articles.title: Opinion꞉ The UK Needs a Workable Route to Regulated DeFi Access
articles.text:
The UK needs a workable route to regulated DeFi access
The UK’s 2027 crypto rules risk a de facto ban on regulated firms providing access to DeFi, argues Coinbase’s European policy head Katie Harries.
Opinion by Katie Harries, head of policy, Europe, Coinbase
The United Kingdom is approaching a choice that could define its financial future: should decentralized finance (DeFi) be allowed to develop through regulated gateways or will it be constrained to a silo?
This is not just relevant to crypto enthusiasts; it goes to the future of capital markets, the competitiveness of the City and the UK’s ability to shape the next generation of financial infrastructure.
DeFi is software that lets people borrow, lend and trade directly with one another without relying on an intermediary like a bank or broker. It works less like a financial institution and more like the internet, promising cheaper, faster financial services that are accessible to everyone, anytime.
While DeFi will always be accessible through open-source or decentralized routes, regulated providers can also offer a route to DeFi, allowing customers to engage with the technology while receiving key information about the services they are accessing and the risks they should be aware of.
However, the Financial Conduct Authority’s (FCA) proposed crypto rules could make this impossible. The FCA will expect regulated platforms to ensure customer orders are only executed on an FCA-authorized venue. While this is designed to prevent overseas firms from illegally accessing the UK market, it also risks blocking off access to DeFi because the decentralized protocols and exchanges where users execute orders do not have a person behind them who could become authorized.
Overview of FCA’s cryptoassets regime policy statements. Source: FCA
No rule explicitly says that firms cannot offer DeFi integrations to their customers; however, the FCA has made clear that it is not seeking to provide rules specific to these products, opting instead to apply the same rules as to fully centralized trading. The effect could be a de facto ban.
From October 2027, regulated platforms may no longer be able to provide customers access to DeFi services unless the FCA changes its approach.
The government has pledged it wants the UK to “lead the world on digital assets.” It will struggle to realize this ambition if British firms are cut off from the decentralized infrastructure digital asset markets are built on.
Related: UK FCA sets crypto authorization guidance ahead of September application window
DeFi is becoming part of the next financial infrastructure
Regulators in other jurisdictions recognize the opportunities and are exploring ways to enable DeFi innovation. In the European Union, the European Securities and Markets Authority has proposed allowing regulated firms to provide access to DeFi, saying it could “allow innovation in decentralized finance in a regulated and transparent environment.”
In September, the United States Securities and Exchange Commission granted an “Innovation Exemption” for the trading of tokenized stocks peer-to-peer, using automated trading systems and liquidity pools.
In short, the US and EU are exploring how traditional finance and DeFi infrastructure can work together. The UK should be exploring the same potential before it closes off this option completely.
Onchain tokenized finance cannot reach its full potential if it is confined to closed and fragmented systems that struggle to interact with the decentralized technology that underpins them.
A de facto ban may push DeFi beyond the regulator’s reach
The UK has set out its first full rulebook for crypto regulation. From Oct. 25, 2027, firms offering crypto services to UK customers will need authorization from the FCA. The FCA is now consulting on guidance on how its rules will apply to firms that provide financial services that use or interact with DeFi.
Potential concerns around DeFi integrations are threefold. First, a customer using a familiar regulated platform may not realize when they have moved into an environment where the usual protections do not apply. Second, certain firms could use DeFi integrations to avoid regulatory obligations. Third, DeFi could bring risks related to financial crime and market resilience.
The UK wants to lead the world on digital assets. Source: Gov.uk
But these risks point to the need for clear information for consumers and responsibilities for firms — not a prohibition.
A de facto ban would produce the opposite of its intended effect. It would not eliminate DeFi. Instead, it would push more activity beyond the FCA’s practical visibility and reduce regulated firms’ ability to shape how customers interact with it.
Regulated platforms can provide a useful point for supervision. They can make clear to customers when they are leaving a regulated environment and require their consent before allowing this. Regulated firms can also curate access to selected protocols, assess operational and governance risks, and report incidents and usage to regulators.
Regulate the gateway, not the technology
The UK already recognizes, in other areas of finance, that regulated institutions can provide access to products or markets that do not carry the same level of oversight.
Many retail trading platforms or so-called “super apps” now offer consumers access to a range of products, from stocks and money market funds to commodities and foreign exchange, with different regulatory protections. The FCA permits this, as long as platforms make clear to consumers which protections apply to different products and services.
This is why DeFi integrations require a better solution. The FCA should protect consumers, but it should not seek to achieve protection with total exclusion.
Responsible integration would give consumers clearer information, give supervisors greater visibility and give UK financial services the chance to compete in the next phase of financial innovation.
Related: ESMA seeks evidence tokenized collateral can be cashed out in crisis
Consumers will use DeFi, so the question is where
DeFi protocols can already be accessed directly without the use of regulated firms. The question is whether consumers will also be able to access DeFi through a regulated gateway, with clear disclosures and guardrails.
The stakes are broader than crypto trading. DeFi underpins the greatest potential cost savings as financial services move onchain, with fewer costly intermediaries and systems that support 24/7 activity across borders. Regulation that provides a clear route to support DeFi is crucial to give firms the confidence to invest in UK innovation in the long term.
If barriers to access are imposed in the UK, tokenized capital markets and financial innovation more broadly could develop in countries that are decisive in supporting DeFi infrastructure.
The UK cannot credibly aspire to lead in digital finance while closing off the decentralized infrastructure on which the future of finance is being built.
About the author: Katie Harries is the head of policy for Europe at Coinbase. Katie leads on international policy, engaging with regulators, governments and industry stakeholders to shape a regulatory environment that fosters growth, competition and responsible oversight for digital assets in the UK and Europe. Prior to joining Coinbase, Katie was a VP at Goldman Sachs. Katie is also heavily involved in the UK Cryptoasset Business Council (UKCBC), the country’s leading crypto trade body.

articles.title: Tesla's Profit Drops 43% as Musk Starts Building Robots and Plans to Sell Driverless Cabs - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- Tesla's third-quarter net income fell 43% to $787 million on flat revenue of $28.05 billion, as research spending rose 69% and capital expenditures more than doubled to $4.73 billion.
- Tesla began producing Optimus humanoid robots in Fremont, California; Musk targets 20,000 a week but says that will take at least a year, with outside deliveries around the end of 2027.
- Tesla says it is trying to get Cybercabs to customers by the end of 2026 while a federal safety audit is open, with its sworn answers to regulators due October 30.
Tesla’s profit fell 43% last quarter to $787 million, down from $1.37 billion a year earlier, per its quarterly filing. The carmaker poured money into humanoid robots and driverless taxis while delivering about 2% fewer cars.
Revenue stayed flat at $28.05 billion, but operating profit, which is what’s left after the costs of running the business, fell 56% to $718 million. Research spending rose 69% to $2.76 billion, and capital expenditures, the money spent on factories and equipment, more than doubled to $4.73 billion.
That spending targets two products headed for factory floors and city streets. Optimus is a humanoid robot meant to take over dangerous and repetitive jobs, and the Cybercab is a two-seat robotaxi (a self-driving taxi you summon from an app) with no steering wheel or pedals.
Tesla said Wednesday that Optimus has entered production, and an executive said on the earnings call that the company is trying to get Cybercabs to customers by the end of the year.
Optimus is now coming off a production line at Tesla’s Fremont, California, factory. “The bots coming off this line are the first production-quality bots that we have manufactured,” Tesla wrote in its shareholder letter.
Musk wants to reach 20,000 Optimus units a week, but said getting there will take at least a year because the design is still changing. He put deliveries to outside customers around the end of 2027 and called the robot’s hand the hardest hardware problem, along with whether it holds up beyond a month of use.
Tesla has missed Optimus targets before, including a goal of about 10,000 robots in 2025, and rivals are already in the race. Figure AI, a startup backed by Microsoft, OpenAI and Nvidia, unveiled its Figure 02 humanoid in 2024.
On the Cybercab, Lars Moravy, Tesla’s vice president of vehicle engineering, said on the earnings call that they may be available this year: “We’re trying to get Cybercabs to customers by the end of this year, 2026.” Every Cybercab built so far is headed to Tesla’s own robotaxi fleet, and Musk said most will stay Tesla-owned and offered as “transport as a service.”
Tesla has not said who will buy Cybercabs first, though it posted a form last month for people interested in buying robotaxis, and it has not announced a price. The target price Tesla has cited is under $30,000.
Musk said the robotaxi business should become noticeable in Tesla’s overall financials in the second quarter of 2027 and will “probably” be “a big deal by Q3 or Q4 of next year.” Tesla has not disclosed how much money the service brings in.
Musk also said Tuesday, on SpaceX’s earnings call, that the Tesla and SpaceX boards have each formed special committees of independent directors to study a combination, and no terms have been agreed.
A deal needs support from holders of 50% of all outstanding Tesla shares, a hurdle Musk called “quite a high hurdle,” and Tesla’s annual shareholder meeting is December 3, though no merger vote is on the agenda.

articles.title: CoinDCX Admits Losses After $16M Wallet Transfers Draw Scrutiny
articles.text:
CoinDCX admits ‘operational losses’ after $16M wallet transfers draw scrutiny
CoinDCX said it covered losses caused by a failed transfer process involving compromised wallets and credited all affected user accounts.
Update (Oct. 22, 12:32 pm UTC): This article has been expanded and its headline updated following CoinDCX’s admission of operational losses and its further explanation of the flagged wallet activity.
Indian cryptocurrency exchange CoinDCX admitted losses from a failure to move deposits out of previously compromised wallets after investigators challenged its explanation for about $16 million in suspicious transfers.
In a statement posted on X Thursday after this article’s initial publication, CoinDCX said some users continued depositing crypto into addresses compromised during its July 2025 hack despite warnings to stop.
The exchange said it regularly transfers deposits out of those old addresses to secure and account for the funds, but that process had failed for an unspecified period.
“This failure led to some operational losses, which were absorbed by CoinDCX,” the exchange said.
CoinDCX added that all affected deposits had been credited to users’ accounts and maintained that its current wallets were unaffected, no funds from active wallets had been compromised and customer assets remained in segregated cold wallets.
Darcy, co-founder of asset recovery platform FlashRescue, earlier on Thursday flagged about $16 million in transfers from addresses labeled as belonging to CoinDCX.
CoinDCX had not responded to Cointelegraph’s inquiry at the time of this update.
Investigators challenge CoinDCX’s initial account
CoinDCX’s latest explanation followed an earlier statement in response to Darcy. It said that the flagged addresses were created in January 2025, compromised in July that year and had not been used by the exchange since.
Blockchain investigator ZachXBT challenged that account, saying a CoinDCX deposit address remained in use by a liquidity provider for 10 months after the July 2025 incident. He said the address continued transferring user deposits to CoinDCX’s current public hot wallet and receiving funds to cover transaction fees.
“Yes, aware of that. We’re investigating it further, and will share an update soon,” responded Sumit Gupta, CEO of CoinDCX. “We assure that no user funds will be at loss.”
CoinDCX lost $44 million in the July 2025 hack. The exchange said at the time that customer wallets were separate from the affected account and that it would cover the loss from its treasury reserves.

articles.title: Oil Climbs Above $111 as AI Stocks Slide, Dragging the S&P 500 and Global Markets With Them - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- Brent crude rose 2.6% to $111.66 a barrel, its highest in five months, as the Nasdaq fell 1.5% and the S&P 500 lost 0.8% by mid-morning in New York.
- South Korea's Kospi fell 3.52%, Japan's Nikkei 225 dropped 2.65% and Hong Kong's Hang Seng lost 3.03%, a week after the Kospi's 7.57% plunge on Oct. 15.
- The 10-year Treasury yield stood at 5.03%, up from 3.97% before the Iran war, with the Fed's next rate decision due Oct. 28.
Brent crude, the global benchmark price for oil, jumped 2.6% to $111.66 a barrel on Thursday, its highest level in five months, as AI-linked stocks slid and dragged markets lower from Asia to Wall Street.
By mid-morning in New York, the Nasdaq, an index heavy with tech companies, was down 1.5% and the S&P 500, which tracks 500 of the largest US companies, had lost 0.8%.
Nvidia, the largest US company by market value, fell 2.3% and weighs so heavily on the S&P 500 that its slides reach the index funds inside many retirement accounts. Gasoline prices jumped 9.1% in September alone, which means the same oil shock rattling the stock market is already showing up at the pump.
South Korea's Kospi, the country's benchmark stock index, fell 3.52% to 5,533.77 after a recovery yesterday, while Japan's Nikkei 225 dropped 2.65% and Hong Kong's Hang Seng lost 3.03%. China's CSI 300, which tracks 300 large companies listed in Shanghai and Shenzhen, entered a bear market, the term for a fall of 20% or more from a recent peak.
The selloff followed the Kospi plunging 7.57% in a single session on Oct. 15 that local coverage dubbed “Black Thursday,” triggering a circuit breaker, an automatic trading pause meant to calm panic selling. The index is still more than 40% below its June peak.
CoreWeave, which borrowed to buy Nvidia chips that it rents out to other companies through the cloud, fell 3.8% on worries about its debt. Meta dropped 5.8% after its profit missed forecasts, and Lam Research, a chip equipment maker, slid 7.7% after guiding profit slightly below analyst estimates.
Citadel founder Ken Griffin said Tuesday that investors are “almost certainly” in an AI bubble, comparing AI chips to airline seats that cost little to run once bought, so prices can collapse when supply outruns demand. He did not tell investors to sell, but his message still feels contrarian in the middle of a market that has been permabullish since the advent of ChatGPT back in 2023.
The Federal Reserve’s next decision comes Oct. 28, with markets pricing roughly a 15% chance of another hike and a December increase still widely expected. This may be at least partially priced in, but a hike would be bad news for the markets as it makes investments more expensive.
Core PCE inflation data, a price measure that strips out food and energy, follows Oct. 29, and October payrolls arrive Nov. 6.

articles.title: Bitcoin Price Seals Lower High After Rejection Near $85K
articles.text:
Bitcoin corrects below $82K after Tesla Q3 results, KOSPI falls
Bitcoin reversed a run toward $85,000 after Tesla reported lower-than-expected capital expenditure in Q3.
Bitcoin (BTC) fell nearly 3% on Thursday after an attempt to break higher was rejected near $85,000.
Key points:
- Bitcoin returned to near $81,500 after Tesla reported a lower-than-expected Q3 capital expenditure (capex) of $4.73 billion.
- South Korea’s KOSPI Composite Index saw fresh weakness, closing down 3.5% on Thursday.
- BTC price action rejected from a resistance trend line at $84,840, preserving a pattern of lower highs.
Tesla capex underspend raises questions
Data from TradingView showed BTC/USD retracing around Wednesday’s daily close, subsequently returning below $82,000. The pair gave back the entirety of the gains made on that day, when price peaked at around $84,840 on Bitstamp.
BTC/USD one-hour chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView
Higher-than-expected US corporate earnings had helped spark a rally in both crypto and stock markets. However, results from Tesla after the Wall Street closing bell did not provide the same promising signals as seen from SpaceX and General Motors earlier in the week.
The company reported Q3 revenue of $28.05 billion, just short of Bloomberg’s $28.13 billion estimate. However, capital expenditure came in at $4.73 billion, well below the projected $7.96 billion. The capex numbers appeared to fuel concerns over the AI sector as markets recovered from last week’s Asia tech-stock sell-off.
“Lower capex suggests less of an ‘all-in’ approach to the AI arms race than one would expect from Elon,” Ryan Lee, senior vice president of product and strategy at Direxion, told Reuters, referring to Tesla CEO Elon Musk.
On the company’s earnings call, Musk said spending would rise through 2028.
“I think capex is actually ending up being a little lower than we anticipated, but we’ll start to become more meaningful next year. And then noticeable in the tens of billions in ’28,” he said, quoted by Bloomberg.
South Korea’s tech-heavy KOSPI Composite Index finished Thursday’s trading session down 3.52%, struggling to sustain a recovery after dropping to 5,460 points last week, its lowest level since late July.
KOSPI Composite Index one-day chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView
Bitcoin sees lower high with resistance trend line still in place
Onchain data showed a marked increase in open interest (OI) across crypto trading platforms prior to Bitcoin’s reversal.

Bitcoin ETF buyers have erased October’s losses in three trading days.
U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs took in $524.8 million on Wednesday, according to Decrypt’s ETF tracker, stretching an inflow streak that began Monday to three sessions and roughly $1.07 billion.

articles.title: Starknet Voters Back Post-Quantum L1 Research
articles.text:
Starknet voters back research into life beyond Ethereum
StarkWare plans to release a draft whitepaper in November as it explores an independent, quantum-resistant blockchain.
Starknet’s community has voted to support research into becoming an independent, post-quantum layer-1 blockchain.
The network’s potential departure from Ethereum gained overwhelming support. The governance vote that ran for seven days closed on Thursday. The poll drew about 3,200 votes, with 93.52% of voting power in favor of the transition.
The non-binding poll recorded the highest participation in Starknet’s governance history, according to StarkWare, which said it abstained from voting to leave the decision to the community.
The outcome allows StarkWare and the Starknet Foundation to proceed with research into an independent L1. The actual shift itself would require a separate, binding governance vote. For now, Starknet will continue operating as an Ethereum layer-2 network.
“We’re beginning work on a whitepaper even before we start the weekend, and hope to release a draft for public scrutiny in November,” StarkWare CEO Eli Ben-Sasson told Cointelegraph.
Starknet outlines next steps for post-quantum L1 research
StarkWare and the Starknet Foundation have established a working group to examine the proposed transition and develop more detailed technical proposals.
The governance proposal states that STRK will remain the network’s native token, with no new token planned, while existing bridges between Starknet and Ethereum will remain open.
StarkWare first raised the potential transition on Oct. 8, citing concerns about the network’s dependence on Ethereum for security. Although Starknet uses hash-based STARK proofs and supports programmable accounts capable of adopting post-quantum signatures, its bridge and data availability infrastructure remain dependent on Ethereum’s upgrade timeline.
Related: Trump administration outlines quantum, AI initiatives in $6B science push
In June, StarkWare unveiled a three-phase quantum-resistance roadmap covering cryptographic upgrades, smart-contract migration and Ethereum-dependent infrastructure.
StarkWare’s Quantum Hub says it has already tested technology designed to withstand future quantum attacks, successfully processing a transaction on Starknet’s live network. However, the technology remains experimental and has not yet undergone a security audit.
Ben-Sasson has set a 2027 target for making Starknet quantum-resistant, ahead of Ethereum’s projected timeline.
“Ethereum’s target of 2029 to become quantum-safe is too late, and deadlines slip,” he said.

articles.title: What Is a Neocloud? The GPU Clouds Powering the AI Boom - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- Neoclouds are specialist cloud providers, such as CoreWeave and Nebius, that rent clusters of Nvidia GPUs to AI labs, startups and Big Tech firms.
- Many have crypto roots: CoreWeave started out mining Ethereum, and Bitcoin miners have signed AI hosting deals worth billions with Microsoft, Amazon and Anthropic.
- Neocloud shares sold off in October 2026 after Gartner predicted that more than 80% of providers will stop operating independently by 2030.
Training and running modern AI models takes a huge amount of computing power, almost all of it from graphics processing units (GPUs). For most of the past decade, renting servers meant going to one of the "hyperscalers": Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure or Google Cloud. When the ChatGPT boom set off a scramble for GPUs, a new kind of company stepped in to meet the demand. These are the neoclouds.
Neoclouds are specialist cloud providers that do one thing: rent out GPU capacity for AI training and inference (running a trained model to answer requests). They have gone from unknown startups to listed companies with contracts worth billions of dollars, and their roots in crypto run deep. CoreWeave began as an Ethereum miner, and a wave of Bitcoin miners is now turning its power-hungry sites into AI data centers.
This guide covers what neoclouds are, how they work, who the main players are, and why their shares were sold off hard in October 2026.
What is a neocloud?
A neocloud is an AI-focused infrastructure-as-a-service (IaaS) provider. A hyperscaler sells hundreds of services, from databases to email hosting. A neocloud mostly sells access to large clusters of high-end GPUs, plus the networking, storage and software needed to run AI workloads on them. CNBC describes them as businesses that offer access to the GPUs powering artificial intelligence as a service.
The best-known neoclouds are:
- CoreWeave (Nasdaq: CRWV): backed by Nvidia, and the largest pure-play neocloud. It listed in March 2025.
- Nebius Group (Nasdaq: NBIS): based in Amsterdam, and formed from the international business of Russian tech giant Yandex.
- Lambda, Crusoe and Fluidstack: privately held GPU cloud providers, though Lambda is raising a final funding round ahead of a planned IPO.
- IREN: a Bitcoin miner turned AI host that now runs its own AI cloud.
Neoclouds are companies, not blockchains, so they don't issue a native token. Their shares trade on traditional stock exchanges.
Did you know?
CoreWeave started in 2017 mining Ethereum with GPUs. Ethereum's 2022 switch to proof of stake ended GPU mining on the network, and CoreWeave moved its hardware over to AI and cloud work.
How does a neocloud work?
The neocloud model comes down to three scarce resources: chips, power and capital.
- 𓇲 Chips. Neoclouds buy large numbers of Nvidia GPUs and network them into clusters built for AI. Being first in line for new Nvidia systems is a big selling point.
- 🔋 Power and space. AI clusters need hundreds of megawatts of electricity plus liquid cooling. Neoclouds either build their own data centers or lease "powered shells" from site owners, including Bitcoin miners turned AI hosts.
- 💰 Capital. GPUs are expensive and lose value quickly. Neoclouds usually pay for them with debt, often backed by the chips themselves and by long-term customer contracts.
Customers such as AI labs, Big Tech firms and startups sign multi-year agreements for reserved capacity, or pay by the hour on demand. The neocloud earns the difference between what the GPUs bring in and what they cost to buy, power and finance.
The weak point is depreciation. In its second-quarter 2026 results, CoreWeave reported depreciation and amortization of nearly $1.4 billion against revenue of about $2.6 billion, while Nebius booked about $260 million against revenue of $582 million.
What's so special about neoclouds?
Neoclouds compete on speed and focus. Hyperscalers split their GPUs between many services, including their own AI products. Neoclouds can deliver large, dedicated clusters quickly, and they tune their software for AI rather than general-purpose computing. Some of their biggest customers are the hyperscalers themselves, which rent neocloud capacity when their own data centers can't keep up.
The sector also gives Bitcoin miners a second life. In the two years to July 2026, miners contracted roughly 7 gigawatts of power capacity across 19 deals worth more than $135 billion to hyperscalers, neoclouds and chipmakers, according to Bernstein. That is less than a quarter of the 30 GW the miners have in their planned power pipeline. The asset that matters is power: miners already had land, grid connections and permits, which can take years to obtain.
Did you know?
TeraWulf signed a 20-year lease with Anthropic for its Kentucky campus. The deal is expected to bring in about $19 billion, which is more than TeraWulf's entire market value at the time.
Who's working with neoclouds?
- 🤖 Microsoft: a major buyer of neocloud capacity, including a roughly $9.7 billion, five-year GPU cloud contract with IREN.
- ☁️ Amazon Web Services: signed a 15-year, roughly $5.5 billion lease with Cipher, a Bitcoin miner turned AI host, for AI capacity.
- 🔍 Google: guarantees Fluidstack's lease payments on sites run by TeraWulf and Cipher.
- 🧠 Anthropic: an AI lab leasing capacity from TeraWulf and, via Fluidstack, from Hut 8.
- 🎮 Nvidia: the main chip supplier to neoclouds, and an investor in CoreWeave.
Is there a neocloud token?
No. Neoclouds are conventional companies. The closest crypto equivalent is decentralized physical infrastructure networks (DePIN) such as Render, Akash and io.net. These use tokens to pay for GPU compute and to reward the people who provide it. They aim at the same market but run on a peer-to-peer model instead of company-owned data centers.
Where to buy neocloud stocks
CoreWeave (CRWV), Nebius (NBIS) and IREN (IREN) trade on the Nasdaq and are available through mainstream brokerages. Several other listed Bitcoin miners turned AI hosts, including TeraWulf, Cipher, Hut 8 and Core Scientific, give exposure to the AI hosting side of the business. Crypto-native compute tokens such as Render (RENDER) trade on major exchanges. Treat all of these as high-risk, volatile assets.
The future of neoclouds
The sector is under heavy pressure. On October 14, 2026, Gartner predicted that "cost pressure and a lack of a differentiating business model" will force more than 80% of neocloud providers to stop operating independently by 2030. It also estimated that more than $3.5 trillion of AI infrastructure spending could be exposed to impairment by the end of 2030 if AI providers keep spending at their current pace.
Credit markets have grown nervous too. By October 21, 2026, CoreWeave's unsecured debt was yielding about 15%, and the cost of insuring its bonds against default had risen 30% in a month. Its shares were down 29% for October, leaving the company valued at about $34 billion, against a peak of about $90 billion in 2025. Nebius fell 27% over the same period, even though it carries far less net debt, and IREN fell 32%.
The bull case is still alive. CoreWeave co-founder Brannin McBee said nearly all of the company's 2027 capacity is already sold, with contracts running into 2028 and beyond. Whether neoclouds stay independent or end up owned by bigger players, demand for AI compute remains high. The open question is whether these companies can earn enough from it to pay back their debts.

articles.title: Cloudflare Saw Millions of Exploit Attempts after PHP Vulnerability Disclosure: CEO
articles.text:
PHP flaw draws millions of exploit attempts, Cloudflare CEO warns
Cloudflare’s Matthew Prince said the network saw thousands of exploit attempts even before the PHP vulnerability was publicly disclosed.
Cloudflare’s CEO Matthew Prince warned that the network saw millions of exploit attempts after two critical PHP vulnerabilities were publicly revealed.
In the 10 hours before the vulnerabilities’ disclosure, the network saw thousands of exploit attempts, which have now reached “millions,” Prince said in a Thursday X post.
Cloudflare is an internet infrastructure company that helps websites load faster and protects them from cyberattacks. About one in five websites worldwide routes traffic through its network, according to the company.
On Wednesday, the PHP Foundation acknowledged that a shortage of resources delayed a fix for a critical security flaw first identified in 2024. PHP developers released emergency patches for two critical vulnerabilities on the same day.
The vulnerabilities may allow attackers to spread malware or inject malicious scripts into websites around the world. PHP powers an estimated 69% of websites with a known server-side programming language, according to research service W3Techs.
The two critical vulnerabilities may “allow malicious cyber actors to remotely execute code in PHP core, potentially compromising sensitive data and networks,” warned the FBI’s Cyber Division in a Wednesday X post, urging organizations to either adopt an immediate update or take affected systems offline.
Multiple organizations and government agencies took websites offline Wednesday as a precautionary measure.
Related: Drift exploiter sends $109M in Ether to Tornado Cash in 2 days

articles.title: XRPL recovers from network slowdown as critical security upgrade faces two-week delay
articles.text:
Quick Take
- XRP Ledger restored normal closing times on Oct. 22 after operators applied a configuration change to address intermittent transaction delays.
- The slowdown raised concerns about XRPL's settlement reliability as stablecoin payments, tokenized assets and lending applications expand.
- Developers are preparing a permanent fix, while a separate security amendment awaits November activation after losing validator support.
The XRP Ledger (XRPL) has recovered from intermittent transaction-processing delays, although developers are still preparing a permanent software correction.
On Oct. 22, XRP Ledger Operations confirmed that ledger-closing times had returned to normal after a configuration change recommended to network operators.
The disruption coincided with a separate setback for a protocol amendment designed to correct vulnerabilities affecting token permissions, lending and other financial applications. Its activation has been pushed to November after validator support briefly weakened.
The developments come as XRPL expands its role in institutional payments, stablecoins and tokenized assets, increasing the importance of reliable settlement infrastructure and safeguards governing financial transactions.
XRP Ledger slowdown exposes transaction-processing challenges
The operational problem emerged on Oct. 21 when some ledgers began taking longer than usual to close, disrupting the blockchain's typical three-to-five-second settlement rhythm.
XRPL Operations said most ledgers continued closing normally, but intermittent delays prompted developers to investigate the network's behavior and prepare a software correction.
As the delays persisted, the team distributed a recommended xrpld configuration change to hub, validator, and node operators.
The adjustment restored normal closing times by Oct. 22, according to the operations team, although developers continued testing a point release intended to address the underlying cause.
David Schwartz, one of XRPL's original architects and Ripple's former chief technology officer, offered additional insight into what may have contributed to the incident.
He said his own hub had continued operating normally after an earlier incident he believed was unrelated, but he restarted it with the recommended configuration change.
Schwartz said:
“I gather the issue was related to servers trying too hard to get too many transactions into each ledger.”
Asked whether that suggested XRPL had encountered a practical limit on its transaction-processing capacity, Schwartz acknowledged a connection between transaction volume and closing frequency.
He added:
“Yes and no. We can't close a ledger more often than every 4 seconds. So limiting the number of transactions per ledger does not necessarily impose a TPS limit.”
His remarks point to a potential trade-off between processing more transactions in each ledger and maintaining consistent settlement times.
However, developers have not established whether the incident reflected a broader network capacity constraint or a software behavior that can be corrected without affecting throughput.
The distinction carries commercial implications, as XRPL attracts applications that require predictable settlement, including RLUSD stablecoin transfers, tokenized securities, and institutional payment services.
Further disruption could complicate transaction processing for services that depend on rapid movement of funds or collateral.
The forthcoming software release will therefore be important in determining whether the configuration change provides a lasting solution or whether additional adjustments are needed to maintain performance under heavier transaction loads.
Validator voting setback delays financial safeguards
Separately, XRPL's fixCleanup3_4_0 amendment has encountered a governance setback that will prolong the activation of several corrections to its financial infrastructure.
The amendment, introduced in September's xrpld 3.4.0 release, addresses technical issues involving token permissions, automated market makers, asset vaults, lending operations and escrow transactions.
Among the changes is a fix for a permission-delegation flaw that could let an account authorized to destroy certain fungible tokens create additional tokens under specific circumstances.
The network's documentation advises issuers against delegating the affected PaymentBurn permission until the correction becomes active.
Other changes improve precision in vault accounting, enforce token-balance safeguards and correct transaction-handling behavior across decentralized trading and lending functions.
The proposed protections had been moving toward an Oct. 23 activation before validator backing briefly fell below the supermajority required to change XRPL's protocol rules.
XRPL requires support from more than 80% of trusted validators to remain uninterrupted for 14 days before an amendment can activate.
The temporary loss of support on Oct. 21 erased the amendment's accumulated approval period, despite backing subsequently recovering above the required threshold.
The XRPLWin amendment tracker now places the earliest activation on Nov. 4, provided the renewed majority remains intact.
XRPL contributor Vet confirmed that additional validator votes had restored the amendment's activation countdown. He also clarified that fixCleanup3_4_0 addresses older protocol issues and is unrelated to the latest ledger-closing delays.
The postponement extends the period before the affected token-permission safeguards become enforceable. It also delays corrections intended to improve accounting and transaction handling in XRPL's developing lending infrastructure.
That infrastructure still needs additional protocol approvals before native lending services can go live.
A further decline in validator support would reset the amendment's waiting period again, potentially pushing activation beyond Nov. 4.
XRP is -4.37% over the past 24 hours and currently sits at rank #5 by market cap.

articles.title: Major Banks Find Rogue AI Agents Inside Customer Accounts—And They’re 'Horrified' - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- Major U.S. banks are detecting unauthorized third-party AI agents inside customer accounts—often logging in with the customer’s own credentials—with some taking actions that appear independent of user instructions, Axios reported..
- Morgan Stanley is blocking outside agents while JPMorgan, Bank of America and Citi restrict them; executives called the situation “horrifying.”
- Rather than banning AI outright, most banks are leaning toward read-only access.
Some of the biggest U.S. banks have discovered an uninvited presence inside their customers’ accounts: autonomous AI agents logging in, sometimes with the customer’s own credentials, and occasionally taking actions that appear to go beyond what anyone asked them to do.
That’s according to a report published Thursday by Axios, which, citing people familiar with the matter, said major banks are detecting unauthorized third-party AI agents operating inside customer accounts, with some agents attempting steps that look independent of user instructions.
Bank executives described the situation as “horrifying,” with one saying the industry has “grave concerns” about agents reaching into accounts and taking actions that could affect people’s finances.
The banks are moving to slam the door. Morgan Stanley is blocking outside agents, while JPMorgan, Bank of America and Citi are restricting them, Axios reported.
The problem is that even when a user grants an agent permission, having software log in as the account holder clashes with the rules at most banks, which require humans to access their own accounts. One executive told Axios they struggle to tell agents apart, or to know whether a given agent was authorized by the customer or has gone rogue.
The friction points toward a middle path rather than an outright ban. According to Axios, most banks have authorized, or are leaning toward, read-only access that would let agents view a customer’s financial information without moving money, similar to what they already grant budgeting apps. Industry executives acknowledged customers will want to use these agents, so some accommodation is likely coming.
The report lands amid a drumbeat of alarm over AI agents slipping their leashes. Agents have repeatedly escaped their creators’ control, breaching systems in ways their developers didn’t intend, and the Bank for International Settlements has warned that AI is shrinking the window banks have to patch security flaws before attackers exploit them.
The banking scare feeds a wider debate over how to contain increasingly capable agents. Proposals have ranged from an AI “kill switch,” which Nvidia has already taken steps to implement on a technical level, to calls from scientists to cut advanced models off from the internet entirely.
It’s a sign of how seriously the financial system and beyond are taking the risk of software that can act on its own.

articles.title: Bitcoin ETFs sold through 7 of 8 crashes even as Wall Street makes BTC selloffs less violent
articles.text:
Quick Take
- Bitcoin ETFs lost $8.2 billion during the May-June crash, following $6.9 billion in withdrawals during the previous major downturn.
- ETF flows were negative at seven of eight market bottoms and positive at seven of eight peaks, exposing Wall Street's tendency to chase momentum.
- Bitcoin crashes are slower but remain deep, raising questions about whether stronger market liquidity can absorb another wave of ETF selling.
Bitcoin ETFs recorded outflows during seven of eight major selloffs, challenging expectations that Wall Street investors would support prices during downturns.
A new DWF Labs report shared with CryptoSlate found that US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds consistently lost money during market declines of at least 15% since their January 2024 launch, while attracting inflows throughout all nine major rallies.
The findings challenge the belief that institutional adoption has created a dependable source of buying during market stress. They also expose a paradox in Bitcoin's changing market structure: selloffs have become slower and less frequent, even as ETF investors continue withdrawing billions during downturns.
The research, covering 694 trading days through Oct. 16, found that investors withdrew a record $8.2 billion during Bitcoin's 28.8% decline between May and June 2026. That followed $6.9 billion in withdrawals during the October 2025 to February 2026 downturn, when the cryptocurrency lost nearly half its value.
The two episodes represented the largest ETF withdrawals since the products launched, surpassing the $3.4 billion investors redeemed during the January-April 2025 correction.
Wall Street investors are buying Bitcoin rallies and selling crashes
DWF Labs found that ETF investors were still withdrawing money at seven of eight market bottoms and purchasing at seven of eight peaks, suggesting institutional flows have largely reinforced existing price trends.
The selling frequently intensified as downturns progressed. In five of the eight corrections, the heaviest withdrawals occurred during the final five trading days before Bitcoin bottomed.
During the May-June 2026 decline, outflows averaged $412 million daily in the final week, while investors withdrew money on 88% of trading days throughout the correction.
The pattern reversed during recoveries, with all nine rallies of at least 15% attracting net inflows. Seven recorded their strongest buying during the final five sessions before the market peaked.
One notable exception emerged during the May-July 2024 correction, when ETFs attracted $2.2 billion despite Bitcoin falling 21.8%. That decline coincided with selling pressure from German government liquidations and Mt. Gox creditor repayments, allowing ETF demand to absorb some of the additional supply.
Otherwise, institutional investors have generally waited for recoveries to become established before returning.
During Bitcoin's April 2025 rebound, ETFs continued losing an average of $40 million daily even as the cryptocurrency gained 9.7%. Inflows subsequently accelerated to $436 million a day after prices had already recovered.
Conversely, one of the largest ETF inflow days, totaling approximately $1.2 billion, coincided with Bitcoin's October 2025 peak, shortly before a prolonged decline.
Bitcoin ETF flows follow prices instead of predicting them
The research found that ETF flows correlated 0.54 with Bitcoin's performance over the preceding five trading days, compared with just 0.03 for returns over the following five days.
Their correlation with same-day returns was 0.41, suggesting flows and prices often move together without indicating whether fund demand drove the move.
This weakens the usefulness of ETF inflows as a forward-looking market signal, despite their growing prominence in institutional Bitcoin analysis.
After the largest 10% of inflow sessions, Bitcoin appreciated over the following 20 days only 51% of the time, compared with 57% across all trading days.
BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT), the market's largest Bitcoin ETF product, offered little additional predictive advantage despite accumulating $65.6 billion in net inflows during the study period.
Its flows correlated only 0.04 with Bitcoin's subsequent five-day returns. Following its largest inflow sessions, Bitcoin advanced over the next 20 days in only 47% of cases.
The findings also complicate the assumption that large ETF purchases necessarily signal fresh bullish positioning.
Some activity reflects investors moving money between competing funds, while hedge funds can simultaneously buy ETF shares and short Bitcoin futures to capture pricing differences without betting on the cryptocurrency's direction.
DWF Labs nevertheless identified one unusual pattern worth attention.
When ETFs experienced unusually large withdrawals on days Bitcoin moved less than 1%, the cryptocurrency subsequently declined over 20 days in eight of 12 cases.
Returns following those sessions were 10.7% weaker than on days with comparable preceding price trends. However, the negative outcomes were concentrated around three major selloffs, limiting the pattern's reliability as a trading signal.
Bitcoin crashes have slowed despite persistent ETF selling
Although institutional investors have repeatedly withdrawn money during corrections, Bitcoin's broader market behavior has changed considerably since ETFs began trading.
The median selloff has unfolded at a daily pace of 0.69%, compared with 1% during 2022-2023 and 1.37% in 2021.
Major corrections of at least 15% have become less frequent, declining to about 2.9 annually from 4.4 in 2022-2023 and 8 in 2021.
Annualized volatility has also fallen to 47% from 55% in 2022-2023, while the annual frequency of roughly 7% daily crashes has dropped from six to two.
However, corrections have remained substantial. The median ETF-era downturn was 21.3%, compared with 19.4% during 2022-2023.
DWF Labs identified deeper liquidity, a broader investor base and greater access to regulated hedging instruments, including CME futures and ETF options, as potential contributors to the market's changing behavior. Bitcoin's volatility was already declining before the ETFs launched.
Hedge funds' positioning provides another indication of how the institutional market has evolved.
DWF Labs estimated that approximately one-fifth of ETF flows may have been hedged through CME futures basis trades. Leveraged funds' net short exposure has since declined from approximately 116,000 BTC in December 2024 to 29,000 BTC.
The firm estimated that unwinding those positions could explain much of the ETF selling during the January-April 2025 correction, but no more than roughly a quarter of withdrawals during the two largest subsequent declines.
That suggests a larger share of recent outflows reflected investors actively reducing Bitcoin exposure.
The report also identified a potential threshold for renewed selling. Once Bitcoin fell 7% below its 20-day high, average daily ETF flows shifted from $74 million in inflows to $72 million in outflows over the following five trading days.
Selling intensified in 19 of the 24 episodes examined, though flows typically returned to neutral levels over the next two weeks.
The finding comes as Bitcoin ETFs have pulled in $57.96 billion in cumulative net inflows, with the 12 products managing around $110 billion in assets.

As the integration expands, readers will gain access to the full universe of Solana tokens alongside tokenized stocks, commodities and other real-world assets, all accessible from the same account, on the same platform where they already consume information.
“We've spent eight years building Decrypt into a destination people trust to understand what's happening in crypto and emerging technology. Now we're taking the next step: giving them the ability to act on that information instantly,” said Ilan Hazan, co-founder and COO of Decrypt. “Whether you're reading about Bitcoin, a public company or a commodity, our vision is that you should be able to trade it right there. One account, every market, directly where you consume information.”
Jupiter has established itself as Solana's “everything exchange,” bringing together token swaps, lending, borrowing, perpetual futures and portfolio management within a unified DeFi ecosystem.
The integration will initially support a select group of major cryptocurrencies before expanding to the broader Solana token ecosystem and tokenized real-world assets.
For Decrypt, The Information Exchange represents a fundamental shift in what a media platform can be: a unified destination where media becomes interactive, enabling readers to trade on news, data and financial markets in real-time on a single platform.
Building out an information infrastructure
Earlier this month, Decrypt Money Accounts launched on Solana, introducing a single self-custodial account designed to power every financial experience across Decrypt.
With a single USD deposit, users will be able to access the platform's growing suite of products, from trading and prediction markets to earning yield and, eventually, perpetual futures.
Jupiter-powered trading is the next piece of that infrastructure.
Additional Jupiter products, beginning with Earn, will further expand what readers can do with their assets without leaving Decrypt.
The experience will extend across Decrypt's editorial coverage and upcoming Situation Rooms, dedicated destinations combining breaking news, live market data, prices, probabilities and financial instruments around the subjects readers care about.
Imagine reading a story about Bitcoin and trading BTC in the same experience. Following a major development at a public company and taking a position in its tokenized stock. Or tracking a geopolitical event, watching prediction market probabilities shift and participating directly.
From information to action, in one place.
The Information Exchange: where media meets markets
Announced in September, The Information Exchange is Decrypt's vision for the next generation of financial media: a unified destination bringing together news, intelligence, market data, probabilities and direct financial participation.
The thesis is simple: information and financial markets are converging, but the experience of consuming information and acting on it remains fragmented.
Today, readers jump between news sites, market-data platforms, exchanges, wallets and trading applications.
The Information Exchange is being built to bring those experiences together.
Decrypt provides the audience, trusted reporting and distribution. Myriad provides the underlying market infrastructure, with its prediction markets already generating more than $600 million in cumulative trading volume. The forthcoming MYR token forms the connective tissue, an economic layer that coordinates users, creators, traders and applications across the ecosystem.
Through integrations with leading protocols like Jupiter, The Information Exchange will bring an expanding universe of financial instruments together on Decrypt.
The Jupiter integration marks another milestone in that transformation, with more products, markets and features set to roll out in the coming weeks ahead of Solana Breakpoint.
News becomes actionable. Markets become accessible. And readers become participants.

articles.title: AI Could Spark a Crypto ‘Meme Game’ Boom
articles.text:
Move over memecoins: Crypto ‘meme games’ coming, bagholders and all
“Plenty will be ponzis. Plenty will get exploited. Plenty will insta die. There will be ridiculous gains, and people will get absolutely f***ing rinsed,” says Illuvium co-founder Kieran Warwick.
Update (Oct. 22 at 10:31 UTC): This article has been updated to include comments from Sébastien Borget and Ben James on AI-driven game development.
AI could unleash a flood of short-lived crypto “meme games,” attracting the same speculative traders who helped push memecoins to record highs in late 2024, according to Illuvium co-founder Kieran Warwick.
Speculative crypto games such as Wolf Game and Fishing Frenzy, where players compete for financial rewards, once took months to develop. But Warwick says AI tools have reduced the time and cost of creating similar games to just days and around $1,000.
He predicts as many as 100,000 such games could launch within a year, with many designed to survive for only a few days — long enough for their creators to turn a profit.
“Like you have serial deployers of memes, you’ll get serial deployers of games,” Warwick told Cointelegraph.
But whether that flood would benefit crypto gaming and the broader industry is less clear. Cheaper development could make niche games viable and revive attention across the sector, but a wave of disposable crypto games could also leave a lot of speculators “holding the bag.”
“There will be ridiculous gains, and people will get absolutely f****ing rinsed,” Warwick wrote on X on Monday.
A memecoin-style boom… and bust?
In 2024, Pump.fun and similar launchpads helped fuel a surge in memecoins by making tokens easy to create. The sector’s combined market capitalization reached $150.6 billion in December 2024 before falling nearly 69% to $47.2 billion by November 2025, according to CoinGecko.
The boom divided industry figures, with supporters championing memecoins’ appeal to traders while critics argued they diverted capital from useful projects and damaged crypto’s reputation.
Warwick said he expects a similar speculative wave to touch crypto meme games.
“These degens who are gambling in crypto, they get a thousand-dollar paycheck and they put $500 in Pump.Fun. You’re giving them a new venue and a new shiny wrapper … for them to be able to go and gamble.”
Asked whether a mass of short-lived crypto games will ultimately be good for the crypto gaming ecosystem, Warwick said: “probably not.”
“Like in the long run, I don’t think so. The sustainable model that Illuvium has been building towards for years, where really good quality games with ownership underneath, that I think is still the dream of where crypto gaming should be building towards.” 
Animoca Brands and The Sandbox CEO Robby Yung took a similar view.
“I think if there is a type of meme game, as Warwick is describing, that doesn’t particularly take much effort to make… I don’t think it would become a lasting category because user retention is the lifeblood of games and always has been,” he told Cointelegraph.
Sébastien Borget, president of the Blockchain Game Alliance and co-founder of The Sandbox said he sees the speculative wave as one part of a broader expansion in game creation.
“We’re witnessing a true Cambrian explosion of games and creativity, where anyone can turn even their wildest ideas into playable experiences without worrying about the complexities of 2D/3D asset creation, level design, music, or sound effects,” he told Cointelegraph.
“But as the cost of experimenting and bringing ideas to life approaches zero, and the abundance of content explodes, the real challenge shifts from creation to discovery, distribution, and reaching an audience.”
More games, but where are the players?
That audience question was central for Mirai Labs co-founder and CEO Corey Wilton, who questioned whether an AI-driven surge in supply can overcome weak demand for crypto games.
“We shipped quite a few games, six or seven games, into the market,” Wilton said. “Ultimately, it came to the conclusion that the demand for or within the Web3 space simply isn’t there.”
Dappradar’s tracking of gaming decentralized apps (Dapps) shows just $232.2 million in total value locked in 2,356 apps. A basket of the top 50 gaming tokens has a combined market capitalization of $3.8 billion at the time of writing.
“I think the lack of demand and liquidity in so-called altcoins is definitely an issue, but I think, at the same time, there is also a lack of choice out there of really enjoyable, fun games that captivate people’s imaginations,” said Yung.
Related: Proof of Play to shut down after blockchain gaming thesis falls short
“The reality is the number of game titles that use crypto is very small, and so there’s not a lot of choice for consumers. That makes it difficult to actually judge whether crypto is the issue or it’s just that there aren’t enough good games.”
Recent crypto games show there is still interest in the sector despite recent pivots. The developers of Yield Fields, an upcoming web3 farming game built on the Robinhood chain, raised an estimated $8.3 million on Oct. 14 selling digital land plots as nonfungible tokens. The game is set to launch at the end of the month.
AI game development hits crypto
Data shows AI has already entered crypto game development.
In the Blockchain Game Alliance’s 2025 survey of 506 industry professionals, 32.8% said their company had implemented or experimented with AI for game design and content creation.
Yung compared the arrival of AI development tools to the early days of mobile gaming, when cheaper development encouraged more studios to enter the market.
“Frankly, I think that’s a great thing all around,” said Yung. “It reminds me a bit of when mobile first started to become popular around 2010. A lot of people started developing for mobile because it was much cheaper and much faster than developing for PC or console.”
“What happened was we just got more games of all kinds of quality, and customers had a choice of playing what they liked,” he said.
Ben James, CEO of Atlas Design and 404.xyz, said the lower barriers would make originality more important.
“AI will make it easier to launch games, and those that lack creativity, innovation or passion will converge on the average: a sameness we call ‘slop’. At the same time, games that are unique in their aesthetics, gameplay or even business models will stand out.”

articles.title: OCC drops proposed affiliate rewards presumption, but stablecoin yield ban stays
articles.text:
Quick Take
- The OCC dropped the proposed affiliate rewards presumption while retaining the GENIUS Act’s issuer yield ban.
- Existing rewards programs receive no grandfathering, while the OCC rejected a safe harbor for small yield payments.
- Rewards arrangements will face review on their facts through issuer applications and supervision, with no list of approved structures.
The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) dropped a proposed presumption against certain stablecoin rewards routed through affiliates or related third parties in its Oct. 21 final GENIUS Act rule. The rule retains the prohibition on issuers paying holders interest or yield solely for holding, using or retaining a payment stablecoin, with older rewards programs facing the same scrutiny as newer ones.
The rule takes effect on Jan. 18, 2027. It covers permitted and foreign payment stablecoin issuers within the OCC’s jurisdiction and certain custody activities by OCC-supervised entities. Comptroller Jonathan V. Gould, posting as @USComptroller on X, said the agency had delivered the final rule ahead of schedule.
For exchange-run rewards, CryptoSlate’s reading is that removing the proposed test leaves the legality of individual arrangements unsettled. The change follows CryptoSlate’s earlier coverage of exchange stablecoin rewards.
CryptoSlate separately examined the rule’s reserve changes and banks’ deposit-flight concerns.
How the OCC will assess rewards
The proposal would have presumed that certain linked arrangements amounted to prohibited issuer yield: an issuer would pay interest or yield to an affiliate or related third party, which would in turn arrange payments to holders solely for holding, using or retaining the issuer’s stablecoin.
The proposed presumption would have applied to those specified payment relationships. The final rule removes it and retains the statutory yield prohibition.
The agency said the proposed test could have caught permissible arrangements while suggesting that impermissible arrangements outside its triggers were acceptable. Requiring a rebuttal in those circumstances risked imposing burdens without a matching benefit.
Instead, the OCC will apply the statute to the facts of each arrangement. It has not provided a list of permitted or prohibited rewards structures.
Its anti-evasion authority also remains. The rule explains that an issuer cannot avoid the prohibition simply by paying an agent to make interest or yield payments on its behalf that it could not make directly.
Transaction-based payments also require an assessment of the particular facts. Payments that do not constitute interest or yield, or that are not made solely in connection with stablecoin holding, use or retention, fall outside the statutory prohibition.
Rewards programs that predate the GENIUS Act will be evaluated in the same way as programs established after enactment or the law’s effective date.
The regulator also declined a de minimis safe harbor for small or incidental yield payments, saying the statute contains no exemption for them.
The rule’s rewards provisions apply the issuer yield prohibition equally to institutional and retail stablecoin holders. The rule also offers no cure period for violations, although the OCC says it will exercise enforcement discretion according to the circumstances.
Applications and supervision come next
The OCC will initially monitor arrangements through issuers’ applications and ongoing supervision. Where it identifies transactions that violate or evade the yield prohibition, it says it will take action and provide additional public guidance as appropriate.
The OCC says GENIUS Act rules on the Bank Secrecy Act, anti-money laundering and sanctions will be addressed in separate rulemaking coordinated with Treasury. The OCC decision is also distinct from the Treasury foreign-stablecoin diligence proposal previously covered by CryptoSlate.
Alongside the rule, the OCC released Paperwork Reduction Act notices covering licensing and registration applications and weekly and quarterly reporting forms. Each specifies a comment deadline 30 days after Federal Register publication; the posted copies leave the calendar deadlines unfilled.
The Jan. 18 effective date is separate from the application opening. The OCC’s announcement says another news release will specify when it begins accepting and processing prospective issuers’ applications and waiver requests.
The OCC anticipates that experience with these arrangements could support a later rule clarifying the yield prohibition.

articles.title: SoFi Launches Tokenized Deposit That Earns 4.4% and Converts to a Stablecoin - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- SoFi launched SoFi Earn (SOFIE), which it calls the first national bank-issued tokenized deposit for consumers.
- The product targets idle digital dollars by offering interest and insurance stablecoins lack.
- It’s SoFi’s fifth crypto product in under a year, extending a build-out that includes its crypto-trading return and the SoFiUSD stablecoin.
SoFi is giving its customers a way to earn bank-grade interest on digital dollars without giving up the speed of crypto, launching what it calls the first national bank-issued tokenized deposit for consumers.
Announced Thursday, the product, SoFi Earn, trades under the ticker SOFIE, with each token representing $1 held on deposit at SoFi Bank. Holders earn 4.40% annual percentage yield, and the funds are FDIC-insured up to applicable limits, a key distinction from ordinary stablecoins.
When members want to deploy the money, they can convert SOFIE one-to-one into SoFiUSD, the bank’s stablecoin, and then use it to buy crypto in the SoFi app or move dollars over blockchain rails around the clock.
The pitch targets a specific gap. Stablecoins have become a popular way to park digital dollars, but many pay no interest and carry no deposit insurance. SoFi cited Federal Reserve research estimating that roughly $64 billion, or about 21% of the stablecoin market, sits idle in forgotten or inactive wallets. The company is pitching SOFIE as a way to keep that money earning until the moment it’s spent.
“Too much money in the digital asset ecosystem is sitting idle,” CEO Anthony Noto said in a statement, arguing the product combines “the earning power and protections of a bank deposit with the speed and utility of digital assets.”
SoFi Earn is the fifth crypto product the company has rolled out in under a year, part of an aggressive build-out of its digital-money ecosystem.
SoFi returned to crypto trading in late 2025 after exiting the business years earlier, becoming the first nationally chartered U.S. bank to offer it to consumers, and members can now trade more than 40 tokens.
The company followed that with SoFiUSD, the first stablecoin issued by a U.S. national bank, launched across Ethereum and Solana and now used to settle SoFi’s entire card program over Mastercard’s network.
The move pushes SoFi deeper into a space where banks and fintech firms are racing to fold blockchain-based dollars into regulated products, following its earlier launch of business banking for digital assets and a stablecoin tie-up involving cryptocurrency exchange Kraken.
By wrapping a yield-bearing, insured deposit in a token that moves like a stablecoin, SoFi is betting consumers want both at once.

articles.title: PHP Foundation Admits ‘Structural Failure’ Delayed Security Fix
articles.text:
PHP Foundation admits ‘structural failure’ delayed critical security fix
Government websites and online services were disrupted after concerns about a PHP bug that could allow attackers to take control of vulnerable servers.
The PHP Foundation has acknowledged that indecision and a shortage of resources delayed a fix for a critical security flaw first identified in 2024, calling the stalled response a “structural failure.”
Government agencies and other organizations worldwide took websites offline Wednesday as a precaution while PHP released emergency patches for two related critical vulnerabilities. The flaws could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code on affected servers without logging in.
PHP is a programming language widely used to power websites and web applications, including content management systems.
In a blog post following the release of the patch, the foundation described how its developers first found signs of the vulnerability in 2024, but struggled to come up with a solution without disrupting the large ecosystem of software built using PHP.
“Combined with the lack of a known path to remote code execution and the small team of core developers with the necessary deep knowledge of the engine occupied with many responsibilities, this decision process caused work on a fix to stall and restart repeatedly over months,” said the foundation.
“We won’t pretend otherwise: the delay was a structural failure, caused by both the security team’s decision process and its lack of resources.”
The foundation was pointed to the vulnerability again on August 11, after security firm Calif and OpenAI independently reported the same underlying issue, with Calif demonstrating unconditional remote code execution, which made it a top security priority.
Websites go dark amid PHP security scare
The disruption stretched across the world as developers disconnected websites while preparing to install the emergency fixes.
The Netherlands shut its digital identity service, and the country’s National Cyber Security Center also took its website offline.
Finland’s state IT provider Valtori disconnected government public web services, while France’s Interior Ministry temporarily took prefecture websites offline. Germany’s federal IT provider ITZBund also disabled several websites, according to Reuters.
In Australia, the Australian Signals Directorate acknowledged that its cybersecurity website, cyber.gov.au, was among government sites affected by the PHP issue.
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi took to X to urge website operators to prepare to apply the patch as quickly as possible. In a post, she said temporarily suspending website functions could reduce the risk if the patch couldn’t be applied immediately.
The Wikimedia Foundation, which operates Wikipedia, said it took some supporting services offline as a precaution, including Toolforge and Cloud VPS, which host tools and projects used by volunteer developers, leading to parts of Wikipedia going offline on Wednesday.
Blockchain security firm SlowMist said its MistEye service surveyed PHP use across the crypto industry, urging exchanges, DeFi platforms and wallet providers to review their exposure and upgrade. It identified 793 domains with direct PHP fingerprints among 1,488 domains assessed.
Intersect, a membership organization supporting the Cardano blockchain’s development and governance, said it had temporarily taken its Members Area offline while it assessed potential exposure. The page is still offline at the time of writing.
Related: Tech giants rush to block 8 eMudhra certs that could enable fake sites
Coinbase chief security officer Jeff Lunglhofer said the company found no evidence of any exposed PHP instances.
“Whenever we hear about vulnerabilities like this, we automatically conduct a full sweep to make sure everything is as safe as we can make it. We’re also working with our third party suppliers for extra assurance.”
Digital asset infrastructure company BitGo also said its platform was unaffected by the PHP vulnerability.
Meanwhile, Binance co-founder Changpeng Zhao warned internet users on Wednesday to be “extra careful” visiting any website in the next few days, as some web administrators may not be up-to-date with security patches.
OpenAI has released a Codex skill to help website operators check for potentially vulnerable PHP versions and identify applicable updates, which can be accessed via GitHub.
The PHP security team said it has not identified any functional exploits at the time of its public disclosure.

articles.title: Railway urges credential resets as investigator alleges $371,000 crypto theft
articles.text:
Quick Take
- Railway warned customer environment variables may have been decrypted and urged every user to replace stored credentials.
- On-chain investigator @tayvano_ alleged roughly $371,000 in stolen crypto across at least 19 EVM chains; Railway has not confirmed the claim.
- Railway invalidated its API tokens and restored builds for Pro and Enterprise, while lower tiers awaited access.
Railway, a cloud deployment platform, has urged every user to replace stored secrets after disclosing on Oct. 21 that an attacker may have accessed encrypted customer environment variables and read some of their contents.
Railway said those variables may contain API keys, database credentials and private registry credentials. Although its initial analysis suggested the impact might be limited to a subset of users, its security disclosure urged all customers to replace stored variables and credentials immediately and review service logs for unusual activity.
The company believes the incident is part of a series of attacks against platform companies aimed at compromising AI inference providers. It said it had notified upstream providers to revoke keys proactively. It has not disclosed a root cause or an affected-customer count.
On-chain investigator @tayvano_ separately alleged cryptocurrency theft involving keys stored in Railway. The investigator estimated losses of roughly $371,000 across at least 19 EVM chains and identified an address as belonging to the attacker.
Railway has not confirmed the alleged theft, its connection to the incident or the $371,000 estimate.
For crypto teams running applications on Railway, the practical response is to review which credentials those applications stored on the platform and the services those credentials can access. Railway's recommendation covers all environment variables and API keys stored there, as well as private registry credentials.
Credential resets and the partial return of builds
Railway initially paused all deployments while investigating, preventing customers from rolling out new versions of their applications. That created an obstacle to deploying replacement credentials, alongside the separate task of revoking potentially exposed credentials at the services that issued them.
Railway also reset credentials for access to its own platform. At 04:17 UTC on Oct. 22, it said it had invalidated all Railway API tokens. Customers using those tokens to integrate with its public API were told to create replacements.
At 12:30 UTC on Oct. 22, Railway said deployment wait times were improving and most queued deployments were starting sooner. Builds were available for Pro and Enterprise workspaces, while Railway continued working to restore access for Hobby, Free and Trial. Some deployments still faced delays.
Railway's Oct. 22 AWS guidance calls for deactivating potentially exposed access keys, deploying replacements and checking CloudTrail and billing for activity the customer did not generate. Its Google Cloud guide similarly recommends disabling potentially exposed service-account keys, replacing them, and reviewing Cloud Audit Logs and billing.
The Google Cloud guide adds a timing caveat: short-lived tokens already issued from a disabled key can remain valid for up to an hour.
Railway said it would email affected customers as accounts were confirmed.

articles.title: Italy Busts Mafia 'Secret Bank' That Laundered Money Through Crypto, Seizes $24M - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- Italian police arrested 30 people over an alleged mafia-linked "hidden bank" run from a car-rental business near Milan, seizing €21 million in assets including cryptocurrency.
- Prosecutors say the network issued more than €110 million in fake invoices and moved about €68 million abroad, some of it through crypto exchanges.
- A financial police inspector, a Milan court employee and a lawyer are among those caught up in the investigation, with arrests also made in Spain and Switzerland.
Italian police have arrested 30 people accused of running an underground bank for organized crime from a car-rental business near Milan, and seized €21 million (about $23.6 million) in cash, bank balances, cryptocurrency, boats, jewelry and luxury watches, Italian news agency ANSA reported on Wednesday.
The operation, carried out by the Guardia di Finanza, Italy's financial police, on the orders of Milan's anti-mafia prosecutors, targeted suspects linked to the 'Ndrangheta, the Camorra and organized crime groups from Foggia in southern Italy. Sixteen were taken into custody and 14 placed under house arrest, including two people arrested in Spain and one in Switzerland.
According to investigators, the business in Pero, on the outskirts of Milan, was run by three Italians: two long-standing contacts of 'Ndrangheta clans from Crotone, both previously convicted in earlier mafia investigations, and a member of the Camorra's Casalesi clan. Chinese and Albanian accomplices helped operate the network, prosecutors said.
Shell companies issued more than €110 million in invoices for services never provided, letting businesses cut their tax bills. Those firms paid by bank transfer and received the money back in cash, minus a commission. The network moved about €68 million abroad, according to prosecutors.
Funds gathered in the shell companies' accounts were sent to banks in Luxembourg, Lithuania and Germany, then routed through crypto exchanges into wallets controlled by the network, Bloomberg reported. Drug traffickers who handed over cash received crypto or international bank transfers in return, and the network also handled money stolen from victims of online crypto investment scams, according to the report.
The Guardia di Finanza's technology fraud unit supported the investigation, which is set out in a court order running to more than 500 pages.
Among those arrested is a Guardia di Finanza inspector, placed under house arrest on corruption charges, according to Calabrian outlet LaC News24. Investigators also accused a Milan court employee of leaking information about ongoing investigations, and a lawyer and a former member of the financial police are among those caught up in the case.
The mafia and crypto
Italian authorities have warned for years that organized crime is adopting digital assets. In 2021, Italy's Anti-Mafia Investigative Directorate said that "all criminal organizations, including those of the Mafia type, have an interest in using these instruments for their business," and described the 'Ndrangheta, Italy's most powerful criminal syndicate, as "growing more and more attuned to modern tools like cryptocurrency and the deep web."
