articles.title: Scientists discover a surprising link between vitamin C and cancer survival
articles.text:
Scientists discover a surprising link between vitamin C and cancer survival
- Date:
- October 20, 2026
- Source:
- Van Andel Research Institute
- Summary:
- A surprising clinical trial suggests that taking vitamin C daily could improve survival in people with precancerous blood disorders and early-stage blood cancers. Patients receiving the supplement had fewer adverse events and showed a promising survival advantage, raising hopes that a common vitamin could help protect against leukemia-related complications.
- Share:
Vitamin C plays an important role in keeping the immune system healthy, helping wounds heal, and protecting cells from damage. However, people with precancerous blood disorders and blood cancers often have persistently low vitamin C levels. Researchers have been investigating whether correcting this deficiency could improve their health and treatment outcomes.
New findings from the phase 2 EVITA clinical trial suggest that vitamin C supplementation may offer important benefits for people with precancerous blood conditions and early-stage blood cancers. The randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study was conducted by the Van Andel Institute-Stand Up To Cancer® Epigenetics Dream Team.
The results, published in the American Cancer Society journal CANCER, revealed that patients who received 1,000 mg of oral vitamin C every day for one year experienced fewer adverse events during the study and its follow-up period. The supplement also changed the levels of certain immune signaling molecules, known as cytokines, in ways associated with more favorable outcomes. These changes suggest that vitamin C could influence inflammation-related processes involved in the growth and progression of abnormal blood cells.
Although vitamin C did not significantly affect the rate at which abnormal blood cells expanded, the researchers identified an encouraging result. An exploratory analysis showed that participants who received vitamin C were significantly more likely to be alive after approximately three years of follow-up than those who took a placebo. Scientists emphasize that this potential survival benefit must be verified in a larger phase 3 clinical trial.
Vitamin C Shows Promise for Patients at Risk of Leukemia
"We are tremendously excited and cautiously optimistic that our results could one day translate into a simple way to improve care and outcomes for people with pre-leukemia disorders," said Peter A. Jones, Ph.D., D.Sc. (hon), a distinguished professor at Van Andel Institute. Jones is also a co-corresponding author of the research and co-leader of the VAI-SU2C Epigenetics Dream Team.
"Our approach reflects a growing emphasis on cancer interception -- intervening before cancer becomes established. We are working to build on the trial findings by exploring how exactly vitamin C interacts with pre-cancerous cells, including the idea that it may help restore normal epigenetic function in blood cells at risk of becoming leukemia."
The international research effort was led by Kirsten Grønbæk, M.D., Ph.D., a leading hematologist, professor at the University of Copenhagen, and member of the VAI-SU2C Epigenetics Dream Team.
"These exciting preliminary findings lay the groundwork for a larger clinical trial to explore vitamin C as a possible way to improve patient outcomes," said Grønbæk. "It is too early to make definitive recommendations based on our results, but we are hopeful that a more expansive study will provide further insights."
First Clinical Trial Tests Daily Vitamin C for Precancerous Blood Disorders
The study enrolled 109 patients with either clonal cytopenia of undetermined significance (CCUS) or myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS). Both conditions can develop into acute myeloid leukemia (AML), an aggressive form of blood cancer that is often difficult to treat. The likelihood of developing CCUS and related blood disorders rises with age, making these conditions particularly common among older adults.
Currently, no approved treatment can prevent CCUS from progressing to leukemia. Although stem cell transplantation is an option for treating MDS, many patients cannot undergo the procedure because of age or other medical conditions. None of the people enrolled in the trial were receiving cancer treatment when the study took place.
To determine whether vitamin C might offer benefits, researchers randomly divided participants into two groups. One received 1,000 mg of vitamin C by mouth each day for 12 months. The other received a placebo designed to be indistinguishable from the supplement in appearance, taste, and smell, but containing no vitamin C.
Neither the participants nor the clinical staff knew who was receiving vitamin C until the study concluded. This double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled approach is considered the gold standard in clinical research because it reduces potential bias and allows investigators to assess treatment effects more objectively.
The research was carried out at four hospitals: Copenhagen University Hospital-Rigshospitalet, Copenhagen University Hospital-Herlev, Aalborg University Hospital, and Keck Hospital of the University of Southern California.
What makes EVITA particularly notable is that it was the first randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial to investigate oral vitamin C in patients with conditions that can precede leukemia or with lower-risk myeloid cancers. Earlier studies had primarily examined vitamin C administered intravenously and had focused on solid tumors rather than precancerous blood disorders or early-stage blood malignancies.
EVITA instead evaluated a daily oral dose comparable to that available in many over-the-counter vitamin C supplements.
More Than Half of Patients Had Low Vitamin C Levels
Blood samples collected throughout the study allowed researchers to track participants' vitamin C concentrations and determine whether supplementation corrected deficiencies.
At the beginning of the trial, more than half of the participants had insufficient vitamin C levels. Among those assigned to the supplementation group, blood concentrations returned to normal after they began taking vitamin C.
For patients living with conditions that could eventually develop into leukemia, the possibility of an accessible intervention is especially important. In many cases, physicians have little choice but to monitor the disease and watch for signs that it is progressing.
"The standard approach for patients with pre-cancer blood disorders is to monitor their blood cell counts over time. This is, understandably, very frustrating -- no one wants to hear that they have a condition that increases leukemia risk but there's nothing that can be done other than watch and wait," said Casey O'Connell, M.D., FACP, the Lawrence and Jane Kelly Chair in Hematology at the University of Southern California and lead clinician at USC's trial location.
"The EVITA trial took on this challenge by exploring vitamin C's potential to address the underlying factors that drive leukemia development."
How Vitamin C Could Influence Cancer Development
Scientists have investigated whether vitamin C could play a useful role in cancer treatment for more than seven decades. For much of that time, the evidence remained uncertain because studies produced inconsistent findings and employed different experimental methods.
During the past decade, however, improved research technologies have revealed that vitamin C has important functions beyond its familiar roles in nutrition and immunity. In particular, scientists have uncovered its involvement in controlling gene activity and guiding normal cell development.
One of the most important discoveries concerns TET2, an enzyme that helps prevent cancerous growth by controlling whether particular genes are switched "on" or "off." Vitamin C supports the activity of this enzyme, which helps maintain normal patterns of gene regulation.
Mutations affecting TET2 are frequently found in leukemia and related blood disorders. When the enzyme's normal function is disrupted, abnormal cells can gain an opportunity to multiply and potentially develop into cancer.
Experiments using cancer models have provided additional evidence of vitamin C's possible protective effects. These studies found that supplementation could interfere with cellular changes associated with cancer and slow the progression of leukemia. Notably, the strongest effects appeared when vitamin C was introduced before cancer had become established.
This research helped inspire the idea of using vitamin C as a form of early intervention, potentially targeting the biological changes that precede the development of leukemia.
Building Toward Larger Clinical Trials
Before launching EVITA, the VAI-SU2C Epigenetics Dream Team conducted a pilot clinical study in 2016 to determine whether taking vitamin C orally could meaningfully raise its concentration in the blood.
The initial findings suggested that oral supplementation was a practical approach. Encouraged by those results, the researchers launched the phase 2 EVITA trial in 2017.
"This early work was critical because it offered a foundation from which to develop the present trial," said Stine Ulrik Mikkelsen, M.D., Ph.D., the study's first author and a clinician researcher in Grønbæk's laboratory.
"Vitamin C is important because it is involved in a range of biological functions, including the activity of enzymes that regulate normal cell function."
Researchers are continuing to examine the EVITA data to better understand the biological processes that might explain why patients receiving vitamin C showed improved survival.
Although the findings offer a promising direction for future research, additional clinical studies will be essential to determine whether vitamin C supplementation can reliably improve outcomes for people with precancerous blood disorders and early-stage blood cancers.
Other authors include Ali Al-Mousawi, M.D., Amalie Bach Puglisi, M.D., Anders Pommer Vallentin, M.D., Astrid Østergaard Mortensen, Heidi Naomi Ottesen, Linn Gillberg, M.Sc., Ph.D., Morten Tulstrup, M.D., M.Sc., Ph.D., Jakob Werner Hansen, M.D., Ph.D., and Mette Klarskov Andersen, M.D., D.MSc., of the University of Copenhagen and Copenhagen University Hospital-Rigshospitalet; Zachary Madaj, M.S., Toshinori Hinoue, Ph.D., Stacey L. Thomas, Ph.D., Christine N. Isaguirre, Ryan D. Sheldon, Ph.D., Marie Adams, M.S., Ryan Burgos, and Peter W. Laird, Ph.D., of Van Andel Institute; Jakob Schmidt Jespersen, M.Sc., Ph.D., Niels Richard Hansen, M.Sc., and Jens Lykkesfeldt, Ph.D., D.MSc., of the University of Copenhagen; Stephen Baylin, M.D., of Johns Hopkins University and Van Andel Institute; Bo Kok Mortensen, M.D., Ph.D., of Copenhagen University Hospital-Rigshospitalet and Copenhagen University Hospital-Herlev; and Marianne Tang Severinsen, M.D., Ph.D., of Aalborg University Hospital.
Funding for the study was provided by Van Andel Institute through the Van Andel Institute-Stand Up To Cancer® Epigenetics Dream Team, the Danish Cancer Society, and Greater Copenhagen Health Science Partners.

articles.title: Scientists reach the ultimate quantum limit on a surface
articles.text:
Scientists reach the ultimate quantum limit on a surface
- Date:
- October 19, 2026
- Source:
- Max Planck Institute for the Science of Light
- Summary:
- Scientists have achieved a quantum breakthrough by creating an ultra-clean surface where individual molecules can maintain their delicate quantum properties at the fundamental limit. The discovery could unlock unprecedented control over molecules and help drive the next generation of quantum technologies.
- Share:
Scientists at the Max Planck Institute for the Science of Light (MPL) have achieved a breakthrough in quantum physics, developing a way to study individual molecules on a surface with extraordinary precision. For the first time, researchers have demonstrated that molecules attached to a surface can reach the ultimate quantum limit of optical coherence, overcoming a major obstacle that has long restricted molecular quantum research.
The findings, published in Science, could open new possibilities for investigating how molecules interact with surfaces and developing advanced quantum technologies.
Why Surfaces Have Been a Major Obstacle in Quantum Physics
Many emerging quantum technologies depend on extremely small objects, such as individual atoms and molecules, that interact with light. Known as quantum emitters, these tiny systems can produce single particles of light called photons, store quantum information, and help establish quantum connections between distant systems. These capabilities are important for future applications in quantum computing and secure quantum communication.
To study a single quantum emitter, scientists must keep it stable and confined to one location for extended periods. Traditionally, researchers have accomplished this by trapping atoms or molecules in a vacuum or embedding them inside solid materials.
Placing quantum emitters directly on a surface, however, offers an intriguing advantage. Scientists could potentially manipulate individual molecules by "touching them" with an extremely sharp probe. Techniques such as scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) and atomic force microscopy (AFM) already use tips with atomic precision to investigate matter at incredibly small scales.
The difficulty is that surfaces are rarely as clean and stable as quantum experiments require. Contaminants from the surrounding environment can accumulate on them, creating disturbances that interfere with the delicate quantum behavior of nearby atoms and molecules. Until now, researchers had struggled to preserve the quantum optical properties of individual emitters attached to surfaces.
Scientists in MPL's Nano-Optics Division have now found a way around this problem.
A Clever Crystal Cleaning Method Solves the Problem
The research team, led by Prof. Vahid Sandoghdar, director at MPL and head of the "Nano-Optics" Division, developed an unusual cleaning method that takes advantage of a natural property of organic crystals.
At room temperature, the crystal material gradually evaporates through a process known as sublimation, in which a solid transforms directly into a gas without first becoming a liquid.
The researchers placed a small crystal inside a vacuum chamber equipped for extremely low temperatures, called a cryostat. As the crystal's uppermost layers slowly evaporated, they carried away unwanted contaminants, leaving behind a remarkably clean surface.
The team then cooled the crystal to just a few degrees Kelvin above absolute zero, the lowest theoretically possible temperature. This extreme cooling halted further sublimation and helped maintain the pristine surface.
Finally, the scientists used a tiny, specially fabricated oven to evaporate molecules onto the cold crystal, allowing them to settle on the clean surface.
Molecules Reach the Ultimate Quantum Limit
With this exceptionally stable environment in place, the researchers could investigate whether the molecules retained their fragile quantum properties.
Dr. Alexey Shkarin, a researcher in the Nano-Optics Division at MPL, explained: "The quality of quantum emitters can be evaluated by their coherence times, which indicate how long they keep their quantumness."
Coherence time describes how long a quantum system can maintain the properties needed for quantum behavior. The longer this coherence persists, the better the emitter can perform in applications that depend on precise interactions with light.
However, there is a fundamental physical restriction on how long coherence can last. Known as the Fourier limit, this boundary is determined by the time required for a quantum emitter to release its energy into its surroundings.
In an unstable or 'noisy' environment, disturbances can cause coherence to disappear hundreds or even thousands of times faster than this theoretical limit allows.
The scientists discovered that molecules deposited on their exceptionally clean crystal surface consistently reached the Fourier limit. This demonstrated that the surrounding environment was sufficiently quiet and stable to preserve the molecules' quantum coherence for the maximum physically permitted duration.
It is the first time researchers have achieved this fundamental limit with molecules attached to a surface.
New Possibilities for Controlling Individual Molecules
The breakthrough also allowed the team to investigate how a crystal surface influences the molecules resting on it.
Further experiments revealed that interactions with the surface can cause molecules to align in particular directions and alter their energy levels. The researchers also found indications that the surface might influence the molecules' shapes or the ways they vibrate.
These effects could provide valuable clues about how matter behaves at the molecular scale, while also offering new opportunities to control quantum systems.
"Our future work will focus on combining this method with AFM and STM to gain local nanometer control over individual quantum emitters," says Vahid Sandoghdar.
By combining their ultra-clean surface technique with powerful microscopy methods, the researchers hope to manipulate individual quantum emitters with precision measured in billionths of a meter.
Such capabilities could reveal previously inaccessible details about interactions between molecules and surfaces, while laying the groundwork for engineering new quantum states of matter and advancing future molecular quantum technologies.

articles.title: NASA solves a strange mystery hidden inside asteroid Bennu’s boulders
articles.text:
NASA solves a strange mystery hidden inside asteroid Bennu’s boulders
- Date:
- October 19, 2026
- Source:
- University of Arizona
- Summary:
- NASA scientists have finally uncovered why asteroid Bennu loses heat so quickly despite being covered in massive boulders. Samples returned to Earth reveal that its rocks are filled with hidden cracks, solving a mystery that has puzzled researchers for years.
- Share:
NASA's OSIRIS-REx mission encountered an unexpected mystery when it arrived at asteroid Bennu in 2018. Instead of the relatively smooth terrain that earlier observations had suggested, the spacecraft found a rugged landscape dominated by enormous boulders, with very few areas suitable for collecting samples.
"When OSIRIS-REx got to Bennu in 2018, we were surprised by what we saw," said Andrew Ryan, a scientist at the University of Arizona's Lunar and Planetary Laboratory, who led the mission's working group responsible for analyzing the physical and thermal properties of its samples. "We expected some boulders, but we anticipated at least some large regions with smoother, finer regolith that would be easy to collect. Instead, it looked like it was all boulders, and we were scratching our heads for a while."
The discovery was especially confusing because of what astronomers had previously learned about Bennu's ability to retain heat. Measurements from NASA's Spitzer Space Telescope in 2007 indicated that the asteroid's surface warmed and cooled rapidly as it rotated through sunlight and darkness.
Scientists describe this property as low thermal inertia. Materials with low thermal inertia, such as beach sand, quickly gain heat in sunlight and lose it once the Sun disappears. Large, solid rocks behave differently. Much like concrete, they typically hold on to warmth and release it gradually.
Bennu's boulder-covered surface appeared to contradict those earlier measurements, leaving researchers with a puzzling question: How could an asteroid covered in massive rocks cool so quickly?
Hidden Cracks Reveal the Secret of Bennu's Boulders
Observations collected by OSIRIS-REx while surveying Bennu offered an early clue. The asteroid's boulders might contain far more empty space than scientists had assumed, allowing them to lose heat faster than ordinary solid rocks.
When samples from Bennu were returned to Earth, researchers finally had an opportunity to examine that possibility directly.
Ryan and his colleagues used several laboratory techniques to investigate tiny rock fragments collected from the asteroid. Their findings, published in Nature Communications, confirmed that the rocks were indeed highly porous. However, porosity alone could not fully explain Bennu's unusually rapid heat loss.
The researchers discovered another important feature. Many of the rock particles contained extensive networks of cracks running through their interiors.
To investigate how these fractures influence the movement of heat, researchers at Nagoya University in Japan examined the samples using a technique called lock-in thermography. This method uses a laser to heat a tiny area of a sample while measuring how the heat spreads through the surrounding material, much like ripples expanding across the surface of a pond.
"That's when things became really interesting," Ryan said. "The thermal inertia measured in the lab samples turned out to be much higher than what the spacecraft's instruments had recorded, echoing similar findings obtained by the team of OSIRIS-REx's partner mission, JAXA's (Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency) Hayabusa-2."
The difference between laboratory measurements and spacecraft observations suggested that the size and internal structure of Bennu's rocks were essential to understanding their behavior.
Because the returned samples were much smaller than the enormous boulders covering Bennu, scientists needed a way to determine how heat would move through the material on a much larger scale.
NASA Uses 3D Scans to Look Inside Asteroid Rocks
At NASA's Johnson Space Center in Houston, researchers prepared the samples for detailed X-ray imaging while taking special precautions to prevent contamination.
Inside a glove box filled with protective nitrogen gas, team members sealed individual rock particles in airtight containers. They then transported the containers to a laboratory for X-ray computed tomography, or XCT scanning. After imaging, the particles were returned to the glove box without being exposed to Earth's environment.
"The sample goes into its own 'spacesuit,' gets a CT scan, and then comes back to its pristine environment, all without having any exposure to the terrestrial environment," said Nicole Lunning, lead OSIRIS-REx sample curator within the Astromaterials Research and Exploration Science division at NASA Johnson and one of the study's co-authors. "We can image right through these airtight containers to visualize the shape and internal structure of the rock that's inside."
The scans gave scientists a detailed view of the samples' interiors, revealing structures that could not be examined simply by looking at their surfaces.
"X-ray computed tomography allows us to look at the inside of an object in three dimensions, without damaging it," said study co-author and NASA Johnson X-ray scientist Scott Eckley.
Each scan also produced a permanent three-dimensional digital record of the particle's exterior and internal features. These records were added to a publicly accessible database, allowing the samples to be studied without repeatedly handling the original material.
Ryan's team then incorporated the X-ray scan data into computer simulations designed to track how heat travels through asteroid rocks. By extending the calculations from individual particles to the much larger boulders found on Bennu, they were able to reproduce the low thermal inertia observed by the spacecraft.
A Discovery That Could Change How Scientists Study Asteroids
The results resolved a key mystery about Bennu's unusual surface. Scientists had previously considered whether the asteroid's boulders might be extremely porous, with a soft, fluffy, or even sponge-like internal structure.
Although the rocks do contain substantial pore space, the researchers found that their widespread internal fractures were equally important to understanding how they retain and release heat.
"It turns out that they're really cracked too, and that was the missing piece of the puzzle," Ryan said.
The discovery has implications beyond Bennu. Astronomers frequently rely on measurements of how an asteroid absorbs and releases heat to estimate the physical properties of its surface. Until now, interpreting those observations has been difficult without actual rock samples to examine.
Ron Ballouz, a scientist at the Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory in Laurel, Maryland, and the study's second author, explained that the findings provide a valuable connection between measurements made remotely and the true internal structure of asteroid material.
"We can finally ground our understanding of telescope observations of the thermal properties of an asteroid through analyzing these samples from that very same asteroid," Ballouz said.

articles.title: Why painful arthritis can return stronger after cancer treatment
articles.text:
Why painful arthritis can return stronger after cancer treatment
- Date:
- October 19, 2026
- Source:
- University of Texas M. D. Anderson Cancer Center
- Summary:
- Researchers discovered that recurring arthritis triggered by cancer immunotherapy may be driven by immune cells that remember previous attacks and return in a more aggressive state. The findings could pave the way for treatments that prevent painful flare-ups while preserving the immune system's ability to fight cancer.
- Share:
For some cancer patients, the effects of immunotherapy can linger in an unexpected place: their joints. Painful arthritis may return repeatedly, sometimes becoming more severe with each episode. Now, scientists have uncovered a possible explanation involving the immune system's ability to remember previous attacks.
Researchers at The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center have found evidence that arthritis triggered by certain cancer immunotherapies behaves like a disease driven by immune memory. Rather than launching an entirely new inflammatory response during each flare, the immune system appears to reactivate cells involved in earlier episodes.
The discovery could eventually help doctors identify patients at risk of recurring arthritis and develop treatments that control joint inflammation without interfering with the immune system's ability to fight cancer.
The study, published in Cancer Immunology Research, was led by scientists at UT MD Anderson and Yale University. The research team included Roza I. Nurieva, Ph.D., professor of Immunology; Synat Keam, Ph.D., a postdoctoral fellow in the Nurieva Laboratory; and Yuanteng Jeff Li, M.D., assistant professor of General Internal Medicine. Sang Taek Kim, M.D., Ph.D., an assistant professor at Yale University, also co-led the investigation.
"Cancer immunotherapy works by creating a lasting immune response against tumors, but that same persistence may also contribute to recurring inflammatory side effects that can be debilitating for patients," Nurieva said. "By identifying the immune cells that drive recurrent arthritis, we can inform treatment strategies that reduce the risk of future flares while preserving the therapy's effectiveness against cancer."
Why Cancer Immunotherapy Can Trigger Painful Arthritis
Immune checkpoint inhibitors are widely used cancer treatments that help the body's natural defenses recognize and attack tumor cells. These drugs are a form of immunotherapy that works by removing some of the molecular restraints that normally keep immune activity under control.
Although this approach can help the immune system destroy cancer cells, it can sometimes cause immune cells to attack healthy tissues as well. When the joints become targets, patients may develop inflammatory arthritis, a condition that causes pain, swelling, and inflammation.
For some patients, the problem does not disappear after the first episode. Approximately 20% to 50% of patients who develop this complication experience repeated arthritis flares, and symptoms can persist for months or even years after immunotherapy ends.
These recurring episodes are often more intense than the initial attack, raising an important question: Why does the immune system continue to produce inflammation, and why can its response become increasingly aggressive?
Scientists Discover Immune Cells That Remember Previous Attacks
To investigate, the researchers examined fluid taken from the joints of six patients during both their first arthritis episode and a later recurrence.
Their analysis revealed two distinct populations of immune cells that appeared during both flares. One consisted of inflammatory CD8 T cells, while the other was a specialized group of CD4 T cells expressing two markers known as PD-1 and CXCL13.
T cells are immune cells that help coordinate the body's defenses and respond to potential threats. Some can also persist after an initial immune response, allowing the immune system to react more quickly when it encounters a familiar target.
The presence of the same immune cell populations during separate arthritis attacks suggests that recurring inflammation may arise from cells already involved in the earlier episode. Instead of starting from scratch, the immune system appears to reactivate an established inflammatory response.
This immune memory mechanism could help explain why arthritis can repeatedly return even after cancer treatment has stopped.
Why Arthritis Flares May Become More Severe
The researchers also found that the recurring immune cells appeared more active during subsequent arthritis episodes. They produced increased amounts of inflammatory signaling molecules, which immune cells use to communicate and influence one another.
Another finding was particularly unexpected. Regulatory T cells, which normally act as a braking system to prevent excessive immune activity, also began producing inflammatory molecules during recurring flares.
This suggests that some of the cells responsible for keeping inflammation under control may instead contribute to it, potentially weakening the body's ability to shut down the response.
The researchers also identified extensive communication networks connecting inflammatory cells within affected joints. These signaling networks became more pronounced during the second arthritis episode.
Together, the findings suggest that recurring flares involve a coordinated and increasingly active inflammatory environment, rather than just a handful of immune cells acting independently.
Could Immune Memory Help Predict Future Arthritis Flares?
Despite growing recognition of inflammatory arthritis as a complication of cancer immunotherapy, scientists still do not fully understand why it affects certain patients while others never develop the condition.
The newly identified immune cell populations could provide an important starting point. Future studies may determine whether these cells can serve as biomarkers, meaning measurable biological indicators that help doctors recognize patients who are more likely to experience recurring arthritis.
Understanding which immune cells sustain the inflammation could also guide the development of more precise treatments. Ideally, such therapies would prevent or reduce painful arthritis flares while leaving the beneficial cancer-fighting effects of immunotherapy intact.
Because the investigation examined samples from only six patients, additional research will be needed to confirm the findings and establish whether the identified immune cells can reliably predict future episodes.
Still, the results offer a promising explanation for a difficult complication of cancer treatment: an immune system trained to remember and fight tumors may also retain inflammatory responses that continue to harm the joints.
This work received support from the Wilkes Family Melanoma Autoimmune Research Fund, the National Institutes of Health, the Advanced Technology Genomics Core Facility, the Rheumatology Research Foundation Fund, the National Cancer Institute (NCI), the Andrew Sabin Family Fellowships, the Gateway for Cancer Research, the U.S. Department of Defense, the Kidney Cancer Association, the V Foundation for Cancer Research, the Finneran Family Endowment in Translational Research, philanthropic donations from the family of Mike and Mary Allen, and institutional funding from UT MD Anderson.

articles.title: Vì sao truyện cổ tích Hàn Quốc không bắt đầu bằng "Ngày xửa ngày xưa..."
articles.text:
Truyện cổ tích Hàn Quốc thường bắt đầu bằng một cụm từ độc nhất vô nhị: "Xưa, xưa lắm ở cái thời mà loài hổ còn hút thuốc...".
Với những người may mắn có được một tuổi thơ êm dịu, các câu chuyện cổ tích được kể trước giờ đi ngủ bằng giọng nói thân thương của ông bà, cha mẹ là một ký ức ngọt ngào của tuổi thơ. Gần như mọi nền văn hóa đều nuôi dưỡng tâm hồn trẻ thơ bằng những câu chuyện cổ tích, vừa là để truyền lại sợi chỉ văn hóa ngàn đời, vừa giáo dục nhân cách thuở còn bế bồng.
Kho tàng cổ tích của nhân loại dường như là vô tận, với hàng trăm nền văn hóa và vô số kể những mô-típ, mẩu truyện, cách lý giải thế giới khác nhau. Nhưng có một điều mà gần như ai cũng còn nhớ về những câu chuyện đầy màu sắc ấy dù có ngủ quên giữa chừng đi chăng nữa, là 4 chữ thần kỳ "Ngày xửa ngày xưa...".
Không chỉ ở Việt Nam mới có 4 chữ dẫn nhập mở ra cả thế giới diệu kỳ đó, mà một số ngôn ngữ khác như: tiếng Anh (Once upon a time) hay tiếng Pháp (il était une fois) và tiếng Nhật (Mukashimukashi) đều có nghĩa tương tự.
Tranh hổ ngậm tẩu thuốc trong văn hóa Hàn.
Chỉ riêng ở Hàn Quốc, cụm từ đó lại luôn đi kèm một ví von có một không hai "Xưa, xưa lắm ở cái thời mà loài hổ còn hút thuốc..." là cụm từ đã thấm sâu vào tâm trí trẻ em Hàn bao thế hệ trước mỗi câu chuyện cổ tích. Như mọi thành ngữ của mọi ngôn ngữ khác, cụm từ này ẩn chứa trong nó bao tâm tư, lịch sử, sáng tạo và thậm chí cả châm biếm của người Hàn.
Theo Bảo tàng Quốc gia Hàn Quốc, loài hổ có một dấu ấn văn hóa sâu đậm trong truyền thuyết nước này. Nhờ địa hình nhiều đồi núi và thung lũng, loài vật này rất phổ biến ở đất nước châu Á.
Trong hình tượng dân gian, hổ duy trì một tính nhị nguyên thú vị: vừa là kẻ dẫn đường cho các vị anh hùng trên con đường chinh phục khi đại diện cho những linh hồn nhân ái, lại có khi là kẻ thù hung dữ chắn đường họ.
Hơn nữa, về mặt ẩn dụ, hổ mang hình tượng uy quyền và sức mạnh đối với con người. Chẳng hạn, chúng thường được khắc họa trong tranh vẽ và bích họa với hình ảnh canh giữ mộ phần hoàng tộc. Nói cách khác, hổ tượng trưng cho tầng lớp thống trị trong xã hội xưa.
Mặt khác, thuốc lá dù chưa có lịch sử xuất hiện quá lâu lại là một biểu tượng thú vị khác trong văn hóa Hàn Quốc, thường gắn với sự phân chia giai cấp. Du nhập vào đây từ những năm 1600, người dân lúc đó tin rằng hút thuốc là một phương pháp trị liệu tốt cho sức khỏe và trở thành thói quen "quốc dân" khi người già, trẻ nhỏ, ai ai cũng có thể hút thuốc, theo Korean Times.
Trong thời kỳ đó, dù vẫn được hút thuốc, giới bình dân không được phép buôn lậu hay hút thuốc trước một lễ kỷ niệm nhất định, cũng không được phép hút trước mặt những người ở tầng lớp cao hơn.
Chính vì lý do đó, cụm từ trên đã ra đời như một cách đả kích dân gian và ẩn dụ về việc tầng lớp thống trị phong kiến được thoải mái hút thuốc, trong khi thường dân nhìn với vẻ ghen tị.
Mô-típ hổ hút thuốc đặc biệt phổ biến trong hội họa.
Qua nhiều thế hệ với những sự thêm mắm dặm muối nhất định, cụm từ "Xưa, xưa lắm ở cái thời mà loài hổ còn hút thuốc..." dần trở thành "văn mẫu" bắt đầu cho những câu chuyện cổ xưa hơn cả lịch sử thuốc lá. Dù nét nghĩa đả kích của nó đã phai mờ qua thời gian, nguồn gốc của nó vẫn rõ rệt, là minh chứng cho một xã hội vốn luôn mong muốn đấu tranh vì sự bình đẳng.

articles.title: Phát hiện “xương sống” của sinh vật trên mặt trăng sao Mộc
articles.text:
Siêu kính viễn vọng James Webb đã có phát hiện "vàng" khi soi kỹ mặt trăng sao Mộc Europa, một trong những nơi mà NASA tin tưởng nhất về khả năng có sinh vật ngoài hành tinh.
Theo The Guardian, các quan sát mới nhất của kính viễn vọng không gian mạnh nhất thế giới này khẳng định carbon dioxide (CO2) trên bề mặt Europa có nguồn gốc từ đại dương ngầm của nó.
"Đây là một phát hiện lớn. Chúng tôi vẫn chưa biết liệu sự sống có thực sự hiện diện hay không, nhưng phát hiện mới này bổ sung thêm bằng chứng cho thấy đại dương của Europa sẽ là nơi đặt cược tốt cho việc tìm kiếm sự sống còn tồn tại" - tiến sĩ Christopher Glein từ Viện Nghiên cứu Tây Nam (SwRI - Mỹ) nói.
Tàu Juno của NASA bay trên mặt trăng sao Mộc Europa - (Ảnh đồ họa: NASA)
Europa là một trong 4 mặt trăng Galilean của sao Mộc, là 4 mặt trăng lớn nhất trong hàng chục mặt trăng của nó, được nhà bác học Galileo Galilei phát hiện từ đầu thế kỷ 17.
Từ lâu, NASA rất tin tưởng về khả năng sinh sống của nó, khi các tàu quỹ đạo sao Mộc liên tiếp bị hơi nước từ đại dương ngầm dưới vỏ băng - chứa các thành phần hóa học đại diện cho sự sống - phun trúng.
Một sứ mệnh mang tên Europa Clipper đang được NASA chuẩn bị sẽ đưa tàu đổ bộ mang robot siêu nhỏ lên "miền đất hứa" này, chui xuống đại dương ngầm để tìm sinh vật ngoài hành tinh.
Phát hiện mới này khẳng định thêm điều đó. Trước đây, CO2 rắn đã được tìm thấy ở trên bề mặt Europa. Nhưng việc chứng minh được nó thuộc về đại dương ngầm mới quan trọng, vì carbon chính là nguyên tố "xương sống" của sự sống.
Các quan sát cận hồng ngoại của James Webb đã giúp các nhà khoa học lập bản đồ phân bố CO2 trên Europa, cho thấy một điểm tích tụ nhiều CO2 là Tara Regio trên mặt trăng sao Mộc này.
Đó là một khu vực rộng 1.800km2, có địa hình hỗn loạn, với các vết nứt băng và rặng băng, được hình thành khi các khối băng bị đẩy từ sâu bên dưới lên bề mặt thông qua các quá trình địa chất.
Nói cách khác, carbon cấu thành CO2 là từ đại dương ngầm bên dưới vỏ băng.
Ở Trái đất, 6 nguyên tố chính tạo nên nền tảng cho mọi sự sống là carbon, hydro, oxy, lưu huỳnh, phốt pho, ni-tơ. Với phát hiện mới, 4 cái quan trọng nhất - carbon, hydro, oxy, lưu huỳnh - đã được xác định trên Europa.
Giáo sư Andrew Coates, người đứng đầu về khoa học hành tinh tại Phòng thí nghiệm vũ trụ Mullard thuộc University College London (UCL - Anh), người không tham gia nghiên cứu, bình luận: "Để có sự sống, bạn cần nước lỏng, chất hóa học phù hợp, nguồn năng lượng và đủ thời gian để sự sống phát triển. Tôi nghĩ tất cả những thứ đó có thể có mặt trên Europa".

articles.title: Alaska’s monster tsunami sent water 1,580 feet up a mountain
articles.text:
Alaska’s monster tsunami sent water 1,580 feet up a mountain
- Date:
- October 19, 2026
- Source:
- The Conversation
- Summary:
- A massive landslide in Alaska triggered the second-highest tsunami ever recorded, sending water and debris 1,580 feet up a mountainside just hours after tourists visited the area. Scientists discovered that the disaster was preceded by several warning signs, including rapid glacier retreat, heavy rainfall, and thousands of tiny seismic tremors. As glaciers retreat, similar disasters could become a growing danger in mountainous coastal regions.
- Share:
On the evening of Aug. 9, 2025, passengers on the Hanse Explorer finished taking selfies and videos of the South Sawyer Glacier, and the ship headed back down the fjord. Twelve hours later, a landslide from the adjacent mountain unexpectedly collapsed into the fjord, initiating the second-highest tsunami in recorded history.
We conduct research on earthquakes and tsunamis at the Alaska Earthquake Center, and one of us serves as Alaska state seismologist. In a new study with colleagues, we detail how that landslide sent water and debris 1,580 feet (481 meters) up the other side of the fjord – higher than the top floor of the Taipei 101 skyscraper – and then continued down Tracy Arm. The force of the water stripped the fjord’s walls down to bare rock.
It was just after 5 o’clock in the morning on a dreary day, and fortunately, no ships were nearby. In the months after, some cruise lines started avoiding Tracy Arm. However, the conditions that led to this event are not at all unique to this fjord.
Landslides are common in the coastal mountains of Alaska where rapid uplift, caused by tectonic forces and long-term ice loss, converges with the erosive forces of precipitation and moving glaciers. But a curious pattern has emerged in recent years: Multiple major landslides have occurred precisely at the terminus of a retreating glacier.
Though the mechanics are still poorly understood, these mountains appear to become unstable when the ice disappears. When the landslide hits the water, the momentum of millions of tons of rock is transferred into tsunami waves.
This same phenomenon is playing out from Alaska to Greenland and Norway, sometimes with deadly consequences. Across the Arctic, countries are trying to come to terms with this growing hazard. The options are not attractive: avoid vast swaths of coastline, or live with a poorly understood risk. We believe there is an obvious role for alert systems, but only if scientists have a better understanding of where and when landslides are likely to occur.
Signs that a landslide might be coming
The Tracy Arm landslide is a powerful example.
The landslide occurred in August, when warm ocean waters and heavier precipitation favor both glacier retreat and slope failure. The glacier below the landslide area had experienced rapid calving – large chunks of ice breaking off and falling into the water – and it had retreated more than a third of a mile in the two months prior. Heavy rain had been falling. Rain enters fractures in the mountain and pushes them closer to failure by increasing the water pressure in cracks.
Most provocative are the thousands of small seismic tremors that emanated from the area of the slide in the days prior to the mountainside collapsing.
We believe that this combination of signs would have been sufficient to issue progressive alerts to any ships in the vicinity and homes and businesses that could have been harmed by a tsunami at least a day prior to the failure – had a monitoring program existed.
Escalating alerts are used for everything from terrorism and nuclear plant safety to avalanches and volcanic unrest. They don’t remove the risk, but they do make it easier for people to safely coexist with hazards.
For example, though people are still killed in avalanches, alert systems have played an essential role in making winter backcountry travel safer for more people. The collapse at Tracy Arm demonstrates what could be possible for landslides.
What an alert system could look like
We believe that the combination of weather and rapid glacier retreat in early August 2025 was likely sufficient to issue an alert notifying people that the hazard may be temporarily elevated in a general area. On a yellow-orange-red scale, this would be a yellow alert.
In the hours prior to the landslide, the exponential increase in seismic events and telltale transition to what is known as seismic tremor – a continuous “hum” of seismic energy – were sufficient to communicate a time-sensitive warning for a specific region.
These observations, recorded as a byproduct of regional earthquake monitoring, warranted an “orange” alert noting immediate concern. The signs were arguably sufficient to recommend keeping boats and ships out of the fjord.
Our research over the past few years has demonstrated that once a large landslide has started, it is possible to detect and measure the event within a couple of minutes. In this amount of time, seismic waves in the surrounding area can indicate the rough size of the landslide and whether it occurred near open water.
A monitoring program that could quickly communicate this would be able to issue a red alert, signaling an event in progress.
The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s tsunami warning program has spent decades fine-tuning rapid message dissemination. A warning system would have offered little help for ships in the immediate vicinity, but it could have provided perhaps 10 minutes of warning for those who rode out the harrowing tsunami farther away.
There is no landslide monitoring system operating yet at this scale in the U.S. Building one will require cooperation across state and federal agencies, and strengthened monitoring and communication networks. Even then, it will not be fail-proof.
Understanding risk, not removing it
Alert systems do not remove the risk entirely, but they are a better option than no warning at all. Over time, they also build awareness as communities and visitors get used to thinking about these hazards.
Many of the most alluring places on Earth come with significant hazards. Arctic fjords are among them. The same processes that create this hazard – glacier retreat, steep terrain, dynamic geology – are also what make these landscapes so compelling. The mix of glaciers, ice-choked waters and steep mountains is exactly what draws people to these places. People will continue to visit and experience them.
The question is not whether these places should be avoided altogether, but how to help people make more informed decisions. We believe that stronger geophysical and meteorological monitoring, coupled with new research and communication channels, is the first step.
On Aug. 9, visitors unknowingly passed through a landscape on the cusp of failure. An alert system might have given tour companies and people in the area the information they needed to make more informed choices and avoid being caught by surprise.

articles.title: Why some people escape Alzheimer’s despite carrying a high-risk gene
articles.text:
Why some people escape Alzheimer’s despite carrying a high-risk gene
- Date:
- October 19, 2026
- Source:
- Columbia University Irving Medical Center
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered why some people with a high genetic risk of Alzheimer’s remain mentally sharp into their 80s, uncovering a rare mutation that protects the brain from harmful protein buildup. The findings reveal a potential new way to prevent early brain damage and could pave the way for treatments that mimic this natural defense.
- Share:
Some people carry one of the strongest genetic risk factors for Alzheimer's disease yet never develop it, remaining mentally sharp well into their 80s. For years, scientists have wondered what protects these individuals despite their increased genetic vulnerability.
Now, researchers at Columbia University have uncovered a biological mechanism that could help explain this remarkable resistance. Their findings point to a rare genetic mutation that protects the brain's blood vessels from damage, potentially opening a new path toward Alzheimer's treatments.
The discovery builds on research the team published two years ago involving APOE ε4, a gene variant strongly associated with Alzheimer's risk. The scientists found that some people carrying APOE ε4 also possess a rare protective mutation in the fibronectin (FN1) gene.
Fibronectin is a protein that helps support the structure of tissues. However, in people with APOE ε4, excessive amounts can accumulate around blood vessels in the brain, potentially compromising a critical protective system known as the blood-brain barrier. The rare FN1 mutation appears to limit this buildup and the damage associated with it.
That earlier discovery suggested an intriguing possibility: What if scientists could develop a treatment that recreates the protection provided by this rare mutation?
A new study published in Nature Aging brings that possibility closer by identifying how excess fibronectin damages the brain's protective barrier and revealing potential ways to interrupt the process.
"This new study takes us from a genetic clue to a disease mechanism," says Caghan Kizil, the study's corresponding author and professor of neurological sciences in the Department of Neurology and the Taub Institute for Research on Alzheimer's Disease and the Aging Brain at Columbia University Vagelos College of Physicians and Surgeons.
"We knew that changes in fibronectin could protect against Alzheimer's, but we didn't know why excess fibronectin was harmful in the first place. This study gives us that detailed mechanism -- and with it, ideas for how to reproduce that natural protection."
How an Alzheimer's Risk Gene Weakens the Blood-Brain Barrier
The blood-brain barrier serves as a protective boundary between the bloodstream and the brain. Made up of tightly connected cells surrounding the brain's blood vessels, it carefully regulates which substances can enter brain tissue while helping maintain conditions necessary for removing potentially harmful waste.
When this barrier becomes damaged or excessively permeable, substances that would normally be kept out can enter the brain more easily. Such disruptions may contribute to inflammation and other processes involved in neurological diseases, including Alzheimer's.
To investigate the role of fibronectin, the Columbia team combined several advanced research approaches. They examined human brain tissue and cerebrospinal fluid, the clear liquid surrounding the brain and spinal cord, using genetic and epigenetic analyses to explore changes in DNA and gene activity.
Their investigation also included single-cell sequencing, which reveals the activity of individual cells, and spatial imaging to examine where biological changes occur within tissues. Additional experiments involved human stem-cell models, three-dimensional cultures of blood vessels, and studies in zebrafish and mice.
Despite the variety of methods, the findings consistently pointed to the same mechanism: APOE ε4 promotes the production and accumulation of fibronectin around the brain's blood vessels.
In mice engineered to carry human APOE ε4, researchers measured nearly twice as much fibronectin in the brain as in mice carrying APOE ε3, another common version of the gene. The greater accumulation was accompanied by evidence that the blood-brain barrier had become leaky.
Scientists Discover How Fibronectin Causes Brain Damage
One experiment provided especially important evidence that fibronectin does more than simply accumulate in damaged blood vessels.
The researchers increased human fibronectin specifically in astrocytes, specialized support cells that help maintain the blood-brain barrier and keep the brain functioning properly.
Increasing fibronectin in these cells was enough to disrupt the barrier, allowing it to become more permeable. Conversely, reducing fibronectin improved the barrier's ability to function normally.
These results provided experimental evidence that excess fibronectin can directly contribute to blood-brain barrier damage rather than merely appearing alongside it.
"The animal experiments allowed us to move beyond association," says co-first author Prabesh Bhattarai, an associate research scientist in the Kizil lab. "When we increased fibronectin in astroglia, the barrier became permeable. When we reduced fibronectin, barrier function improved."
The team then investigated the molecular events responsible for the damage.
They found that excessive fibronectin interferes with communication between cells by activating abnormal signals through integrins, proteins that help cells sense and respond to their surroundings, and an enzyme known as focal adhesion kinase.
These abnormal signals disrupt a network of growth factors called VEGF, HBEGF, and IGF1. Although growth factors are often associated with cell development and repair, these particular signaling molecules also help astrocytes and blood vessel cells coordinate their activities to maintain a healthy blood-brain barrier.
When their communication becomes disrupted, the barrier can lose its integrity, potentially leaving brain tissue more vulnerable to damage.
"Single-cell analysis allowed us to examine this pathway in the different cells that maintain the brain's blood vessels," says co-first author Elanur Yilmaz, an associate research scientist in the Kizil lab. "We observed the same biological pattern across experimental models and human Alzheimer's tissue, making the mechanism especially compelling."
Evidence From Human Brains Strengthens the Alzheimer's Connection
Importantly, the researchers found signs of similar biological disturbances in human samples, suggesting that the process identified in laboratory experiments may also contribute to Alzheimer's disease in people carrying APOE ε4.
Analyses of brain tissue and cerebrospinal fluid showed that elevated fibronectin levels were associated with inflammation in astrocytes.
Genetic and gene-regulation analyses also connected FN1 to blood vessel disease and changes involving VEGFA, a growth factor that plays an important role in maintaining healthy brain blood vessels.
Together, these findings provide multiple lines of evidence linking excess fibronectin to the vascular damage associated with APOE ε4.
"The convergence of these independent human datasets strengthens the case that fibronectin is part of the APOE ε4-related vascular disease process," says Badri Vardarajan, associate professor of neurological science in the Department of Neurology, Gertrude H. Sergievsky Center, and Taub Institute, who collaborated on this discovery of the FN1 mutation.
A Rare Genetic Defense Could Inspire New Alzheimer's Treatments
The potential implications are significant because APOE ε4 is the strongest common genetic risk factor for Alzheimer's disease. Approximately one in five people carries at least one copy of this gene variant.
Although carrying APOE ε4 does not guarantee that someone will develop Alzheimer's, it increases their likelihood of developing the disease. Understanding why certain carriers remain unaffected could reveal new opportunities for prevention and treatment.
The latest findings suggest several possible approaches.
One strategy would be to prevent harmful amounts of fibronectin from accumulating around the brain's blood vessels. Another would involve blocking the abnormal cellular signals triggered by excess fibronectin. A third possibility would be to restore the growth factor signaling that allows astrocytes and blood vessel cells to maintain the blood-brain barrier.
Researchers are already investigating these possibilities through laboratory experiments.
However, translating the discovery into a treatment will require considerable care. Fibronectin performs essential functions throughout the body, including supporting tissue structure and helping damaged tissues heal. Any future therapy would therefore need to target its harmful accumulation or effects without disrupting these beneficial activities.
By identifying the molecular mechanisms involved, scientists now have a more precise framework for designing such treatments. The findings may also help researchers determine when interventions would be most effective and how to measure whether they are successfully protecting the brain.
"By showing how fibronectin contributes to early vascular damage, this study gives us new therapeutic targets and potential ways to measure whether treatments are working," says Richard Mayeux, chair of the Department of Neurology and a collaborator on the project. "Clinically, it connects a major genetic risk factor for Alzheimer's to an early disease process that may be possible to modify."
Although these potential therapies remain experimental, the discovery offers a promising new direction in Alzheimer's research. Rather than focusing only on the damage that develops as the disease progresses, scientists may eventually be able to reproduce a natural genetic defense that helps protect vulnerable brains before significant damage occurs.

articles.title: Tại sao đồ ăn của Ấn Độ chủ yếu là ở dạng sệt?
articles.text:
Người Ấn Độ đặc biệt thích chế biến các loại thực phẩm và gia vị thành dạng sệt, vì vậy khi nhắc đến đồ ăn Ấn Độ, người ta nghĩ ngay đến các loại bột nhão. Vậy tại sao người Ấn Độ thích ăn đồ ăn dạng sệt?
Trước hết, để hiểu tại sao người Ấn Độ thích ăn thức ăn nhão và sệt, chúng ta phải hiểu về lịch sử và văn hóa ấm thực của Ấn Độ.
Ấn Độ có truyền thống ăn chay lâu đời trong lịch sử, điều này khiến người Ấn Độ chế biến hầu hết các nguyên liệu thành dạng sệt, điều này khiến nguyên liệu trông ngon miệng hơn.
Ẩm thực Ấn Độ có đặc trưng bởi việc sử dụng các loại gia vị, các loại rau gia vị và rau quả khác và đôi khi trái cây được trồng ở Ấn Độ và cũng như chế độ ăn chay phổ biến trong một bộ phận của xã hội Ấn Độ.
Ngoài ra, ẩm thực Ấn Độ còn mang nhiều ý nghĩa văn hóa phong phú. Trong Ấn Độ giáo và Phật giáo, ăn chay là biểu tượng của tâm linh, được coi như một hình thức bảo vệ và tôn kính sự sống, vì vậy, rất nhiều người Ấn Độ ít ăn thịt mà thích ăn rau, đậu và gạo.
Đồng thời, người Ấn Độ cũng rất coi trọng mùi vị và mùi thơm của thức ăn. Nhiều loại gia vị thường được sử dụng trong ẩm thực Ấn Độ, chẳng hạn như nghệ, gừng, tỏi, thảo quả, quế… có thể làm cho hương vị của món ăn đậm đà hơn, đồng thời tăng kết cấu của món ăn.Thức ăn dạng sệt có cảm giác mềm và dễ nhai, cũng có thể mang lại trải nghiệm hương vị độc đáo. Do đó, người Ấn Độ cũng thích làm thức ăn dạng sệt.
Mỗi khu vực ở Ấn Độ có đặc trưng món ăn và kỹ thuật nấu ăn khác nhau. Kết quả là, phong cách ấm thực sẽ thay đổi theo vùng, phản ánh cơ cấu nhân khẩu khác nhau của tiểu lục địa Ấn Độ đa dạng về sắc tộc, nhưng hầu hết chúng đều có dạng sệt. Ẩm thực Ấn Độ được biết đến với những món ăn có hương liệu và gia vị cay nồng, điển hình là món cà ri, đất nước này cũng nổi tiếng về các món chay.
Thói quen chế biến thức ăn của người Ấn Độ cũng là một yếu tố quan trọng ảnh hưởng đến độ sệt của thức ăn Ấn Độ.
Trong văn hóa ẩm thực của Ấn Độ, nấu nướng không chỉ nhằm thỏa mãn nhu cầu vị giác mà còn nhằm nâng cao giá trị dinh dưỡng của món ăn. Do đó, người Ấn Độ thường áp dụng nhiều kỹ thuật nấu ăn khác nhau như chiên, luộc, hầm… để thức ăn dễ tiêu hóa và bổ dưỡng hơn.
Niềm tin tôn giáo và văn hóa Ấn Độ đã đóng một vai trò có ảnh hưởng trong sự tiến hóa của ẩm thực của quốc gia này. Tuy nhiên, ẩm thực trên khắp Ấn Độ cũng đã dần thay đổi do sự tương tác văn hóa quy mô lớn của tiểu lục địa này đồi với Hy Lạp cổ đại, Ba Tư, Mông Cổ và Tây Á, khiến cho ẩm thực quốc gia này có một nét độc đáo pha trộn của các nền ẩm thực khác nhau trên khắp châu Á.
Trong chế độ ăn uống của người Ấn Độ, nghiền các nguyên liệu thành bột nhão cũng là một phương pháp chế biến phổ biến. Ví dụ, cà ri Ấn Độ, súp cà ri… được làm bằng cách nghiền các loại gia vị và rau củ thành dạng sệt, sau đó thêm các nguyên liệu khác để nấu.
Ngoài ra, thói quen ăn uống của người Ấn Độ cũng có tác động nhất định đến độ sệt của thức ăn. Ví dụ, ở Ấn Độ, nhiều người ăn bằng ngón tay để họ có thể cảm nhận rõ hơn mùi vị và mùi thơm của thức ăn. Và thức ăn dạng sệt có thể giúp cho việc ăn bằng tay dễ dàng hơn.
Trong khi hầu hết mọi người trên thế giới nghĩ rằng các món ăn của Ấn Độ đều là cà ri. Nhưng nó không đúng. Nhiều loại ẩm thực Ấn Độ được làm từ cá, thịt, đậu lăng hoặc rau. Điểm đặc biệt của ẩm thực Ấn Độ là sự đa dạng trong các loại gia vị khiến mỗi món ăn trở nên lạ miệng và nổi bật so với một vài nền ẩm thực khác trên thế giới.
Cuối cùng, điều đáng chú ý là thức ăn nghiền của Ấn Độ cũng có khía cạnh giá trị dinh dưỡng của nó.
Người Ấn Độ tin rằng những nguyên liệu mà họ thường sử dụng như đậu nành, đậu phụ, đậu xanh… có thể cung cấp nhiều chất dinh dưỡng cần thiết cho cơ thể con người, chẳng hạn như protein, chất xơ, vitamin…
Các món ăn ở Ấn Độ được biết là được làm từ cùng loại ngũ cốc và nguyên liệu mà người Ấn Độ đã từng ăn hàng ngàn năm trước. Ngày nay, lương thực chủ yếu của họ bao gồm bột mì nguyên cám, gạo và các nguyên liệu bổ dưỡng khác.
Nghiền các thành phần này thành bột nhão không chỉ có thể cải thiện hương vị của thức ăn mà còn giúp cơ thể hấp thụ các chất dinh dưỡng này dễ dàng hơn.
Ngoài ra, các loại gia vị thường được sử dụng trong ẩm thực Ấn Độ như gừng, tỏi, ớt có tác dụng chống oxy hóa mạnh, giúp nâng cao khả năng miễn dịch và sức đề kháng. Do đó, ăn thức ăn Ấn Độ ở mức độ vừa phải cũng có thể có lợi cho cơ thể.
Ẩm thực Ấn Độ phổ biến nhất có 6 hương vị: chua, ngọt, mặn, đắng, chát và hăng. Ấn Độ còn được mệnh danh là “xứ sở của gia vị”, chỉ riêng quốc gia này đã sản xuất hơn 70% lượng gia vị của thế giới, nhiều hơn bất kỳ quốc gia nào khác trên thế giới.

articles.title: Something strange is happening beneath a volcano near 2 million people
articles.text:
Something strange is happening beneath a volcano near 2 million people
- Date:
- October 19, 2026
- Source:
- Penn State University
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered evidence of two hidden magma sources beneath Nicaragua’s Masaya volcano, where satellite observations revealed mysterious ground movements suggesting magma is shifting deep underground. The findings could improve eruption forecasting for the active volcano, which sits near 2 million people and attracts tourists to its spectacular lava lake.
- Share:
A volcano famous for its glowing lava lake is hiding a surprisingly complex system of magma deep underground. Scientists at Penn State have uncovered evidence of two previously unrecognized magma sources beneath Nicaragua's active Masaya volcano, raising new questions about how molten rock moves beneath the surface.
The discovery is particularly important because approximately 2 million people live within 13 miles of the volcano, which is also a popular tourist destination. Understanding its underground activity could help scientists recognize warning signs of future eruptions and better protect nearby communities.
Using six years of satellite observations, researchers tracked subtle changes in the ground around Masaya. They discovered that one part of the volcano initially sank before beginning to rise, possibly indicating that fresh magma was entering a deep reservoir. Meanwhile, the ground around its active Santiago crater and lava lake continued to sink, suggesting that a separate, shallower magma reservoir was behaving differently.
The findings, published in Geophysical Research Letters, reveal that the volcano's underground magma system may be considerably more complicated than previously understood.
"These observations help scientists better understand how magma moves beneath Masaya and may improve monitoring and eruption forecasting in the future," said lead author Lizzie Johnson, who earned her bachelor's degree in geosciences from Penn State in May.
Why Masaya Volcano Is Closely Monitored
Located near Managua, Nicaragua's capital, Masaya is a geologically complex volcano featuring multiple overlapping craters and calderas. Calderas are large depressions that generally form when the ground collapses after magma is removed from an underground chamber.
Although scientists have studied Masaya for years, the movement of magma through its underground reservoirs and passageways remains poorly understood. These systems can change over time, making it difficult to determine exactly what is happening beneath the volcano.
"Having a thorough understanding of Masaya's volcanic activity and its related hazards is critical as around 2 million people live near Masaya and the caldera is a national park and popular tourist destination," Johnson said. "Although Masaya last produced a major lava flow in 1772, its persistent degassing often produces dangerously high concentrations of sulfur dioxide volcanic gas."
Sulfur dioxide is a potentially harmful volcanic gas released as magma approaches or remains near the surface. Even without a major eruption, elevated concentrations can create dangerous conditions for visitors and surrounding communities.
Young Cheol Kim, who completed his doctorate in geosciences at Penn State this summer, explained that monitoring the volcano continuously is essential for distinguishing normal activity from changes that might signal increasing volcanic hazards.
"Doing continuous monitoring allows us to understand the baseline activity and identify see if things are changing," he said, explaining that certain shifts in volcanic behavior could indicate a period of heightened activity or a possible eruption. "And then if there is a need to warn people, we can do that in a timely manner."
Satellites Reveal Hidden Movements Beneath the Volcano
To investigate Masaya's underground activity, the researchers analyzed measurements collected by the Sentinel-1 satellite, which observes the volcano approximately once every 12 days.
The team used a technique called interferometric synthetic aperture radar (InSAR), which can detect extremely small changes in the elevation of Earth's surface. By comparing satellite measurements taken at different times, scientists can identify areas where the ground is rising or sinking.
The technique combines two important capabilities. Synthetic aperture radar sends microwave signals toward Earth's surface, allowing satellites to collect measurements even when clouds obscure the ground. Interferometry compares the returning radar signals to detect changes in distance between the satellite and the surface.
This is especially valuable in tropical regions, where frequent cloud cover can make conventional satellite imagery less reliable.
"Cloud penetration is important for volcanoes because many of them, like Masaya, are in tropical areas where there is often cloud cover," Kim explained. "And when we look at all the different satellite images across multiple years, we can see how the distance between the satellite and the ground changes, where it is uplifting or subsiding."
By examining these subtle movements over time, researchers can investigate processes happening far below the surface without directly observing the magma itself.
Two Magma Reservoirs Behaving in Different Ways
The satellite measurements revealed an intriguing pattern between 2018 and 2024. During the first part of the study, the ground within Masaya's caldera gradually subsided, meaning it moved downward. Later, the same general area began to rise.
Scientists believe this transition could reflect changes in the amount of magma stored underground. When magma drains away from a reservoir, the overlying ground can sink. When additional magma enters and increases pressure within a reservoir, the surface may rise.
The most surprising finding was that the area surrounding Santiago crater did not follow the same pattern. Instead, it continued to sink throughout the six-year study, even as the broader caldera began rising.
"When it's subsiding, that means that there's probably magma draining away from the volcano, but once the ground starts uplifting again, that can mean that there's potentially new magma moving in," Johnson said. "At the same time, the area directly around the active Santiago crater deflated over the entire study period independently of the transition to inflation of the main reservoir. This indicates that the plumbing system is more complex and could be due to decreasing magma in a second, shallower reservoir."
Together, these observations suggest that Masaya may have at least two distinct parts of its magma storage system undergoing different changes. A deeper source could be supplying additional magma to the main reservoir, while a shallower reservoir near Santiago crater may be losing magma.
This would help explain why different sections of the same volcano moved in opposite directions.
What the Discovery Means for Future Eruptions
Understanding these underground movements is important because changes in the ground can provide clues about where magma is accumulating, where it is moving, and how it might eventually reach the surface.
The researchers emphasized that their observations did not reveal any immediate danger to communities surrounding Masaya. However, identifying the volcano's normal behavior and understanding its magma supply system could make it easier to recognize unusual changes in the future.
Continued satellite observations, combined with more detailed computer models, could also help scientists better understand the connections between underground magma reservoirs and volcanic activity at the surface.
"Further long-term geodetic and modeling studies will provide a more thorough understanding and allow for effective hazard monitoring and mitigation at Masaya and other lava-lake hosting basaltic volcanoes," Johnson said.
The findings may therefore have implications beyond Nicaragua, particularly for other active volcanoes that contain persistent lava lakes and complex underground magma systems.
From Undergraduate Research to Volcano Science
Johnson became involved in the project after attending a presentation by Christelle Wauthier, a Penn State professor of geosciences and computational sciences hub director at the university's Institute for Computational and Data Sciences.
She completed the research as part of her Schreyer's Honors College thesis, working alongside graduate researchers, including Kim, to analyze satellite measurements and develop her scientific skills.
"I appreciated learning how a research group works," said Johnson, who has recently started a doctoral program in Earth sciences at the University of Hawaii at Manoa, where she will continue studying volcanoes using seismic waves to image below the surface of Kilauea volcano. "I had never had any experience with research, so it was great to be able to join in the group meetings and get to hear about everybody's work. And learning coding was also useful as I continue with my Ph.D."
The research received support from the U.S. National Science Foundation through awards 1945417 and 2523375, along with computational resources provided by Penn State's Institute for Computational and Data Sciences. The authors are solely responsible for the findings and conclusions, which do not necessarily represent the views of the funding organizations.
Story Source:
