articles.title: Phóng to 400 lần bức họa "Mona Lisa" nổi tiếng, chuyên gia phát hiện 3 bí mật ẩn giấu
articles.text:
Là một trong những bức họa nổi tiếng nhất thế giới, "Mona Lisa" được cho là ẩn chứa nhiều bí mật không ngờ tới.
Với tài năng hội họa và những cống hiến của mình trong lĩnh vực khoa học, Leonardo da Vinci luôn được các học giả hiện đại gọi với biệt danh "đại diện hoàn hảo nhất của thời kỳ Phục hưng", là người toàn năng độc nhất vô nhị trong lịch sử loài người.
Leonardo da Vinci.
Trong những kiệt tác mà danh họa người Ý sáng tác, bức "Mona Lisa" có thể coi là một trong những tác phẩm đình đám nhất của ông và cho đến thời điểm hiện tại, nó vẫn là một kiệt tác vô giá.
Không chỉ nổi tiếng bởi kỹ thuật vẽ, nụ cười của nàng Mona Lisa trong bức họa cũng đã trở thành đối tượng nghiên cứu của nhiều chuyên gia bởi sự bí ẩn của nó. Trong mắt các học giả, nụ cười của Mona Lisa chứa đựng 83% hạnh phúc, 9% ghê tởm, 6% sợ hãi và 2% tức giận.
Nhưng ngoài sự bí ẩn của nó, sau khi sử dụng công nghệ cao để phóng đại bức tranh lên 400 lần,các nhà nghiên cứu cũng đã phát hiện ra ba bí mật đã bị che giấu trong bức họa suốt nhiều năm trời.
Bức tranh ẩn chứa nhiều bí mật ít ai biết.
Đầu tiên là bí mật ẩn dưới phần nền của bức tranh. Nếu chỉ nhìn bằng mắt thường, chúng ta chỉ có thể nhìn thấy cảnh núi sông phía sau nàng Mona Lisa. Nhưng sau khi phóng to, các nhà nghiên cứu cho rằng họ đã phát hiện hình dáng của 4 con vật ẩn sau là vượn, sư tử, trâu và rắn. Một họa sĩ tên Ron Picinello đã đưa ra suy đoán rằng 4 con vật ẩn trong bức tranh tượng trưng cho sự đố kỵ và cái ác. Đồng thời, bàn tay phải cong của Mona Lisa ám chỉ sự coi thường cái thiện hơn cái ác.
Điều bí ẩn thứ hai được phát hiện sau khi phóng to bức tranh là khuôn mặt ẩn của một phụ nữ đằng sau mặt của Mona Lisa. Do nằm ở vị trí đặc biệt và bị màu sắc bao phủ xung quanh nên chi tiết này rất khó có thể nhận ra. Các nhà nghiên cứu cho rằng, so với Mona Lisa, khuôn mặt này về tổng thể rất nhỏ. Sau khi so sánh, người ta nhận định rằng người phụ nữ này thực chất rất có thể mẹ của Da Vinci, bởi bà ấy trông rất giống Da Vinci.
Bức tranh tiết lộ bí mật khi được phóng to 400 lần.
Về bí mật thứ ba, có thể thấy nàng Mona Lisa trong bức tranh không có lông mày và lông mi. Khi phóng to bức tranh lên nhiều lần, người ta phát hiện có hai chữ cái trong mắt phải của Mona Lisa, có thể là LV, được cho là hai chữ cái viết tắt theo tên của Leonardo da Vinci.
Sau khi 3 bí mật này được đưa ra, rất nhiều cuộc tranh luận liên quan đến bức tranh đã nổ ra. Những giả thuyết này đã góp phần khiến cho bức tranh nhận được nhiều sự quan tâm hơn từ công chúng. Tuy nhiên, người duy nhất có thể kiểm chứng được những giả thuyết này chỉ có thể là Leonardo da Vinci mà thôi.

articles.title: Physicists create a bizarre new quantum state called a fractional fermi sea
articles.text:
Physicists create a bizarre new quantum state called a fractional fermi sea
- Date:
- October 18, 2026
- Source:
- University of Innsbruck
- Summary:
- Physicists have discovered a strange new state of quantum matter in which ultracold atoms defy familiar organizational rules, forming a highly excited yet surprisingly orderly configuration called a "fractional Fermi sea." The discovery challenges established quantum theories and hints at exotic quasiparticles that scientists have dubbed potential "super-Fermions."
- Share:
Physicists have uncovered a strange new form of quantum behavior in which particles organize themselves in ways that challenge established theories. Even more surprising, the particles maintain a remarkable hidden order despite being driven into an extremely energetic state.
In a study published in Physical Review Letters, researchers from the group led by Hanns-Christoph Nägerl, working with theoretical physicist Alvise Bastianello of the CNRS and Université Paris-Dauphine, describe how to engineer an exotic quantum state known as a "fractional Fermi sea."
The breakthrough involves pushing ultracold cesium atoms far beyond their normal conditions by repeatedly changing how strongly they attract or repel one another. Rather than simply becoming disordered, the particles rearrange themselves into an unusual configuration that behaves differently from the quantum systems scientists have traditionally studied.
The theoretical findings provide the foundation for recent experimental research conducted by Nägerl's team at the Department of Experimental Physics.
Pushing Quantum Particles Beyond Their Normal Limits
Under ordinary conditions, quantum particles follow well-established rules that determine how they arrange themselves, particularly at extremely low temperatures.
One important example involves fermions, a category of particles that includes electrons. These particles cannot all occupy the same quantum state, so they fill available energy levels according to specific restrictions. At very low temperatures, this arrangement produces what physicists call a Fermi sea.
But what happens when researchers deliberately disrupt the conditions that normally govern how particles behave?
As Alvise Bastianello explains: "Fermions, for instance, stack neatly into the available energy states to form the so-called 'Fermi sea'. But what happens if one forces interacting atoms to continuously cycle through extreme conditions, smoothly shifting them from strongly repelling each other to strongly attracting each other?"
To investigate this possibility, the researchers studied ultracold cesium atoms confined to a one-dimensional system. This means the atoms are restricted to moving along a single direction, creating an environment in which their quantum interactions can be studied with exceptional control.
The team examined what happens when the interactions between these atoms are repeatedly adjusted, cycling between powerful repulsion and attraction.
Their calculations revealed something unexpected. Starting from the ground state, the lowest energy configuration available to the system, the atoms could be driven into a highly excited state without losing their underlying organization.
The researchers call this unusual arrangement a fractional Fermi sea because its particles appear to obey a modified rule governing how quantum states are occupied.
"Instead of simply heating the system, the interaction cycle reorganizes the atoms into a new many-body state," says Yi Zeng, the leading author of this study. "This gives us a controlled way to explore quantum matter beyond the usual equilibrium paradigms."
A Strange New Quantum State With Hidden Order
One of the most intriguing features of the fractional Fermi sea is that its particles remain organized even though the system has been pushed far from equilibrium.
In physics, equilibrium describes a condition in which a system's overall properties have settled into a stable balance. Systems driven far from equilibrium can behave in complicated and unexpected ways, making them particularly challenging to understand.
Yet the fractional Fermi sea is not simply a collection of excited particles behaving randomly. Instead, it contains distinctive mathematical patterns that reveal a deeper structure.
Among these patterns are pronounced ripples called Friedel oscillations. These are wave-like variations associated with the way quantum particles influence one another. The researchers also identified unusual patterns in how correlations between particles weaken with increasing distance, even when the repulsive interactions are relatively weak.
These signatures are important because they differ from predictions associated with Tomonaga-Luttinger liquid theory, a long-established framework for describing how interacting quantum particles behave in one-dimensional systems.
The findings therefore point toward a previously unexplored type of quantum behavior that cannot be fully described using this familiar theoretical picture.
"This state is highly excited, but it is not random," says Hanns-Christoph Nägerl, the group leader. "It has a hidden order that becomes visible in its correlations."
The strange behavior also raises questions about the effective particles that emerge within the system. Physicists call these collective excitations quasiparticles because they can behave like individual particles even though they arise from the coordinated motion of many interacting particles.
Nägerl suggests that the unusual excitations might eventually deserve a name of their own.
"We are not yet sure how we should name these new quasiparticles. Perhaps 'super-Fermions'?"
Opening a New Frontier in Quantum Physics
The discovery suggests that fractional Fermi seas represent an exotic critical phase of quantum matter, with characteristic patterns of particle correlations that extend beyond existing descriptions of one-dimensional quantum systems.
It also demonstrates the growing power of quantum simulation, a technique that allows scientists to use carefully controlled quantum systems to investigate physical behavior that would otherwise be difficult to reproduce or study.
Ultracold atoms are particularly useful for this purpose because researchers can precisely adjust their interactions and observe how the resulting quantum states change.
Rather than limiting these experiments to recreating phenomena already understood through established theories, scientists can now explore deliberately engineered states that reveal entirely new possibilities.
As Hanns-Christoph Nägerl says: "The discovery of fractional Fermi seas shows how far we can push quantum simulation: not only reproducing known models, but creating and probing states that go beyond established paradigms."
The current publication establishes the theoretical framework for fractional Fermi seas. A companion study describing their experimental realization through quantum simulation is undergoing peer review.
Together, the research points toward new ways of investigating the fundamental behavior of quantum matter, including unusual collective excitations and hidden forms of order that emerge only when particles are pushed far outside their normal conditions.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Innsbruck. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal References:
- Alvise Bastianello, Yi Zeng, Sudipta Dhar, Zekui Wang, Xudong Yu, Milena Horvath, Grigori E. Astrakharchik, Yanliang Guo, Hanns-Christoph Nägerl, Manuele Landini. Exotic Critical States as Fractional Fermi Seas in the One-Dimensional Bose Gas. Physical Review Letters, 2026; 136 (23) DOI: 10.1103/j3s5-gjpf
- Yi Zeng, Alvise Bastianello, Sudipta Dhar, Zekui Wang, Xudong Yu, Milena Horvath, Grigori E. Astrakharchik, Yanliang Guo, Hanns-Christoph Nägerl, Manuele Landini. Realization of fractional Fermi seas. arXiv, 19 May 2026 DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2602.17657

articles.title: World's first round-trip mission to Mars has launched — and could be a 'transformative leap' for science
articles.text:
World's first round-trip mission to Mars has launched — why it could be a 'transformative leap' for science
The Martian Moons Exploration (MMX) mission, which launched from Japan on Oct. 19, is on its way to Mars. When it arrives, the probe will attempt to land on one of the Red Planet's twin moons and scoop up rocks to bring back to Earth. Experts tell Live Science what these "transformative" samples could teach us.
On Monday (Oct. 19), Japan's space agency launched a first-of-its-kind sample-return mission to Mars. The historic endeavor marks another major step toward humanity's shared goal of understanding — and perhaps eventually colonizing — one of our closest planetary neighbors, experts say.
The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency's (JAXA) Martian Moons Exploration (MMX) probe is an international effort, constructed with help from NASA, the European Space Agency (ESA) and others. Over the next few years, it will closely study the Red Planet's twin moons, Phobos and Deimos. The spacecraft will snap close-up photos of the pair before attempting to land on the larger satellite, Phobos, to scoop up rocky material that will hopefully be carried back to Earth in around five years.
If the mission is successful, the returned samples will finally settle a decades-old mystery about the origins of both moons. The findings could also help paint a picture of Mars' ancient history and provide clues about what the early solar system was like.
"This mission marks a transformative leap in our capacity to investigate the Martian system," Sonia Fornasier, an astronomer at the Paris Observatory who has studied Phobos and Deimos extensively and is a project scientist for MMX's infrared spectrometer instrument (MIRS), told Live Science. It "ranks very high" among the missions we have sent to the Red Planet so far, she added.
What will MMX do?
JAXA launched the MMX probe on board an H3 rocket, which lifted off from Tanegashima Space Center in Kagoshima prefecture at 3:41 p.m. EDT Monday (4:41 a.m. Tuesday local time), Live Science's sister site Space.com reported. (The mission was initially scheduled to launch in 2024, but it was delayed due to initial concerns about the H3 rocket.)
The camper-van-sized spacecraft successfully separated from the rocket's fairing just over an hour later, and on Wednesday (Oct. 21), JAXA announced that the mission had passed the "initial critical operations phase," meaning the probe is now locked into its roughly 140 million-mile-long (225 million kilometers) journey to Mars, which will take around 10 months.
"MMX took its first step today," Naoki Murakami, general manager of Mitsubishi Electric’s space division, which led the design of the MMX probe, said in a postlaunch news conference early Tuesday morning (Oct. 20), according to The Japan Times. "This marks the beginning of a long, five-year journey."
Once the probe arrives at the Red Planet in August 2027, it will insert itself into a "quasi-satellite orbit" around Phobos. In other words, MMX will circle Mars alongside the moon but will not be gravitationally bound to it, similar to around half a dozen "quasi-moons" that currently accompany Earth around the sun.
After collecting data from a distance for a few months, MMX will swoop down and attempt to land on the surface of Phobos — not once, but twice.
During the first landing, MMX will hover just above the moon and deploy a mini rover, dubbed Idefix, onto the moon's surface. The wandering robot, built by the French and German space agencies, will have to contend with extremely weak gravity as it trundles across the surface of Phobos: The rover weighs around 55 pounds (25 kilograms) on Earth but will weigh only around half an ounce (15 grams) on Phobos, according to ESA.
Once Idefix has completed its initial assessment of the moon's surface, the entire MMX probe will set down on Phobos, on top of the spacecraft's four-legged lander module. Mission scientists hope this goes a lot more smoothly than the attempted landings of Japan's "Moon Sniper" and Resilience lunar landers, which crash-landed on Earth's moon in 2024 and 2025, respectively.
Two of the MMX lander's legs contain built-in sampling devices — one that will drill into Phobos and another that will hoover up surface material. The second device, dubbed the Pneumatic Sampler (or P-Sampler), was built by the Blue Origin-owned private company Honeybee Robotics on behalf of NASA and will collect its material in a "matter of seconds," Kris Zacny, vice president of the Exploration Technology Group at Honeybee Robotics, said at an Oct. 15 NASA news conference. "You blink, and it's all done."
In total, JAXA aims to collect around a third of an ounce (10 grams) of material from Phobos. That would be around twice as much material as the space agency managed to snag on its most recent sample-return mission, Hayabusa2, which collected samples from the "spinning-top" asteroid Ryugu in 2019, finding materials rich in surprising organic compounds.
Once the samples have been acquired, at some point between late 2028 and early 2029, the probe will conduct a series of close flybys of Mars' smaller moon, Deimos, before beginning the long trip back to Earth in late 2030 — the first return flight ever attempted by a spacecraft sent to Mars.
When the probe returns to Earth in 2031, it will release its samples in a 20-inch-wide (60 centimeters) container that will fall back to our planet's surface, most likely somewhere in Australia, according to ESA.
What could we learn about Phobos and Deimos?
Mars' twin satellites, which were first spotted by American astronomer Asaph Hall in 1877, are nothing like Earth's constant companion. For starters, they are much smaller; Phobos is around 14 miles (22 km) across, while Deimos is just 7.5 miles (12 km) wide. The duo also have lopsided shapes and are between 12 and 64 times closer to Mars than the moon is to Earth. (Phobos, meaning "fear," and Deimos, meaning "terror," are named after the sons of the Greek war god Ares, the counterpart to the Roman war god Mars.)
Phobos is dominated by the 6-mile-wide (10 km) Stickney crater, which was left by an ancient asteroid impact. The larger moon is also slowly falling toward Mars and may eventually be ripped apart before it reaches the Red Planet's surface.
Other Martian spacecraft, such as the Emirates Mars Mission orbiter, have flown close to the moons, and NASA's Mars rovers have frequently looked up to see the satellites eclipsing the sun in Mars' sky (sometimes both at the same time). Yet many mysteries remain about the pair.
"Mars is right in our cosmic backyard, and yet we haven't explored the planet's moons," Nancy Chabot, a space exploration expert at the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory in Maryland and the deputy principal investigator of NASA's MEGANE instrument on board MMX, told Live Science in an email. "MMX will do this!"
The biggest mystery surrounding Phobos and Deimos is their origin. Some researchers suspect the satellites are asteroids, or maybe even comets, that have been captured by Mars' gravity, while others think the moons emerged from the debris of an ancient impact on the planet's surface, similar to how Earth's moon formed.
EXCLUSIVE TO LIVE SCIENCE PRO
- A secretive Chinese probe has just arrived at one of Earth's 'quasi-moons' and will soon attempt a first-of-its-kind landing
- 'We're not a competitor to fusion. We are fusion': Inside the race to harness unlimited solar power in space
- 'Is having two legs useful' in space?: Astronaut explains what life in orbit might be like for the first physically disabled person in space
Neither theory is conclusive, meaning the moons' origins "remain enigmatic," Christopher Edwards, a planetary scientist at Northern Arizona University and one of NASA's participating scientists for MMX, told Live Science.
For example, explaining how Mars captured the moons is "quite hard from an orbital mechanics perspective," but if they did form from a debris disk from an ancient impact, they should have coalesced into better-defined spheres, Edwards said.
"MMX will solve this debate thanks to the spacecraft observations and the detailed analysis of the samples of Phobos on Earth," Fornasier said. The data the probe collects from its flybys of Deimos will also allow researchers to generate a "full characterization of this body," she added.
Fornasier is "particularly excited" by the possibility that the moons are captured asteroids because that would mean they would likely contain "organic and hydrated materials," which would have a big "astrobiological implication" and would shed light on what the early solar system was like.
What could we learn about Mars itself?
Regardless of how the twin moons formed, researchers also stand to learn a lot about Mars and how planets form and evolve.
"Phobos and Deimos are interesting, but not just in their own right," Tom Statler, an MMX program executive and scientist in NASA's Planetary Science Division, said at the Oct. 15 news conference. "Their presence is a key piece of the larger story of the Mars system. By uncovering the moons' origin, we'll gain new insights into the history of both Mars and Earth."
If the moons did form via an impact scenario, the samples MMX collects may also contain actual pieces of Mars for researchers to study.
"If these objects are in fact pieces from the Martian surface that have coalesced moons, we'll collect the best-preserved samples of the Martian surface," Edwards said. Other fragments of Mars have already reached Earth as meteorites. However, entry into Earth's atmosphere can transform them.
If Phobos is a chunk of Mars, that would be a real boon to NASA, which canceled its Mars Sample Return program — a mission that would have retrieved samples collected by the Perseverance rover — earlier this year. The agency's researchers will receive up to 15% of the MMX samples to analyze.
During its three-year stay in the Red Planet's system, the Japanese probe will also collect lots of data on Mars that could contribute to a wide range of future findings. "MMX will conduct in-depth studies of the Martian atmosphere, with a particular emphasis on dust and water transport mechanisms and the escape processes shaping Mars' atmospheric dynamics," Fornasier said.
This atmospheric data could temporarily fill a gap left by the recent death of NASA's iconic MAVEN spacecraft, which stopped sending data back to Earth late last year.
Analysis of craters on the Martian moons could also provide clues about other events in Mars' history. For example, some researchers think the Red Planet may have once had rings like Saturn or a larger moon.
Other experts are hopeful that the MMX findings could help lay the groundwork for future missions to explore — and perhaps colonize — Mars. "The samples from MMX will bring forth paradigm-shifting science on the Mars system for generations to come, especially as NASA prepares to send the first humans to Mars," Nicky Fox, associate administrator for NASA's Science Mission Directorate, said in a recent statement.
The next sample-return trip to Mars will be China's Tianwen-3 mission, which is scheduled to launch in 2028 and will aim to land on and retrieve samples directly from the Red Planet's surface, according to Space.com.
Harry is a U.K.-based senior staff writer at Live Science. He studied marine biology at the University of Exeter before training to become a journalist. He covers a wide range of topics including space exploration, planetary science, space weather, climate change, animal behavior and paleontology. His recent work on the solar maximum won "best space submission" at the 2024 Aerospace Media Awards and was shortlisted in the "top scoop" category at the NCTJ Awards for Excellence in 2023. He also writes Live Science's weekly Earth from space series.

articles.title: Bát diện 12 mặt đồng: Bí ẩn lịch sử một nền văn minh
articles.text:
Những bí mật đối với nền văn minh La Mã cổ đại là điều mà có dành cả đời nghiên cứu kỹ lưỡng cũng không tiết lộ hết.
Một trong những thứ đó là khối đa diện La Mã. Đó là một vật thể rỗng bằng đồng có hình dạng bát diện gồm mười hai mặt ngũ giác phẳng. Sự hiện diện của nó ở trung tâm châu Âu không cho thấy mục đích nào của nó. Nhưng có một vài giả thuyết đã được đặt ra kể từ lần khám phá đầu tiên cách đây hơn 300 năm.
Các mẫu bát diện 12 mặt với các mẫu hoa và kích cỡ không giống nhau. (Ảnh: Amusingplanet)
Khối đa diện đầu tiên được phát hiện vào năm 1739 bởi một nhà sử học địa phương ở Aston, Hertfordshire dọc theo vùng nông thôn nước Anh. Trong báo cáo của mình với Hiệp hội Cổ vật, ông mô tả vật thể này là “một mảnh kim loại hỗn hợp, hoặc đồng thau cổ đại, bao gồm 12 mặt bằng nhau”. Khám phá kỳ lạ khiến tất cả những nhà nghiên cứu cổ đại đều phải bất ngờ, nhưng vẫn còn nhiều thứ đang đến với họ.
Mỗi vật thể được phát hiện sau đó đều có kích thước và cấu tạo khác nhau. Hầu hết các khối tứ diện đều có kích thước từ 4 đến 11 cm và trọng lượng từ 35 đến 580 gram. Mỗi bề mặt hình ngũ giác đều chứa một lỗ, nhưng kích thước của những lỗ này hầu như luôn khác nhau- trong một khối tứ diện duy nhất cũng như giữa các khối khác nhau. Mỗi đỉnh trong số năm đỉnh có một núm hình cầu. Nhỏ hơn một quả bóng tennis, vật thể này có vẻ giống một viên xúc xắc hơn.
Đến năm 2016, 116 mảnh ghép khối đã được khai quật khắp nơi ở Bỉ, Croatia, Pháp, Đức, Anh, Hungary, Luxemburg, Hà Lan và Thụy Sĩ ngày nay. Một mẫu duy nhất làm bằng bạc đã được tìm thấy ở Geneva. Điều thú vị là không có khối mười diện nào tồn tại ở phía đông đế chế La Mã theo như dự đoán. Những thứ được tìm thấy ở khu vực phía Tây có niên đại từ thế kỷ thứ hai, thứ ba và thứ tư sau Công nguyên. Sự ngẫu nhiên của các vị trí cũng như thiếu tư liệu đã khiến các nhà sử học bối rối thêm.
Năm 1987, một người đàn ông tên Brian Campbell đã phát hiện ra một khối tứ diện trong sân nhà của mình. Những khối khác được đào lên trong các trại quân sự La Mã, đền thờ và nhà tắm công cộng. Một số xuất hiện trong nhà hát và lăng mộ, một số nằm trong đống tiền xu bị bỏ đi.
Các khối bát diện khác nhau về hình dạng, hoa văn, nơi tìm thấy khiến cho việc giải đáp rơi vào bế tắc. (Ảnh: Internet)
Nhiều nhà sử học cũng tìm thấy những đồ vật này trong các cửa hàng đồ cổ, điều này khiến việc truy xuất nguồn gốc của chúng trở nên khó khăn. Hầu hết được trang trí bằng các thiết kế và hoa văn, nhưng không bao giờ là chữ cái hoặc số có thể cho chúng ta biết việc sử dụng chúng. Chỉ có hai khối mười hai mặt được tìm thấy trong các cuộc khai quật khoa học có kiểm soát. Một trong những địa điểm này có thể là một cửa hàng bán đồ kim loại quý, xác nhận khả năng vật thể lạ là vật quý.
Hơn 200 nhà sử học đã đề xuất hơn 50 cách sử dụng có thể có của khối tứ diện La Mã. Khối mười hai mặt chủ yếu xuất hiện ở vùng đất Gallo-La Mã nơi nền văn minh La Mã phủ lên nền văn minh Celtic. Trong bối cảnh đó, 12 mặt của ngũ giác có thể có sự liên quan đến vũ trụ. Có thể chúng đã được sử dụng để tính toán thiên văn với mặt trời chiếu qua các lỗ vào các thời điểm khác nhau trong ngày. Nhà nghiên cứu người Hà Lan Sjra Wagemans đã so sánh nó với khối icosahedron - một khối đa diện lồi 20 mặt - phục vụ mục đích tương tự. G.M.C. Wagemans đã chứng minh thông qua các ước tính khác nhau rằng một số khối hình khối có thể được sử dụng để xác định thời điểm tốt nhất để gieo hạt mùa đông ở Bắc Âu.
Giả thiết cuối cùng vẫn là vật thể thiêng liêng và quan trọng đối với việc thực hành tôn giáo. Khối mười hai mặt được tìm thấy trong Hang động Idaean (Crete) được làm bằng tinh thể đá, và trên mười hai mặt của nó đã tìm thấy các ký tự Hy Lạp thay vì lỗ. Một số người có gợi ý rằng vật thể rỗng nhỏ bé được đeo như một chiếc bùa hộ mệnh hoặc được mang theo trong ví.
Các khối bát diện 12 mặt vẫn là dấu chấm hỏi lớn cho các nhà cổ vật về một nền văn minh. (Ảnh: Amusingplanet)
Mặc dù chúng ta có kho tàng kiến thức, những nhà nghiên cứu hiện đại vẫn gặp khó khăn trong việc xác định công dụng và sự nổi bật của cổ vật 2.000 năm tuổi này. Có thể, một lúc nào đó, một sự nghiên cứu sâu hơn sẽ tiết lộ những bí mật của quả bóng nhỏ đã trở thành một trong những bí ẩn lớn nhất của ngành khảo cổ học này.

articles.title: Eating blueberries every day may have a surprising effect on your mood
articles.text:
Eating blueberries every day may have a surprising effect on your mood
A new study hints that eating blueberries daily could help improve mood in older adults, potentially through surprising effects on the gut microbiome.
- Date:
- October 18, 2026
- Source:
- Hebrew SeniorLife Hinda and Arthur Marcus Institute for Aging Research
- Summary:
- Eating blueberries every day could have surprising effects on mood, according to a small study that found greater reductions in depressive symptoms among older adults who consumed the fruit for three months. Researchers also detected changes in gut microbial enzymes, suggesting a possible gut-brain connection, although the mood benefits were not statistically significant compared with a placebo.
- Share:
A small pilot study suggests that eating blueberries every day may influence gut bacteria and potentially affect mood in older adults. Participants who consumed blueberries regularly experienced a greater and more consistent reduction in depressive symptoms, along with subtle changes in genes associated with gut microbial enzymes.
However, the improvements in depressive symptoms were not statistically significant when compared with the placebo group. Although the findings do not establish that blueberries can relieve depression, they offer preliminary clues about a possible connection between blueberry consumption, the gut microbiome, and mental health.
"Fiber and anthocyanins in blueberries have potential to modify the gut microbiome and metabolites that are relevant to depression in older adults," said lead author Courtney L. Millar, PhD, assistant scientist II at Hebrew SeniorLife's Hinda and Arthur Marcus Institute for Aging Research and assistant professor of medicine at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Harvard Medical School. "Our objective was to preliminarily determine the effect of blueberry consumption on the gut microbiome, metabolites, and depressive symptoms."
Testing the Effects of Daily Blueberry Consumption
To investigate the potential connection, researchers recruited adults aged 65 and older who were physically inactive and experiencing mild depressive symptoms. The pilot study used a randomized, double-blind, parallel-arm, placebo-controlled design to evaluate whether consuming blueberries could influence gut microbes and mood.
Over three months, participants consumed either 48 grams of blueberry powder each day (approximately two cups of fresh berries) or a matching placebo powder.
Researchers examined the participants' gut microbiomes using metagenomic sequencing, which allowed them to measure the abundance of different microbial species and genes. They also used liquid chromatography/mass spectrometry to analyze gut-derived fecal short-chain fatty acids, compounds produced through microbial activity. Depressive symptoms were assessed using validated questionnaires administered before and after the three-month intervention.
Blueberries Linked to Subtle Changes in Gut Microbial Activity
A total of 18 participants completed the study. Most were women, and the group was predominantly white (placebo group, n = 8; mean age: 75 ± 6; blueberry group, n = 10; mean age: 71 ± 4).
Despite the encouraging pattern in depressive symptoms among participants consuming blueberries, the researchers found no statistically significant difference in mood improvements between the blueberry and placebo groups.
The gut microbiome results also revealed a mixed picture. The overall abundance of microbial species, MetaCyc metabolic pathways, and short-chain fatty acid metabolites remained unchanged.
However, researchers identified statistically significant changes within the blueberry group in the abundance of genes associated with several gut microbial enzymes. One of these was EC 3.6.3.31 Polyamine Transporting ATPase, which is involved in the production of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), a neurotransmitter that plays a role in brain signaling.
These findings suggest that blueberries may influence specific aspects of gut microbial function even without producing measurable changes in the overall composition of the microbiome. Larger studies will be needed to determine whether these changes are connected to meaningful improvements in mood or depressive symptoms.
The study, "A pilot study of daily blueberry intake modulates the gut microbiota enzyme commissions in older, sedentary adults with mild depressive symptoms," was published in the Journal of Nutrition, Health and Aging.
Other contributors included Mohit P. Chopra, MD, of the Deanna and Sidney Wolk Center for Memory Health at Hebrew SeniorLife and the Department of Psychiatry at UMass Chan Medical School; Xochitl Morgan, PhD, and Emily A. Green, PhD, of the Department of Biostatistics at Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health; Alex Wolfe of the Hinda and Arthur Marcus Institute for Aging Research at Hebrew SeniorLife; Kerry A. Pierce of the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard; and Lidan Gao, PhD, and Christopher N. Blesso, PhD, of the Department of Nutritional Sciences at the University of Connecticut.
Additional contributors were Alyssa B. Dufour, PhD, of the Hinda and Arthur Marcus Institute for Aging Research at Hebrew SeniorLife and the Department of Medicine at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Harvard Medical School; Douglas P. Kiel, MD, MPH, of the Hinda and Arthur Marcus Institute for Aging Research at Hebrew SeniorLife, Harvard Medical School, and Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center; and Lewis A. Lipsitz, MD, of the Hinda and Arthur Marcus Institute for Aging Research at Hebrew SeniorLife and professor of medicine at Harvard Medical School.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Hebrew SeniorLife Hinda and Arthur Marcus Institute for Aging Research. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Courtney L. Millar, Mohit P. Chopra, Xochitl Morgan, Emily A. Green, Alex Wolfe, Kerry A. Pierce, Lidan Gao, Christopher N. Blesso, Alyssa B. Dufour, Douglas P. Kiel, Lewis A. Lipsitz. A pilot study of daily blueberry intake modulates the gut microbiota enzyme commissions in older, sedentary adults with mild depressive symptoms. The Journal of nutrition, health and aging, 2026; 30 (10): 100958 DOI: 10.1016/j.jnha.2026.100958

articles.title: Will plants survive climate change? The 'Great Dying' reveals clues about their resilience.
articles.text:
Will plants survive climate change? The 'Great Dying' reveals clues about their resilience.
Plants can't easily pick up and move when environmental conditions get rough, so they've evolved strategies to weather harsh conditions in place. That could help some plants survive in the face of a warming climate.
About 251 million years ago, volcanic eruptions wiped out most life on Earth. For about a million years, the Siberian Traps in Russia spewed huge clouds of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere, leading to the most severe extinction event in our planet's history.
Equatorial temperatures spiked, making much of the land too hot for life. Meanwhile, the oceans became acidic and most of the creatures in them suffocated from lack of oxygen. Known as the Permian-Triassic mass extinction or the "Great Dying," it ultimately destroyed more than 90% of ocean life and 70% of terrestrial species.
However, in a corner of what is now China, a refuge of pollen-producing plants avoided that fate and created an oasis for surviving animals. Research suggests that this was not the only place where plants were able to weather catastrophic climate change during the Great Dying, and that plants may have been better able to withstand the extinction event than other organisms.
"Plants do indeed sometimes have a lot of resilience because they can't move individually, and even as a population, they're not very good at moving," Chris Thomas, an ecologist and evolutionary biologist at the University of York in the U.K., told Live Science. As a result, many plants have evolved mechanisms to survive in place despite difficult conditions, he said.
As climate change raises global temperatures and throws ecosystems into upheaval, plants will need to draw once more upon this resilience. Many plant species have evolved unique adaptations that help them weather harsh conditions. Experts told Live Science that these adaptations — along with a hefty dose of luck — will now decide the difference between survival and extinction.
Growing with the flow
Unlike most animals, many plants have the ability to regenerate limbs — and those limbs can make them better able to adapt to new environment conditions. Plants in general have higher developmental plasticity than animals, which means that they have greater flexibility to change how their cells and tissues grow and develop.
"Many plants have what we call indeterminate growth and modular body plans," Amy Angert, a botanist at the University of British Columbia in Canada, told Live Science. Indeterminate growth means that an organism continues to grow and develop indefinitely throughout its lifespan.
"If we lost an arm, it would be gone forever. But on plants, if you cut off a branch, they can sprout new ones and those new ones can then receive signals from the current environment instead of being stuck with sort of developmental programs from the past environment."
For example, researchers found that resprouts on holm oak trees (Quercus ilex) are better able to cope with drought than those that had not resprouted.
And because buds can go dormant, many plant species can resprout after catastrophic events, such as fire. Cape Floristic Region in South Africa, for example, is the smallest of the world's six recognized floral kingdoms, and most of its plant species depend on fire — its plants resprout after fire and many of their seeds require fire to germinate.
Some plants, such as the Snow Gum (Eucalyptus pauciflora), have a thick layer of insulating bark to protect their buds, while others like stinging nettles (Urtica dioica) bury them underground in a "bud bank". The soil insulates the seed's buds from extreme heat and cold and protects most of the plant from life-threatening conditions. This widespread adaptation allows herbaceous plants to endure through the winter and plants with bulbs to hide their tissues from the ravages of fire.
Storing seeds for better times
Plants can also store seeds underground when times are difficult. Almost 350,000 plant species produce seeds. For most of these species, the seeds contain dormant tiny versions of the young plant, with all the structures that will turn into leaves and roots.
"Seeds can live essentially in stasis in the soil," Daniel Anstett, an evolutionary ecologist at Cornell University, told Live Science. "You can have the seed bank where certain seeds might come back, and there's access to the backward library of genetic information that many plants can ultimately draw upon."
Seed banks are a vital tool for resilience in many plant species. They create the opportunity for metabolically inactive individuals to reanimate when environmental conditions improve, according to a 2021 paper published in the journal Nature Communications. "When lucky, at least some of these individuals will awaken in the future when the environment is more conducive for growth and reproduction," the authors wrote.
Rapid evolution
Seedbanks can also be reservoirs of genetic diversity, which is integral to being able to adapt to new environments.
"The raw material for adaptation comes from genetic variation," said Angert. "Genetic variation is larger in large populations, and genetic variation can be shared between populations as the environment changes — if individuals can disperse successfully between them."
In a paper published in journal Science earlier this year, researchers, including Angert and Anstett, showed rapid evolution saved scarlet monkey flower (Erythranthe cardinalis) populations from prolonged drought in the U.S. and Mexico between 2010 and 2018.
"They can either grow really fast, flower and put out seeds before the fall drought takes effect, or they can grow much more slowly and bunker down,” Anstett explained.
The researchers sequenced the genomes of 55 scarlet monkeyflower populations to find areas within their genomes linked to coping with stress and drought. They tracked the populations and how they changed over the period. Some populations experienced rapid evolution to cope with the changing environment.
They found that, based on populations’ genetic diversity, they could predict whether a population would be able to survive the drought — even before it started.
While this is only one plant species, Anstett believes it could be true of other organisms too.
Flexible photosynthesis
Some plants are able to transform how they produce energy to endure a changing environment. This is what Zhen Xu, a paleobotanist at the University of Leeds in the U.K, thinks allowed some plant species to survive the Permian-Triassic mass extinction and might become increasingly important for plants in today's changing climate.
Plants use photosynthesis to convert carbon dioxide and water into sugars and oxygen, and use stomata, or small pores on their leaf surface, to regulate the amount of carbon dioxide entering the plant.
Many plants open their stomata during the day to let in CO2 and release oxygen. Others use CAM photosynthesis, which stands for "Crassulacean acid metabolism," to close their stomata during the day and protect themselves from the heat. At night, they absorb CO2 and transform it into an acid, which they store in their tissues to be used to make sugars during the day.
"CAM photosynthesis is very common in present day desert plants, like the cactus and succulents," Xu told Live Science. "It's a very smart way to escape from the high temperature or aridity during the daytime."
In a study published in journal Nature Ecology & Evolution earlier this year, Xu and colleagues showed that plants that used CAM photosynthesis had an advantage during the Permian-Triassic mass extinction.
They found that Lycophytes, or are ancient vascular plants, switched to CAM photosynthesis around the time of the mass extinction. "We think CAM photosynthesis may be the special strategy to survive" and allowed these plants to dominate after the mass extinction, Xu said.
Hopeful monsters
Some plants go to even more extreme lengths. During cataclysmic events, plants have turned into "hopeful monsters" to survive environmental upheaval, past research shows.
In nine separate events over the past 150 million years, many flowering plants duplicated their whole genome to give themselves a better chance of survival, according to research published in journal Cell earlier this year. The duplicate genome gives them more opportunities to evolve and adapt to challenging environmental conditions.
"We see clusterings of whole genome duplications in time, and every time it corresponds with a described, important geological event, whether it's a global cooling period, whether it's a global warming period, or whether there's an extinction event," study co-author Yves Van de Peer, a genome biologist at Ghent University in Belgium, told Live Science at the time.
Boils down to luck
Still, the survival of specific plant populations or species often boils down to luck, experts told Live Science.
Plants "essentially have this broad toolkit" but "some of the plants have some pathways, and other plants have others, and some have some traits, and some have others", Anstett said. Whether the particular tools they have will help depends on the conditions they face.
During the Triassic-Permian mass extinction, the plants in refugia in China (and elsewhere) were in the right place at the right time, with the right suite of potential adaptations at their disposal and enough genetic variety to tap into them.
Exclusive to Live Science Pro
- 'The apple you eat isn't the apple your granddaughter will eat': What's on the menu in a warming world?
- 'If there's any country that will do it, it's China': Why is China diverting some of the world's mightiest rivers thousands of miles?
- A looming 'insect apocalypse' could endanger global food supplies. Can we stop it before it's too late?
The same holds true for modern-day species facing a changing climate and potential extinction. Angert said there are ways to make plant species "luckier" in the years ahead, such as connecting fragmented populations to increase genetic diversity, which increases the suite of potential tools at a plant species' disposal.
"The best thing we could do is to leave larger and better connected populations on the landscape," she said.
Anstett agreed. "If populations become really disconnected, then potentially we're eroding away whatever toolkit that these plants have to be able to adapt."

Sarah Wild is a British-South African freelance science journalist. She has written about particle physics, cosmology and everything in between. She studied physics, electronics and English literature at Rhodes University, South Africa, and later read for an MSc Medicine in bioethics.
Since she started perpetrating journalism for a living, she's written books, won awards, and run national science desks. Her work has appeared in Nature, Science, Scientific American, and The Observer, among others. In 2017 she won a gold AAAS Kavli for her reporting on forensics in South Africa.

articles.title: Ngọn lửa "địa ngục": Cháy được 4000 năm và không hề có dấu hiệu sẽ ngừng lại
articles.text:
Cho dù là trong mưa gió hay tuyết đổ, những lưỡi lửa của Yanar Dag vẫn nhảy nhót trên sườn đồi của bán đảo Absheron. Đêm xuống, nó tỏa rạng cả một vùng. Mùa đông, những bông tuyết chưa kịp rơi xuống đã vội bốc hơi, tan biến ngay trên không trung.
Azerbaijan là một quốc gia nằm ngay trên ngã tư giữa Đông Âu và Tây Á. Còn bán đảo Absheron thì lừng danh là nơi sản xuất xăng dầu sớm nhất thế giới. Kể từ thập niên 1870, nơi này đã tiến hành chưng cất dầu thô hàng loạt.
Bán đảo Absheron.
Ngoài dầu mỏ, Absheron còn giàu vôi, cát, muối. Nhờ đó mà dù khí hậu khô hạn (lượng mưa dưới cả 200mm/năm) còn đất đai thì cằn cỗi, bán đảo này vẫn hình thành nên Baku, thành phố lớn nhất và đông dân nhất Azerbaijan.
Và chính tại bán đảo này, chúng ta có câu chuyện về một ngọn lửa không bao giờ tắt, và đó là nghĩa đen 100%.
Từ Baku sầm uất tiến theo hướng Bắc khoảng nửa giờ lái xe, trước mắt bạn sẽ là một sườn núi đang bốc cháy. Nó được gọi tên là Yanar Dag, có nghĩa là "ngọn núi đang cháy".
Đúng như cái tên, Yanar Dag đã cháy liên tục được cả 4000 năm và sẽ không bao giờ dừng lại. Bất chấp mưa gió bão bùng hay tuyết rơi giá buốt, những lưỡi lửa của nó vẫn thi nhau nhảy nhót trên một vạt đồi thấp.
Ngọn lửa được gọi tên là Yanar Dag, có nghĩa là "ngọn núi đang cháy".
Từ các lỗ hổng của những phiến sa thạch bao quanh khoảng 10m của sườn đồi này, lửa chui ra, dữ dội bốc cao cả mét và cháy không ngừng nghỉ. Nó khiến cho sườn núi vốn đã nực nội lại càng ngột ngạt hơn.
Sở dĩ Yanar Dag có thể cháy vĩnh viễn là bởi vì Absheron vốn dồi dào trữ lượng khí đốt thiên nhiên. Bên dưới mặt đất nơi Yanar Dag ngùn ngụt bốc lửa là một dòng khí đốt cực kỳ bền bỉ. Trừ khi dòng gas này bị cắt, Yanar Dag sẽ không bao giờ bị dập tắt.
Thực tế thì Yanar Dag giàu khí tự nhiên đến nỗi ngay cả trên bề mặt của các dòng suối ở xung quanh nó cũng tràn ngập thứ khí đốt này. Chỉ cần lấy một que diêm ra đánh lửa là bạn có thể đốt cháy bầu không khí ngay trên mặt nước luôn.
Ngọn lửa này đã cháy suốt từ thời cổ đại.
Khắp Yanar Dag, mùi gas nồng nặc. Theo ghi chép của nhà thám hiểm người Ý Marco Polo (1254-1324) - một trong những người Châu Âu đầu tiên đến Châu Á thông qua Con đường Tơ lụa lừng danh - thì ngọn lửa này đã cháy suốt từ thời cổ đại. Song cũng vẫn có ghi chép cho rằng Yanar Dag chỉ mới được thắp sáng gần đây thôi, vào một buổi nào đó của thập niên 1950 do sự sơ ý của một người chăn cừu.
Thực chất thì những ngọn lửa như Yanar Dag từng đầy rẫy khắp Azerbaijan. Chính nhờ có chúng mà đất nước này từ xưa đã được vinh danh là "vùng đất lửa". Nhưng để cứ để mặc cho chúng cháy thì hoang phí quá, nên người ta đã dập hết phần nhiều.
Kể từ cuối thế kỷ VII trước Công nguyên, tín ngưỡng Hỏa giáo (còn gọi là Hiên giáo, Hỏa hiên giáo, Hỏa yêu giáo hoặc Bái hỏa giáo) đã bắt đầu. Các tín đồ của nó tin rằng, lửa là phương tiện trung gian liên kết giữa con người và thế giới siêu nhiên. Chuyện bói toán, tiên tri thông qua việc nhìn một ngọn lửa rất thịnh hành.
Cũng từ Baku nhưng tiến sang phía Đông, bạn sẽ bắt gặp Đền Lửa Ateshgah, vị trí thờ Thần Lửa đặc biệt quan trọng của tín ngưỡng Hỏa giáo tại Azerbaijan một thời.
Đền Lửa Ateshgah.
Cái độc đáo nhất ở Đền Lửa Ateshgah là nó được xây trên chính một lỗ thoát khí đốt tự nhiên. Thế nên, nó từng có một bàn thờ rực cháy vĩnh viễn. Tiếc là suốt trong thế kỷ 19, Ateshgah bị bỏ hoang. Có lẽ là do sự suy giảm của dân số người Ấn Độ trong khu vực. Trải qua gần một thế kỷ khai thác dầu khí tràn lan, vào năm 1969, ngọn lửa vĩnh cửu trên bệ thờ còn bị tắt.
Song nếu bạn muốn ghé Đền Lửa Ateshgah để chiêm ngưỡng ngọn lửa vĩnh hằng huyền thoại thì đừng lo! Nó đã được tái thắp bằng khí đốt được dẫn qua từ thành phố gần đó.
Ngày nay, cả Đền Lửa Ateshgah lẫn Yanar Dag đều không còn vai trò tôn giáo linh thiêng như thuở xưa nữa. Thực tế thì từ cuối thế kỷ 19, Đền Lửa Ateshgah đã không còn được sử dụng làm nơi thờ cúng.
Vào năm 1975, Azerbaijan quyết định biến khu phức hợp ngũ giác này thành một bảo tàng. Tới năm 1998, Ateshgah được UNESCO công nhận là di sản thế giới. Kể từ lúc này, nó mới trở nên cuốn hút, thường xuyên đón khoảng 15.000 du khách ghé thăm mỗi năm.
Yanar Dag cháy rừng rực cả vào ban ngày, nhưng đặc biệt đẹp rạng ngời vào ban đêm. 
Tương tự với Ateshgah, du khách đến thăm Yanar Dag cũng không còn vì tín ngưỡng mà đơn thuần là để thỏa mãn thị giác. Yanar Dag cháy rừng rực cả vào ban ngày, nhưng đặc biệt đẹp rạng ngời vào ban đêm. Xung quanh ngọn lửa trải rộng này là đồi núi trơ trọi, hoàn toàn hoang vắng. Ánh lửa vì thế mặc sức tỏa rạng, thắp sáng cả một vùng.
Vào những ngày mùa đông, Yanar Dag lại càng lộng lẫy đến kỳ diệu. Những bông tuyết bay trong không khí, chưa kịp rơi xuống đất đã bị lửa sấy khô, tan biến như mất hút vào hư vô.
Và vì sẽ không bao giờ tắt, nên dù có phải mất bao lâu đi chăng nữa, Yanar Dag cũng sẽ vẫn rực rỡ, nhởn nhơ chờ bạn đến chiêm ngưỡng.

articles.title: Scientists link a strange sugar in red meat to a 63% higher diabetes risk
articles.text:
Scientists link a strange sugar in red meat to a 63% higher diabetes risk
- Date:
- October 18, 2026
- Source:
- European Association for the Study of Diabetes
- Summary:
- A study of nearly 90,000 adults found that people consuming the most of a little-known sugar found in red meat had a 63% higher risk of developing type 2 diabetes. Scientists suspect the sugar may trigger chronic inflammation, potentially revealing a hidden connection between red meat and diabetes that goes beyond weight gain.
- Share:
A sugar naturally present in red meat may help explain why eating these foods has been associated with a higher risk of type 2 diabetes. Preliminary findings from a large observational study suggest that people who consume the most of this sugar face a substantially greater risk of developing the disease, potentially because of its effects on the immune system and chronic inflammation.
The sugar, known as N-glycolylneuraminic acid (Neu5Gc), is particularly common in beef and lamb. Researchers found that participants with the highest intake of meat-derived Neu5Gc had a 63% higher risk of developing type 2 diabetes (T2D) compared with those who consumed the least.
The association remained statistically significant after researchers accounted for several established diabetes risk factors, including physical activity, overall diet, smoking, and existing health conditions. It became weaker after body mass index (BMI) was also considered, but remained significant.
The findings were presented at the Annual Meeting of The European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) in Milan, Italy.
“Our findings support chronic inflammation as a specific mechanism linking red meat consumption with T2D, partly beyond the amount of red meat a person eats and partly independent of body fat,” said lead author Dr. Leopold Fezeu from the Université Sorbonne Paris Nord, Bobigny, France.
The researchers also observed that diabetes risk generally increased with greater consumption of meat-derived Neu5Gc, particularly among those with the highest exposure.
“Although we do not know exactly what levels of Neu5Gc trigger an immune response, our data suggest that higher intakes of meat-derived Neu5Gc are associated with a progressively higher risk of T2D.”
Why a Sugar in Red Meat May Trigger Inflammation
Neu5Gc is produced naturally by most mammals, but humans lost the ability to make it following an ancient mutation in the CMAH gene. Despite this evolutionary change, the sugar can still enter the human body through food.
It occurs in red meat (particularly beef and lamb), with smaller amounts also found in dairy products.
After Neu5Gc is consumed, the body absorbs it and can incorporate it into human tissues. Because humans do not naturally produce the molecule, the immune system may recognize it as foreign. Scientists classify it as a xeno-autoantigen, a foreign substance that becomes incorporated into the body's own tissues and can provoke an immune reaction.
In response, the immune system produces antibodies against Neu5Gc. The resulting prolonged immune activity, called xenosialitis (xenosialitis), has previously been associated with cardiovascular disease and cancer.
Researchers suspect that this persistent inflammatory response could also contribute to type 2 diabetes. However, before this investigation, no large prospective study had examined whether dietary Neu5Gc might promote diabetes through chronic inflammation.
Nearly 90,000 Adults Studied Over Several Years
To investigate the possible connection, the scientists analyzed dietary and health information from 89,953 adults participating in NutriNet-Santé, a large French observational study that follows people over time to examine how nutrition and lifestyle influence health.
Participants were 42 years old on average, and 79% were women. None had type 2 diabetes or cancer when they entered the study.
Each person completed three 24-hour dietary records. The research team then used a validated food database to calculate how much Neu5Gc participants were likely consuming based on the measured amounts of the sugar in different foods.
The analysis included a broad range of red meats, such as beef, lamb, pork, rabbit, goat, and game. Processed meats (such as bacon, sausages and cured meats) were evaluated as a separate category, while dairy products were analyzed independently.
Using the dietary information, the researchers estimated total Neu5Gc intake from all reported foods. They then ranked participants separately by sex according to their intake of meat-derived Neu5Gc and divided them into five equally sized groups (quintiles).
Diabetes risk was compared across these groups, using those with the lowest intake as the reference.
During a median follow-up period of 7.2 years, researchers recorded 966 new cases of type 2 diabetes.
Higher Red Meat Sugar Intake Linked to 63% Greater Diabetes Risk
The results showed a significant relationship between meat-derived Neu5Gc consumption and the likelihood of developing type 2 diabetes. The association became particularly pronounced among participants with the highest estimated intake.
Compared with the lowest intake group, individuals in the highest group had a 63% greater risk of developing the disease. Those in the second-highest group had a 41% greater risk (men and women combined).
These estimates accounted for potentially influential factors, including age, sex, exercise habits, overall dietary quality, smoking, and existing medical conditions.
The researchers also examined how much meat participants typically consumed.
Among men in the highest Neu5Gc intake group, median red meat consumption was 97 grams daily (136 g including processed meat). For women, the corresponding amount was 73 grams (96 g).
By comparison, men in the lowest intake group consumed a median of just 5 grams of red meat per day (21 g), while women consumed 0 grams (9 g).
The relationship between Neu5Gc and diabetes was observed in both sexes, with no statistically significant evidence that it differed between men and women (see tables in notes to editors).
The findings were also consistent when differences in total calorie intake were considered.
Researchers noticed that the increase in diabetes risk was especially steep at higher levels of Neu5Gc exposure. One possible explanation is that the immune system begins to respond more strongly after enough of the foreign sugar has accumulated in body tissues, although this proposed threshold mechanism has not been confirmed.
Importantly, when the analysis additionally accounted for the total amount of red meat consumed, the relationship between Neu5Gc and diabetes weakened and was no longer statistically significant. The direction of the association remained the same, however.
This means the researchers cannot determine whether Neu5Gc itself (rather than other components of red meat) is responsible for the increased risk. The findings suggest it could contribute to the relationship, but they do not establish that the sugar acts independently of red meat consumption.
Diabetes Risk May Extend Beyond Weight Gain
Another notable finding was that obesity appeared to explain only a relatively small portion of the association.
According to the researchers' estimates, obesity accounted for approximately 13% of the relationship between meat-derived Neu5Gc consumption and type 2 diabetes.
This suggests that factors unrelated to excess body weight may contribute substantially to the observed connection.
One possibility is that immune reactions to Neu5Gc produce chronic inflammation that interferes with insulin-producing cells or tissues that normally respond to insulin. Such effects could potentially increase the likelihood of developing type 2 diabetes even without substantial weight gain.
However, additional studies are necessary to establish whether these inflammatory processes actually explain the association.
Why Dairy Products Showed Different Results
Although Neu5Gc occurs in both red meat and dairy products, the researchers found an important difference between these dietary sources.
Higher consumption of Neu5Gc from dairy products was not associated with an increased risk of type 2 diabetes.
This finding may reflect the relatively small amounts of Neu5Gc in cow's milk compared with red meats such as beef and lamb. The typically smaller amounts of Neu5Gc consumed through dairy servings may also contribute to the difference.
When the scientists considered Neu5Gc intake from all dietary sources combined, participants in the highest intake group had a 37% greater risk of developing type 2 diabetes compared with those in the lowest group.
That association appeared to be driven primarily by Neu5Gc obtained from red meat.
“Together, these findings suggest that the association between Neu5Gc and T2D may depend on its dietary source, with meat-derived Neu5Gc showing a stronger association with T2D risk than total dietary Neu5Gc,” said Dr. Fezeu. “There may be differences between sources, or other components of red meat may contribute.”
Could Changing Protein Sources Lower Diabetes Risk?
The findings raise the possibility that reducing dietary exposure to meat-derived Neu5Gc could eventually become one approach to lowering diabetes risk.
However, researchers emphasize that studies are still needed to determine whether replacing foods rich in Neu5Gc with other protein sources would actually produce measurable health benefits.
“Given how common red meat is in Western diets, the strong association between meat-derived Neu5Gc and T2D risk is an important finding. Future research should explore whether reducing exposure to meat-derived Neu5Gc, for example by favoring poultry or plant-based proteins over beef and lamb, which have the highest Neu5Gc content, could help prevent T2D. Studies directly measuring anti-Neu5Gc antibodies in large cohorts would also help to directly test the xenosialitis mechanism in humans.”
The research team plans to investigate how Neu5Gc interacts with other substances found in red meat, including heme iron (a form of dietary iron), and how these components may collectively relate to diabetes risk.
They also intend to measure antibodies against Neu5Gc directly. Doing so could help determine whether the proposed immune response is an important biological mechanism connecting red meat consumption with type 2 diabetes.
Important Limitations of the Findings
The researchers caution that their findings are preliminary and have not yet been validated. The reported estimates could change once the final analysis is completed.
Because the study was observational, it cannot establish that Neu5Gc causes type 2 diabetes or identify precisely which factors are responsible for the higher risk.
Although the analysis accounted for several established diabetes risk factors, unmeasured lifestyle and social influences could still have affected the results.
There were also limitations in how dietary exposure was assessed. Neu5Gc consumption was estimated using participants' food records rather than measured directly, and the researchers did not account for possible dietary changes during the follow-up period. Both factors could have introduced errors into the exposure estimates.
The findings therefore offer a potential new explanation for the established connection between red meat consumption and diabetes, but further investigation is needed to determine whether Neu5Gc directly contributes to the disease.
Table 1. Median Meat Consumption by Neu5Gc Intake
The table shows typical daily meat consumption in each of the five groups, ranked according to estimated intake of meat-derived Neu5Gc.
| Neu5Gc intake group | Men: red meat | Men: red + processed meat | Women: red meat | Women: red + processed meat |

Participants were assigned to these groups based on their estimated Neu5Gc intake, calculated from all reported foods and their measured Neu5Gc content.
The meat consumption figures represent the typical amounts eaten by participants in each group. They do not establish a specific risk threshold or indicate how much meat can be considered safe.
Table 2. Type 2 Diabetes Risk by Neu5Gc Intake

The results suggest a similar association in men and women, without a statistically significant difference between the sexes.
However, relatively few diabetes cases occurred within each sex-specific intake group, making the separate estimates less precise. For this reason, the researchers presented their principal findings using the combined data.

articles.title: Climate change is literally altering the shape of our planet
articles.text:
Climate change is literally altering the shape of our planet
The melting of the poles is increasingly shifting Earth's shape at a faster rate, with the planet becoming more and more round.
Climate change is making Earth progressively rounder, new research finds.
The findings are a signal of human-caused climate change, however, and tracking the shape of the Earth can help reveal just how much impact people are having on its ice caps.
Our planet is not a perfect sphere. Because of its rotation, it is a bit flatter at the poles and bulges in the middle. But the new study reveals that Earth is getting rounder at an accelerated rate, largely due to shifts caused by the melting polar ice caps.
This finding applies only to the solid parts of the planet; the ocean continues to bulge outward at the equator.
The study, published Sept. 9 in the journal JGR Solid Earth, used direct measurements from the global navigation satellite system (GNSS) to track the planet's shape-shifting over time. This system provides direct measurements, but there are limits in how it can be used. For example, there are few GNSS stations near the North and South poles and few in remote oceans because they must be deployed on buoys.
Christoforos Kotsakis, a professor of geodesy at the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki in Greece, developed a new method for analyzing GNSS data to better capture the changes in the planet's surface. He found that the poles are rising and the equator's bulge has been shrinking, each by about 0.04 inch (1 millimeter) per year between 2011 to 2015. That's a small number, considering Earth's diameter at the equator is about 7,926 miles (12,756 kilometers). But that change is bigger than between 1997-2000, when Earth was becoming about 0.02 inch (0.5 mm) rounder per year. This means Earth's shape is rounding at 0.016 inch (0.4 mm) more per year with each decade that passes.
Related stories
The shift is being driven by polar ice melt, which takes pressure off the Earth's crust and allows it to rise slowly, similar to how rising bread dough springs back after you press a finger into it, Kotsakis reported. Meanwhile, increased mass toward the equator puts pressure on the crust there, reducing its bulge. However, there's a catch: When considering the solid Earth and the ocean together, the planet is getting flatter by about 0.03 inches (0.8 mm) a year because the ocean is getting bulgier at the equator as water shifts away from the poles. This 'water weight' overwhelms the rounding happening in the rock below.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.
These shifts are also slowing Earth's rotation, other research has shown.
Researchers also track Earth's changing shape using measurements of its gravity field, which varies depending on the mass of particular regions. GNSS changes and gravity field measurements don't match up perfectly, Kotsakis found, which indicates that the planet's shape and gravity field aren't in perfect lockstep. However, the two methods can be used together to track the major effects of climate change, especially the melting of Greenland and Antarctica and the varying movements of ocean water.
Kotsakis, C. (2026b). Mapping Global GNSS vertical velocities to solid Earth figure change. Journal of Geophysical Research Solid Earth, 131(9). https://doi.org/10.1029/2026jb034224
Stephanie Pappas is a contributing writer for Live Science, covering topics ranging from geoscience to archaeology to the human brain and behavior. She was previously a senior writer for Live Science but is now a freelancer based in Denver, Colorado, and regularly contributes to Scientific American and The Monitor, the monthly magazine of the American Psychological Association. Stephanie received a bachelor's degree in psychology from the University of South Carolina and a graduate certificate in science communication from the University of California, Santa Cruz.

articles.title: Loại thịt rẻ nhưng lại chính là "thuốc quý" của người Việt, cuối năm nên ăn nhiều để tăng cường sức khỏe
articles.text:
Những ngày cuối năm bận rộn, nếu gia đình bạn đang cần tìm một loại thực phẩm vừa chế biến nhanh lại đưa cơm thì đừng bỏ qua thịt vịt. Không như các loại thịt khác, thịt vịt dù đem luộc, đem nướng hay nấu lẩu đều có hương vị độc đáo không thể lẫn với bất cứ món nào.
Vịt không chỉ ngon mà còn cung cấp đầy đủ dinh dưỡng cho gia đình bạn. Nghiên cứu cho thấy, trong 100g thịt vịt có chứa khoảng 25g chất protein, tương đương so với thịt bò, heo, dê. Ngoài ra, hàm lượng các chất dinh dưỡng như canxi, phốt pho, sắt, vitamin (B1, B2, A, D, E), acide nicotic cũng rất cao.
Vịt không chỉ ngon mà còn cung cấp đầy đủ dinh dưỡng cho gia đình.
Đánh giá về thịt vịt, lương y đa khoa Bùi Đắc Sáng, Viện Hàn lâm Khoa học và Công nghệ Việt Nam cho rằng loại thịt này ăn ít nhất 1 lần/tuần có thể giúp mọi người bổ sung dinh dưỡng, kéo dài cuộc sống.
Theo Đông y, thịt vịt vị ngọt, hơi mặn, tính lương (mát). Công hiệu thanh nhiệt giải độc, tư âm giáng hỏa. Đặc biệt có hiệu quả đối với các bệnh có sốt, sởi, trừ khử thử nhiệt, đại tiện táo, phụ nữ kinh nguyệt ít...
Thường xuyên ăn thịt vịt có thể giúp bổ âm, dưỡng dạ dày và nhuận tràng. Thịt vịt không chỉ giúp bổ máu, mà còn dưỡng dạ dày và thúc đẩy sản sinh năng lượng, đặc biệt phù hợp cho những người có thể chất yếu hoặc suy nhược sau khi ốm.
Ăn thịt vịt vào thời điểm cuối năm, sẽ đem về tác dụng thế nào?
Từ nguyên liệu quen thuộc là thịt vịt, chúng ta có thể chế biến thành các bài thuốc, món ăn có công dụng trị bệnh hiệu quả. Cụ thể như sau:
Cách làm: Sử dụng vịt mái già 1 con, bách hợp tươi 300g, gia vị. Vịt mổ bụng bỏ lòng đã làm sạch, cho bách hợp vào bụng tưới 2 muỗng rượu, gia vị, bỏ đầu vịt vào bụng buộc chặt lại. Chưng cách thủy cho chín. Ăn thịt, lòng và bách hợp.
Thịt vịt là loại thực phẩm ngon và bổ.
Cách làm: Một con vịt, đại táo, liên nhục, bạch quả, cả 3 vị thuốc đều lấy 49 quả, nhân sâm 3g. Vịt làm sạch, đại táo tách bỏ hạt, liên nhục ngâm bóc bỏ vỏ và tâm sen, bạch quả bỏ vỏ và ruột, nhân sâm thái lát nhỏ vụn. Dùng rượu, tương và dầu quét đều ngoài da và trong bụng vịt, sau đó cho cả 4 vị thuốc vào bụng vịt, khâu lại, hầm chín rồi ăn.
Cách làm: Một con vịt, 200g đậu đỏ, thảo quả 10g, hành sống. Vịt làm sạch, đậu đỏ xay ngâm mềm đãi sạch cùng thảo quả xay nhuyễn, trộn đều rồi cho vào bụng vịt, khâu lại, cho nước đun ninh nhừ, thêm hành, không cho muối rồi ăn sẽ phát huy công dụng chữa bệnh rất tốt.
Cách làm: Thịt vịt 100g nấu 30 phút, đỗ trọng 30g, mộc nhĩ trắng 30g. Cho các nguyên liệu vào nấu thêm 15 phút rồi ăn.
Cách làm: Thịt vịt nạc 300g, băm nhỏ ướp gia vị, gạo tẻ 100g, nước mía 300ml. Cho các nguyên liệu vào nấu cháo, ninh nhừ. Cháo chín cho thịt vịt đảo đều, đun tiếp cho chín vịt. Ăn ngày 3 lần, duy trì liền một tuần.
Cách làm: Chuẩn bị 300g thịt vịt; 20g gừng; 60g kỷ tử; 60g nấm hương; 3 củ cà rốt; 10 quả táo đỏ. Ướp thịt vịt với gia vị, đem xào săn miếng thịt, rồi cho các nguyên liệu khác vào nồi hầm trong 30 phút cho mềm.
Thịt vịt sẽ bổ hơn gấp bội nếu được nấu cùng các loại thực phẩm dưới đây
Nếu muốn có món thịt vịt ngon lành và phát huy được đầy đủ mọi tác dụng khi ăn, lương y Bùi Đắc Sáng gợi ý các gia đình có thể chế biến thịt vịt cùng một số thực phẩm sau:
Hạt sen: Món thịt vịt vốn rất giàu dinh dưỡng, giàu chất béo vì thế, nên ăn thịt vịt chung với hạt sen có thể làm giảm hàm lượng cholesterol trong máu, đặc biệt có tác dụng rất tốt trong việc bồi bổ cơ thể rất tốt.
Ăn thịt vịt chung với hạt sen có thể làm giảm hàm lượng cholesterol trong máu.
Cải thảo: Thịt vịt có chứa nhiều protein, chất béo và cholesterol… vì vậy nếu ăn cùng loại rau chứa nhiều vitamin C như cải thảo sẽ có thể thúc đẩy trao đổi cholesterol trong máu, có lợi cho sức khỏe.
Củ mài: Nếu các gia đình ăn thịt vịt chung với củ mài có thể giảm hàm lượng cholesterol trong máu, đặc biệt hiệu quả bồi bổ rất tốt.
Nấu cháo: Món cháo vịt có thể làm giảm chất béo trong cơ thể, ngoài ra có thể đào thải chất dư thừa.
Kim ngân hoa: Thịt vịt nổi tiếng với công dụng tiêu sưng, trị nhiệt độc, mụn độc. Còn kim ngân hoa lại có công dụng trong giải độc, tiêu trừ mụn, nhuận da… 2 món này ăn kèm với nhau sẽ là liều "thuốc quý" cho da.
Mỡ vịt chứa nhiều chất béo không bão hòa đơn, giúp giảm cholesterol LDL, hay còn gọi là "cholesterol xấu", phù hợp với những người có vấn đề về mỡ máu. Chất lượng mỡ vịt gần giống với dầu ô liu, làm cho nó trở thành lựa chọn tốt hơn so với các loại mỡ động vật khác. Nhiều đầu bếp chuyên nghiệp ưa chuộng mỡ vịt nhờ vào lợi ích sức khỏe và hương vị đậm đà.
Thịt vịt cung cấp lượng chất béo cần thiết cho cơ thể, giúp duy trì độ ẩm và độ đàn hồi cho da, giữ cho làn da luôn tươi trẻ và mịn màng. Thiếu chất béo có thể dẫn đến các vấn đề như da khô, nhăn và xỉn màu.
Thịt vịt cũng giàu riboflavin (vitamin B2), giúp duy trì sức khỏe của tóc và ngăn ngừa rụng tóc. Mỗi 100 gam thịt vịt quay chứa 0,5 mg riboflavin, đáp ứng 28% nhu cầu hàng ngày.
Khoáng chất kẽm trong thịt vịt giúp tăng cường hệ miễn dịch, bảo vệ cơ thể khỏi các tác nhân gây bệnh như vi khuẩn và virus, đồng thời hỗ trợ quá trình lành vết thương.
Thịt vịt cũng chứa các chất chống oxy hóa, giúp bảo vệ cơ thể khỏi các gốc tự do – nguyên nhân gây ra nhiều bệnh tật.

articles.title: Magic mushroom ingredient takes the fight out of aggressive fish
articles.text:
Magic mushroom ingredient takes the fight out of aggressive fish
Scientists discovered that the psychedelic compound in magic mushrooms can calm highly aggressive fish without disrupting their normal social behavior.
- Date:
- October 18, 2026
- Source:
- Frontiers
- Summary:
- A psychedelic compound found in magic mushrooms appears to have an unexpected effect: calming highly aggressive fish. Researchers discovered that low doses of psilocybin significantly reduced aggressive attacks in mangrove rivulus fish without disrupting their normal social interactions. The findings suggest psilocybin may selectively calm escalating aggression rather than simply suppressing all behavior.
- Share:
Psilocybin, the psychedelic substance found in more than 200 species of mushrooms, appears to have an unexpected effect on aggressive fish. Most mushrooms containing this compound belong to the gilled mushroom genus Psilocybe. In mammals, psilocybin interacts with serotonin receptors in the brain, influencing emotions and behaviors such as mood, appetite, and aggression. However, scientists still know relatively little about how the substance affects social interactions among animals.
To investigate this question, researchers in Canada examined the effects of psilocybin on the amphibious mangrove rivulus fish (Kryptolebias marmoratus). Their findings, published in Frontiers in Behavioral Neuroscience, suggest that even a brief exposure to a low dose can significantly reduce aggressive behavior without disrupting normal social interactions.
"We show that an acute, low dose of psilocybin significantly reduces activity and aggressive attack behavior during social interactions in adult mangrove rivulus fish, a species that is naturally highly aggressive," said first author Dayna Forsyth, a research associate and former MSc student at Acadia University in Nova Scotia.
"These findings provide the first evidence that psilocybin can selectively reduce escalated aggression in a vertebrate model without suppressing social interaction," added senior author Dr. Suzie Currie, a biologist at The University of British Columbia.
Why Scientists Studied Aggressive Mangrove Rivulus Fish
Mangrove rivulus fish are naturally combative, particularly when they encounter another member of their species. Their aggressive responses are easy to recognize and measure, allowing researchers to detect even small changes in behavior.
These fish also have an unusual reproductive ability. They can fertilize themselves, producing offspring that are genetically identical. This makes them especially useful for experiments because scientists can minimize genetic variation and more confidently attribute behavioral differences to psilocybin rather than inherited traits.
For the experiment, the researchers worked with three genetically distinct lines of fish bred in the laboratory. One group received psilocybin, another provided the fish used to provoke social interactions, and the third helped researchers measure how much psilocybin entered and accumulated in the animals' bodies.
The researchers first established a baseline for each fish's behavior. They placed a fish into a tank already occupied by another fish, with the two separated by a fiberglass mesh barrier and an opaque cover. The mesh prevented physical contact while allowing the fish to see and smell each other once the cover was removed.
After allowing five minutes for the fish to adjust to their shared environment, the team removed the opaque cover and recorded their interactions.
The following day, 24 hours after the initial observation, the researchers placed the same fish in water containing dissolved psilocybin. Following 20 minutes of exposure, they returned it to the tank with the same fish it had encountered previously. The opaque cover was then removed again so the researchers could observe any changes in behavior.
Magic Mushroom Compound Reduces Aggressive Attacks
The results revealed a striking change. Fish exposed to psilocybin moved around less and displayed fewer bursts of aggressive swimming than fish that had not received the substance.
To assess these changes, the scientists measured overall activity (time spent moving) and several signs of aggression (including swimming bursts). These rapid bursts are particularly important because they indicate that an encounter is escalating toward an attack, even when the fish cannot make physical contact.
"Swimming bursts are high-energy attack behaviors that represent an escalation of aggression towards the stimulus fish without making physical contact," explained Currie. "Other types of aggressive behaviors, like head-on displays, are more about communication and social assessment and require very little energy."
Interestingly, psilocybin did not suppress every form of aggressive or social behavior. While the fish became less likely to engage in intense, energy-demanding attacks, their less physically demanding social displays remained largely unchanged.
"Psilocybin's calming effect appears to selectively reduce energetically costly, escalated behaviors while lower-energy social display behaviors remained largely unchanged," said Forsyth. "This suggests that this compound can selectively dampen escalated social conflict rather than shutting down behavior altogether."
The compound also reduced general activity. When placed alongside another member of their species, fish treated with psilocybin spent less time swimming than untreated controls.
Together, these findings suggest that psilocybin may influence specific aspects of aggressive behavior rather than simply making animals less responsive to their surroundings.
What the Findings Could Mean for Psychedelic Research
The researchers believe animal studies like this one could eventually help scientists better understand how psychedelic compounds influence behavior and identify possible directions for therapeutic research.
By examining which social responses are most sensitive to psilocybin, researchers may be able to uncover biological mechanisms that are difficult to investigate directly in people. Such insights could ultimately inform studies of potential clinical applications.
However, the team emphasized that the findings should not be interpreted as evidence of a treatment for aggression in humans. The experiment involved fish, did not evaluate any clinical intervention, and cannot establish whether similar effects would occur in people.
There are also important questions about how long the calming effect lasts. The researchers examined only single doses and short exposure periods. They did not investigate repeated treatments, long-term behavioral changes, or whether the fish might adapt to the substance over time.
Additional experiments will be necessary to determine whether psilocybin's ability to reduce aggressive attacks can persist beyond the brief period examined in this study.
"Future studies can build on this work to explore how psilocybin alters neural signaling, which serotonin pathways are involved, and why some aspects of social behavior are affected while others are not," concluded Currie. "These are questions that are difficult or impossible to answer directly in humans."
Story Source:
Materials provided by Frontiers. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Dayna Forsyth, Nicoletta Faraone, Simon G. Lamarre, Suzanne Currie. The magic of mushrooms: psilocybin influences behavior in the mangrove rivulus fish, Kryptolebias marmoratus. Frontiers in Behavioral Neuroscience, 2026; 20 DOI: 10.3389/fnbeh.2026.1767175
