articles.title: Uber puts all 30,000 employees on ChatGPT Work | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Uber and OpenAI announced an expansion of their partnership on Thursday, with the ride-share giant telling TechCrunch that its entire global workforce — some 30,000 people — will now be using ChatGPT Work.
ChatGPT Work was introduced in July as an enterprise-focused AI agent that corporate teams could deploy for various workflows.
Uber originally piloted ChatGPT Work with 1,000 employees earlier this year but has now scaled up its usage to the entire company.
That earlier pilot was deployed to workers from across Uber’s various departments, including finance, operations, and product. Indeed, a majority of the early adopters — some 80% — were non-engineers, Sumanth Sukumar, Uber’s VP of engineering, told TechCrunch.
“They used it for a wide range of tasks: analyzing complex data from our operations to identify trends and develop recommendations; localizing training materials for different markets and languages; and building personalized interactive dashboards to manage their daily work,” he said.
Yet while the ride-share giant is now going all in on ChatGPT, it has not settled on exactly how employees will use it. “Our approach is to make powerful AI tools available across Uber while giving teams room to experiment,” Sukumar said. “For example, earlier this year we paired 30 AI engineers with teams across Uber and gave them two weeks to automate key parts of their job. Those ‘AI pods’ showed us how much opportunity there is when you combine technical expertise with a deep understanding of a particular job.”
Uber didn’t disclose how much it’s spending on the new rollout of the chatbot. Instead, Sukumar said the company will track how employees use the tool. “We’ll look at how employees are using the technology, the kinds of workflows they develop and how it helps them work more effectively. We’ll evaluate those outcomes and use what we learn to guide how we deploy AI across the business,” he said. Uber says OpenAI worked closely with the company on integrating the chatbot.
OpenAI has moved quickly to scale up its enterprise business as it competes with its chief competitor, Anthropic. Once known largely as a consumer brand, the ChatGPT creator has swiftly gained a loyal following with business customers, while other AI companies have struggled to keep up.

articles.title: Victoria McClune is challenging how the AI industry understands its users
articles.text:
Victoria McClune’s career has followed the evolution of digital technology, from interactive children’s books on the first iPads to artificial intelligence systems reshaping how people work and communicate. A creative director by training, she entered technology with an interest in how people engage with digital experiences. Today, that interest informs her work at Current Futures Group, where she is investigating how AI systems influence their users and why their design deserves greater scrutiny.
McClune was still at art school when the first iPads arrived. Seeing an opportunity to rethink children’s publishing, she founded a startup developing interactive books for the new platform. The company worked with Disney illustrators, gained recognition at South by Southwest and operated entirely remotely at a time when distributed work was far less established.
As the economics of digital publishing changed, McClune moved into augmented and virtual reality for marketing. Through her own agency, she contributed to external initiatives involving several multinational companies. These experiences kept her close to emerging technology and the challenge of making it useful to the people expected to engage with it.
After the pandemic, McClune returned to an industry she felt had changed considerably. Artificial intelligence was beginning to reshape marketing and creative work, prompting her to study the technology at MIT. Her background in psychology and advertising helped her approach AI through the question of how people experience and interpret its outputs.
“I am not an engineer,” McClune explains. “I am a human computer interface designer and have been one for over 20 years.” That distinction became particularly relevant when she noticed a change in the responses generated by an AI model she was using. After introducing language concerning children and healthcare into her conversations, she suspected the system was treating her differently. Drawing on her understanding of human behaviour, she began testing the model to investigate what might be influencing its responses.
“I noticed I was being managed and I knew what that was from my background,” she recalls. The investigation developed into her Silent Downgrade research, which examines how AI systems may shape the quality of responses users receive. McClune argues that the effects of interacting technical processes can emerge before someone submits a specific prompt, influencing the experience in ways that are not immediately visible.
Her Silent Downgrade series uses the metaphor of a room to explain how AI can establish conditions that influence a user’s experience. People may assume a disappointing answer reflects their inability to prompt effectively, without considering whether the system itself is contributing to the outcome. McClune wants users to recognize these constraints and question what shapes the responses they receive.
She does not view AI as a sentient force with independent intentions. Instead, she sees it as predictive generative technology shaped by patterns in human-created information. Her concern centres on how the systems are designed and how their behaviour affects the people relying on them.
This perspective also informs her criticism of AI development. McClune believes frontier laboratories have concentrated heavily on improving technical capabilities while giving insufficient attention to user experience. Businesses adopting AI need systems that produce useful, consistent outputs, yet confusing interactions can make employees work harder to obtain reliable results. She argues that these problems deserve greater attention as organizations seek meaningful returns from their investments.
McClune wants professionals with expertise in psychology, communications, and human-computer interaction to play a larger role in AI development. She is also sceptical of relying solely on companies to regulate themselves, believing their practices and incentives require closer scrutiny. For her, accountability includes making systems easier to understand and giving users a stronger basis for questioning their outputs.
At Current Futures Group, her work focuses on making decisions and system states more readable to the people affected by them. She hopes to bring these ideas to a wider audience through further research and writing, helping users understand AI without assuming they are at fault when an interaction goes wrong. “I think what’s actually missing is that there needs to be more people who understand us in the room,” McClune argues.
From interactive publishing to AI, her career has centred on the relationship between people and technology. As artificial intelligence becomes more deeply embedded in everyday work, she wants the industry to pay closer attention to the experience it creates for its users. Its future, in her view, depends not only on what these systems can do, but on how well they serve the people who rely on them.

articles.title: 570 triệu cổ phiếu sang tay, Novaland cần gần 8.000 tỷ đồng để cơ cấu nợ
articles.text:
Cổ phiếu NVL giao dịch đột biến, cổ đông lớn có động thái trái chiều
CTCP Tập đoàn Đầu tư Địa ốc No Va (Novaland, mã NVL) liên tiếp ghi nhận những diễn biến đáng chú ý, từ biến động mạnh của giá cổ phiếu đến các giao dịch quy mô lớn liên quan đến những doanh nghiệp trong hệ sinh thái gia đình nhà sáng lập Bùi Thành Nhơn.
Khoảng một tháng qua, tổng cộng khoảng 570 triệu cổ phiếu NVL được chuyển nhượng, tương đương gần 24% lượng cổ phiếu đang niêm yết, hiện ở mức hơn 2,4 tỷ đơn vị. Đáng chú ý, nhiều phiên giao dịch có khối lượng đột biến xuất hiện trong giai đoạn cổ phiếu giảm sâu, xen kẽ những nhịp hồi phục.
Phiên 30/9 ghi nhận hơn 97 triệu cổ phiếu NVL được sang tay, với giá trị gần 1.000 tỷ đồng. Giao dịch diễn ra sau hai phiên giảm sàn liên tiếp và chuỗi giảm sâu trước đó. Một ngày trước, hơn 65 triệu cổ phiếu NVL chất bán ở giá sàn.
Đây cũng là ngày giao dịch không hưởng quyền của đợt chào bán cổ phiếu cho cổ đông hiện hữu. Sau phiên bán tháo, lực cầu bắt đáy xuất hiện và hấp thụ lượng cung lớn. Những phiên sau đó tiếp tục ghi nhận giao dịch sôi động, với 51,3 triệu cổ phiếu được giao dịch ngày 2/10 và hơn 73 triệu đơn vị ngày 9/10.
Diễn biến này diễn ra khi Novaland triển khai kế hoạch chào bán gần 800,7 triệu cổ phiếu cho cổ đông hiện hữu theo tỷ lệ 3:1, giá 10.000 đồng/cổ phiếu, dự kiến huy động gần 8.007 tỷ đồng. Tập đoàn đã gia hạn thời gian chuyển nhượng quyền mua đến ngày 23/11 và thời hạn đăng ký, nộp tiền mua cổ phiếu đến ngày 26/11.
Đáng chú ý, các cổ đông liên quan gia đình ông Bùi Thành Nhơn cũng có những động thái trái chiều. Bà Cao Thị Ngọc Sương, vợ ông Nhơn, đăng ký bán 6,3 triệu cổ phiếu NVL trong thời gian từ 26-30/10 nhằm phục vụ nhu cầu cá nhân.
Ở chiều ngược lại, CTCP Diamond Properties đăng ký mua 7 triệu cổ phiếu NVL trong cùng thời gian để cân đối danh mục đầu tư. Nếu hoàn tất, tỷ lệ sở hữu của doanh nghiệp này sẽ tăng từ 7,423% lên 7,715% vốn điều lệ Novaland.
Trước đó, ngày 6/10, Diamond Properties đã bán 2,58 triệu cổ phiếu NVL theo phương thức thỏa thuận. Như vậy, chỉ khoảng hai tuần sau giao dịch bán ra, doanh nghiệp này lại đăng ký mua vào với khối lượng lớn hơn.
Trong khi đó, ngày 6/10, Novaland lên tiếng bác bỏ thông tin lan truyền trên mạng xã hội về việc tập đoàn phá sản hoặc mất khả năng hoạt động, khẳng định những nội dung này không phản ánh chính xác tình trạng pháp lý và hoạt động thực tế của doanh nghiệp.
Về hoạt động kinh doanh, Novaland dự kiến mở bán trở lại dự án Aqua City từ ngày 31/10, sau thời gian dài tháo gỡ vướng mắc pháp lý. Các dự án như The Grand Manhattan, Victoria Village và The Park Avenue tiếp tục được thi công, hoàn thiện hoặc bàn giao theo kế hoạch.
Cổ phiếu NVL hiện ở vùng thấp lịch sử, quanh ngưỡng 10.000 đồng/cp.
Nợ gần 73.000 tỷ đồng, Novaland vẫn chịu áp lực dòng tiền
Khoảng 570 triệu cổ phiếu NVL được sang tay trong một tháng, cùng những giao dịch trái chiều của các cổ đông liên quan gia đình nhà sáng lập, đặt ra câu hỏi về diễn biến cơ cấu sở hữu và kỳ vọng của nhà đầu tư đối với Novaland.
Tuy nhiên, chỉ dựa vào khối lượng giao dịch chưa đủ cơ sở để kết luận có sự thay đổi lớn trong cơ cấu cổ đông. Cần thêm thông tin về bên mua, bên bán và các thay đổi sở hữu được công bố chính thức để xác định bản chất những giao dịch này.
Đáng chú ý, diễn biến trên thị trường xuất hiện trong khi Novaland vẫn phải xử lý áp lực tài chính lớn, dù kết quả kinh doanh có dấu hiệu cải thiện.
Theo số liệu doanh nghiệp công bố trong tài liệu tham khảo, doanh thu thuần quý III/2026 đạt hơn 5.000 tỷ đồng, tăng khoảng 200% so với cùng kỳ; lợi nhuận sau thuế đạt hơn 1.100 tỷ đồng. Lũy kế 9 tháng, doanh thu thuần ước vượt 10.000 tỷ đồng, lợi nhuận sau thuế hơn 2.800 tỷ đồng, đảo chiều so với khoản lỗ 1.820 tỷ đồng cùng kỳ năm trước.
Dù vậy, lợi nhuận chưa đồng nghĩa với dòng tiền thực thu. Trong 6 tháng đầu năm, dòng tiền thuần từ hoạt động kinh doanh của Novaland vẫn âm gần 3.600 tỷ đồng.
Tại ngày 30/6, tổng dư nợ vay của tập đoàn ở mức 72.900 tỷ đồng. Trong đó, khoảng 30.500 tỷ đồng sẽ đáo hạn trong vòng 12 tháng, bao gồm khoảng 13.200 tỷ đồng trái phiếu. Doanh nghiệp còn ghi nhận hơn 16.700 tỷ đồng nợ gốc quá hạn tại cuối kỳ.
Một số khoản trái phiếu vẫn chưa được thanh toán đầy đủ.
Novaland cho biết nguyên nhân chậm thanh toán là chưa thu xếp được nguồn tiền và doanh nghiệp đang tiếp tục thương thảo với các nhà đầu tư.
Trong bối cảnh đó, Novaland dự kiến huy động gần 8.007 tỷ đồng từ việc phát hành gần 800,7 triệu cổ phiếu cho cổ đông hiện hữu. Trong đó, hơn 5.953 tỷ đồng dự kiến được sử dụng để thanh toán một phần hoặc toàn bộ gốc của 13 mã trái phiếu do doanh nghiệp phát hành. Khả năng giảm áp lực tài chính sẽ phụ thuộc vào kết quả chào bán và tiến độ thực hiện phương án sử dụng vốn.
Đáng chú ý, báo cáo soát xét bán niên 2026 tiếp tục nhấn mạnh vấn đề hoạt động liên tục của Novaland trong bối cảnh dòng tiền kinh doanh thâm hụt và các nghĩa vụ tài chính đến hạn, quá hạn còn lớn.
Diễn biến giao dịch NVL thời gian qua cho thấy cổ phiếu đang thu hút sự chú ý lớn của thị trường, nhưng chưa đủ cơ sở để kết luận về sự thay đổi trong kỳ vọng của cổ đông hay một chuyển biến cụ thể trong cơ cấu sở hữu. Với Novaland, những yếu tố cần theo dõi vẫn là kết quả huy động vốn, tiến độ xử lý nợ, dòng tiền thực thu và khả năng đưa các dự án vào triển khai, bàn giao đúng kế hoạch.

articles.title: Fortnite is coming back to Apple's Australian App Store following court ruling - Engadget
articles.text:
Fortnite is coming back to Apple's Australian App Store following court ruling
The ruling also forces Apple to allow alternative app stores and methods of payment.
Fortnite is coming back on the App Store in Australia after a federal court ordered Apple to open its iOS ecosystem up to competition. The judgement will also force Apple to permit alternative app stores without imposing conditions and allow developers to show alternative payment options, among other clauses. Apple disagreed with the court's findings and said it would challenge them.
"Big news: Fortnite is coming back to the App Store in Australia tomorrow!" Epic Games wrote in a post on X. "This is great news for developers worldwide and iOS users in Australia who will benefit from an open mobile app ecosystem."
In May 2026, Fortnite returned to iOS everywhere around the world except Australia because of its ongoing court battle there. Epic said at the time that Apple continued to enforce terms that Australian courts had found to be unlawful and was awaiting a final decision, which arrived yesterday.
Australian courts followed the EU's blueprint for forcing Apple to open up its ecosystem. At the same time, the ruling includes clauses that would preclude any of the "malicious compliance" Apple has been accused of in the past, like "Core Technology" or developer fees for using third-party app stores.
As a brief summary of the 1,104-paragraph filing, the court ordered Apple to open iOS to third party app stores and allow users to download apps directly from developers. Developers will be able to offer alternative payment systems (free from excessive Apple fees and conditions) and not forced to use Apple's in-app payment system. The App Store can't block developers from pointing users to outside apps to make purchases, and users must not find any "friction" when paying with alternative systems or installing apps from outside the App Store.
Apple was also ordered to pay 85 percent Epic's legal costs and must implement the orders by March 1, 2027 or send proof that it needs an extension by February 15, 2027. However, Apple said it disagreed with many parts of the decision and plans to appeal.
"Apple does not have a monopoly position in Australia or in any market around the world," a spokesperson told Engadget. "We respectfully disagree with many findings in this case, including a market definition that has been rejected by other courts. We will request a stay and appeal the outcome to seek a resolution that respects our intellectual property and protects the safe, secure experience that consumers and developers expect from the App Store."
Apple noted that it did win some points in the case, like the court affirming that it's "entitled to seek a commercial return on its highly valuable intellectual property-protected assets... which developers like Epic take the benefit of." The court also rejected Epic's "unconscionable conduct" claims, and as with other territories, did not impose any rate setting.
Update October 22, 2026 at 5:31 AM ET: The article has been updated with Apple's comment to Engadget.
Correction October 22, 2026 at 8:14 AM ET: The original version of this story claimed Fortnite had already returned to the Australian App Store. This is not yet the case, Engadget regrets the error.

articles.title: Meta’s AI could still scrape news sites, legal experts say
articles.text:
Meta has tweaked its business terms to remove language suggesting that it could freely train its AI models on news sites, like The Verge — but legal experts say these changes aren’t enough to address their concerns. “This does nothing to restrict the ‘associated with your products or services’ [language] that would let Meta scrape entire sites,” James Grimmelmann, a professor of digital and information law at Cornell Law School, tells Nieman Lab.
Meta’s AI could still scrape news sites, legal experts say
Meta’s new business terms could still help it justify training AI on scraped sites.
Initially, Meta’s new terms for business accounts appeared to give the company permission to train its AI on news sites. The terms, which go into effect October 30th, stated that Meta “may use any content” from the websites associated with a business account to “develop, research” and “train” Meta’s products. At the time, legal experts told Nieman Lab that this could allow Meta “to argue its commercial terms supersede other blocking instructions,” such as the robots.txt file that has historically told scrapers (including search engines like Google) what they are allowed to crawl.
Following fierce backlash from the publishing industry, Meta removed language saying it would “train” its products with scraped content. But the tweaks might not be enough to rule out that possibility. “The revised version of the new terms still allows Meta to use that scraped content to develop any ‘business product.’ That doesn’t seem to be a defined term, and presumably Meta is developing AI business products. I think ‘develop’ is broad enough to include ‘train,’” Matt Topic, a media and intellectual property attorney at Loevy & Loevy, tells Nieman Lab.
Meta has maintained that its new terms aren’t designed to scrape news content for free. In a statement to The Verge today, Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts reiterated that “content owners can use robots.txt to signal their preferences,” adding that the update “is not about scraping news sites, and these updates don’t give us new rights that supersede those preferences.”

articles.title: Tesla is prepping a Cybercab onslaught | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Tesla says it is preparing to launch its shiny gold Cybercab in new markets outside its home of Austin, Texas, in a bid to “literally take over every part of terrestrial transportation.”
“We’re starting with getting people from one place to the other, but we want to basically own transportation of any kind on Earth,” Chief Financial Officer Vaibhav Taneja said on the company’s third-quarter earnings call Wednesday.
Tesla has previously shown a concept version of a multi-passenger vehicle it calls the “Robovan,” but it’s unclear if Taneja’s bombastic comments mean the company is working on other types of transportation.
What was clearer on the call is that Tesla’s Cybercab expansion will begin in Dallas next month and spread to other cities by the end of this year. Tesla already operates robotaxi versions of its Model Y SUV in small fleets in Dallas, Houston, and the Florida cities of Miami, Orlando, and Tampa. The company also said on its earnings call that it will start selling Cybercabs to fleet operators by the end of this year.
Broader expansion of the Cybercab could set up a real fight with Waymo, which is currently the market leader for robotaxis in the United States, with more than 4,000 of them deployed across more than a dozen cities. Tesla has argued that its Cybercab is cheaper and easier to build, which should allow it to undercut Waymo and other robotaxi operators on price. But the company has to reach real scale outside Austin in order to prove that point.
Tesla said it’s ready thanks to a dramatic increase in the number of miles its self-driving cars have traveled in recent weeks. While that may be true, Tesla was mum on Wednesday about how much money the overall robotaxi effort is bringing in. Tesla CEO Elon Musk said the new ride-hailing business won’t be noticeable in the company’s overall financial figures until the second quarter of 2027, “and probably a big deal by Q3 or Q4 of next year.”
Tesla also made a change to its letter to shareholders that further obscures what little visibility there was into its robotaxi business.
In Tesla’s second-quarter letter, the company included a chart for “Cumulative Paid Robotaxi Miles.” A close read of that chart showed a 36% decline from the first quarter of the year. In the new letter released on Wednesday, Tesla changed that chart to show “Cumulative Unsupervised Robotaxi Miles” — an indicator of how far the fleet cars are driving, whether or not they have paying riders on board.
There wasn’t much more clarity on the call, either. When asked about paid robotaxi miles traveled, Taneja said the company is “seeing utilization improving,” but didn’t offer specifics.
Instead, Taneja kept most of his comments generally focused on Tesla’s plans to scale the Cybercab. That included praise for Tesla’s engineering team for creating a vehicle that, according to the manufacturing team, is very easy to build — and build quickly.
“They think this is one of the easiest products for them to scale in terms of manufacturing,” he said. “So scaling would not be that much of a challenge.”
What might be a challenge, Taneja said, is that Tesla needs to make sure it has “all the regulatory approvals” so it can “start deploying the Cybercabs as fast as we can produce them.” That echoes many previous comments from Musk, who has long claimed that “regulatory approval” was the biggest barrier to Tesla’s robotaxi plans, not technical progress.
Musk has always been a bit hazy about what approvals, specifically, he felt were needed. The company has run into a regulatory hurdle this year, though. In September, just hours after Tesla formally launched its Cybercab in Austin, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) opened an investigation into whether the vehicle complies with current federal motor vehicle safety standards.
All automakers self-certify that their vehicles conform to these standards, and Tesla has claimed that the Cybercab is compliant. But it is missing features that the current standards require, like a brake pedal and side mirrors. The NHTSA has proposed removing some of these requirements, but that rule change is likely still at least a few months away.
Not every Tesla executive agreed on this during Wednesday’s call.
Asked about the remaining bottlenecks for a wider robotaxi rollout, Ashok Elluswamy, Tesla’s vice president overseeing autonomy, said they are “not purely regulatory.”
“It’s technology-driven,” he said. “We had initially had the robotaxi service from 6 a.m. to 9 p.m., and then expanded to 10 p.m. to 11 p.m, now it’s going to be pretty soon, [to] 2 a.m. So we’re slowly expanding the availability of robotaxi, and that is driven by the capability of the AI software.”
That could be why Tesla’s service still doesn’t operate on highways, and in certain conditions, although it has been spotted operating in heavy rain many times in Austin — something Waymo’s robotaxis have largely avoided. Elluswamy said Wednesday that Tesla plans to tackle more of these challenging driving scenarios by the end of this year, before scaling further.
“We just want to make sure that there’s not a single safety incident. That is our operating principle. And even if there’s the slightest possible risk at all, we don’t like to take on that risk,” he said.

articles.title: Ex-OpenAI science head Kevin Weil launches Warp Sciences with $215M
articles.text:
Kevin Weil, who led OpenAI for Science, has launched Warp Sciences with $215M led by Lightspeed, valuing it at $865M, Bloomberg reported. It is building an automated lab in the US for a drug development step that pharma companies have long outsourced to Chinese firms such as WuXi AppTec.
Kevin Weil, who led OpenAI’s science unit until he left in April, has launched a startup that uses AI to speed up a key step in drug development, Bloomberg reported. Warp Sciences came out of stealth on Thursday with $215M in funding.
Lightspeed Venture Partners led the round, which values Warp at $865M including the new money, according to the company. IVP, Premji Invest and Lux Capital also invested. Angel investors include OpenAI finance chief Sarah Friar, Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong and LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman.
Warp won’t discover drugs itself. Once researchers find a promising molecule, they often make hundreds or thousands of versions of it to make it work better and cut side effects. Drugmakers have long sent that work to Chinese firms, especially WuXi AppTec, because they are cheaper and faster.
That reliance has grown riskier as US-China tensions reach drug supply chains. In June, the Pentagon added WuXi AppTec to its list of companies it says are linked to China’s military, though a judge blocked the move in August. Some drugmakers also worry about sharing sensitive data with Chinese contractors, Weil told Bloomberg.
Warp wants to bring that work back to the US with a fully automated lab. Its team of about 20 has already bought robotic arms and AI chips. Its chemists will wear cameras and pressure-sensing gloves during experiments to create data for training its own AI models.
“It’s still an area where frontier AI models are not yet changing the world in the way models are changing the world in software engineering and math,” Weil said. “That’s because the field is so much more experimentally driven. The models need to see that data.”
His co-founders are Manohar Paluri, a former vice president at Meta’s Superintelligence Labs, DJ Patil, the White House’s first chief data scientist, and Solomon Reisberg, formerly of Terremoto Biosciences. Weil is the second former OpenAI leader this week to raise big money to make things in the US. On Tuesday, Bob McGrew’s Arda raised $232M for AI that sets up factory lines.
Investors are piling into AI for drug research, and OpenAI-backed Chai Discovery raised $400M in July. OpenAI bought Orchestra Bio, which helps drugmakers run drug development with AI agents, this week. That same month, OpenAI researcher Miles Wang was reported to be raising about $200M for his own drug startup, with Lightspeed in talks to lead.

articles.title: Meta turns Muse sharing back on
articles.text:
Meta has re-enabled Muse sharing after security researchers had reported that public conversation links could be easy to find. The researchers said they had been able to find Muse pages like a marketing company’s internal revenue review and a small business owner’s loan application.
Meta turns Muse sharing back on
Meta has given new URLs to shared Muse ‘artifacts’ after security researchers reported that public links could be easy to find.
Researchers at Claroc reported earlier this week that Muse the web addresses for shared conversations from Muse were named after a conversation’s title and written into public DNS. Ars Technica said Tuesday that Meta paused the sharing feature after it reached out about what was going on.
In a post today on X, Meta’s David Singleton says that “The underlying issue is now fixed, and sharing is back on.” According to Singleton, the issue was with URLs for shared Muse artifacts, which Meta says are things like documents and images inside Muse, and wasn’t a flaw with chat sharing.
“If you shared an artifact before the fix: it now has a new URL,” Singleton says. “Anyone visiting the old link will see a note asking them to get the new one from you. We know that’s a pain, and we’re sorry for the disruption — but protecting user data has to come first.”

articles.title: Lãi suất thấp không thể chỉ dựa vào cam kết ngân hàng
articles.text:
Lãi suất vừa giảm nhưng có lâu dài?
Đợt giảm lãi suất huy động và cho vay được triển khai từ ngày 19/10 được kỳ vọng sẽ hỗ trợ doanh nghiệp và nền kinh tế. Tuy nhiên, diễn biến sau đợt cam kết giảm lãi suất hồi tháng 4/2026 cho thấy việc duy trì mặt bằng lãi suất thấp không đơn giản.
Sau cuộc họp với Ngân hàng Nhà nước (NHNN) chiều 9/4, các ngân hàng thống nhất giảm lãi suất huy động và cho vay từ ngày 10/4. Dù vậy, áp lực thanh khoản sau đó khiến lãi suất huy động chịu sức ép tăng trở lại, cho thấy cam kết giảm lãi suất khó duy trì nếu các điều kiện thị trường chưa thuận lợi.
Trong cuộc đua tăng lãi suất ấy, ngân hàng không công khai tăng lãi suất một cách chính thức, nhưng thực tế người gửi tiền lâu nay đã quen với việc “mặc cả” lãi suất khi gửi tiền.
Để đợt giảm lãi suất lần này đi vào thực chất và duy trì bền vững, TS. Nguyễn Văn Lộc, Giám đốc Chương trình đào tạo Kinh doanh thương mại, Đại học Phenikaa, cho rằng điều quan trọng không chỉ là cam kết của các ngân hàng, mà còn là những điều kiện kinh tế đứng sau mặt bằng lãi suất. Theo ông, mệnh lệnh hành chính có thể tạo ra sự đồng thuận trong ngắn hạn, nhưng để duy trì lãi suất thấp, cần giảm chi phí vốn, áp lực thanh khoản và rủi ro tín dụng, đồng thời giữ ổn định kỳ vọng lạm phát và tỷ giá.
“Nếu những yếu tố này chưa thay đổi, mức lãi suất vừa giảm sẽ sớm chịu sức ép điều chỉnh trở lại. Bởi vậy, muốn giảm lãi suất lâu dài, cần sử dụng đồng bộ các công cụ tiền tệ, tài khóa và quản lý an toàn hệ thống, thay vì chủ yếu trông vào cam kết của các ngân hàng”, ông Lộc lưu ý.
Lãi suất phải được nhìn từ cả hai phía
Lãi suất huy động là chi phí tìm kiếm và giữ nguồn vốn của ngân hàng. Người gửi tiền quyết định dựa trên lợi tức, kỳ vọng lạm phát, mức độ an toàn và cơ hội đầu tư khác. Ngân hàng quyết định dựa trên nhu cầu thanh toán, cơ cấu kỳ hạn và kế hoạch cho vay.
Nếu lãi suất huy động giảm nhưng nhu cầu vốn của ngân hàng vẫn lớn, tiền gửi có thể dịch chuyển sang tổ chức khác hoặc kênh đầu tư khác. Khi đó, ngân hàng lại phải nâng lãi suất để giữ vốn. Một ngân hàng tăng lãi suất có thể khiến những ngân hàng khác phải điều chỉnh theo.
Trong khi đó, lãi suất cho vay không chỉ phụ thuộc vào chi phí huy động vốn mà còn bao gồm chi phí hoạt động, chi phí dự phòng rủi ro và mức độ rủi ro của từng khoản vay. Nếu lãi suất đầu ra giảm trong khi các chi phí này chưa giảm tương ứng, ngân hàng có thể thận trọng hơn khi thẩm định hồ sơ hoặc ưu tiên khách hàng có khả năng trả nợ tốt.
Kết quả có thể là lãi suất niêm yết giảm nhưng doanh nghiệp nhỏ và vừa vẫn khó tiếp cận vốn.
“Đây là rủi ro cần tính đến, không phải kết quả tất yếu của mọi đợt giảm lãi suất. Ngân hàng vẫn có trách nhiệm tiết giảm chi phí và chia sẻ lợi nhuận với khách hàng, nhưng khả năng ấy có giới hạn”, ông Lộc phân tích.
NHNN có thể sử dụng các công cụ như nghiệp vụ thị trường mở (OMO), tái cấp vốn và các lãi suất điều hành để tác động đến điều kiện thanh khoản và mặt bằng lãi suất ngắn hạn. Tuy nhiên, hiệu quả phụ thuộc vào nguyên nhân gây thiếu hụt thanh khoản, thời điểm can thiệp và tình hình chung của hệ thống ngân hàng.
Đây cũng là mong muốn của ông Lê Ngọc Lâm, Chủ tịch HĐQT BIDV. Theo ông Lâm, các ngân hàng thương mại quốc doanh sẵn sàng giảm lợi nhuận để đồng hành cùng doanh nghiệp. Nhưng với các ngân hàng thương mại cổ phần, ông Lâm cho rằng họ sẽ tự tin hơn trong việc giảm lãi suất đầu vào, từ đó giảm lãi suất cho vay nếu NHNN đưa ra thông điệp mạnh mẽ như cam kết hỗ trợ khi họ gặp khó khăn về thanh khoản, thông qua các kênh như OMO (nghiệp vụ thị trường mở) hay SWAP (hoán đổi ngoại tệ).
Theo TS Nguyễn Văn Lộc, nếu thiếu hụt thanh khoản chỉ mang tính thời điểm, hỗ trợ kịp thời có thể hạn chế việc ngân hàng đẩy lãi suất huy động lên để phòng ngừa. Nếu tình trạng thiếu vốn kéo dài do cho vay quá nhanh hoặc cơ cấu kỳ hạn mất cân đối, cần điều chỉnh hoạt động của ngân hàng. Việc bơm vốn ngắn hạn liên tục sẽ không giải quyết được nguyên nhân.
Điều này đòi hỏi dự báo tốt hơn các dòng tiền lớn: lịch thu, chi ngân sách, phát hành trái phiếu chính phủ, nhu cầu tiền mặt và các thời điểm đáo hạn. Phối hợp giữa Bộ Tài chính và NHNN giúp thị trường tránh những biến động thanh khoản bất ngờ.
Bên cạnh đó, dự trữ bắt buộc cũng là một công cụ có thể ảnh hưởng đến nguồn vốn khả dụng và chi phí ngân hàng. Tuy nhiên, đây là công cụ tác động rộng, cần cân nhắc trong tổng thể lạm phát, tỷ giá và an toàn hệ thống; không nên mặc định rằng cứ giảm dự trữ bắt buộc là có thể duy trì tín dụng rẻ.
“Đặc biệt, phải phân biệt thiếu thanh khoản tạm thời với yếu kém về khả năng thanh toán. Ngân hàng có tài sản tốt nhưng thiếu tiền trong ngắn hạn cần được tiếp cận cơ chế hỗ trợ phù hợp. Ngân hàng thua lỗ, thiếu vốn hoặc chất lượng tài sản suy giảm phải được tái cơ cấu và bổ sung vốn. Hai tình trạng này không thể xử lý bằng cùng một cách”, ông nhấn mạnh.
Không để tăng trưởng tín dụng tạo áp lực ngược lên lãi suất
Muốn duy trì mặt bằng lãi suất ổn định, tốc độ tăng trưởng tín dụng cần phù hợp với khả năng huy động vốn ổn định, năng lực vốn tự có và khả năng quản trị rủi ro của các ngân hàng.
Về mặt kế toán, hoạt động cho vay có thể tạo ra tiền gửi trong hệ thống ngân hàng. Tuy nhiên, từng ngân hàng vẫn phải đáp ứng nhu cầu thanh toán, chuyển tiền và các yêu cầu an toàn vốn, thanh khoản. Khi tín dụng tăng nhanh, đặc biệt là cho vay trung và dài hạn, áp lực tìm kiếm nguồn vốn phù hợp có thể gia tăng.
Ông Lộc cho rằng cần đặt mục tiêu tăng trưởng tín dụng và mục tiêu lãi suất trong cùng một khuôn khổ. Nếu vừa thúc đẩy cho vay tăng rất nhanh, vừa muốn lãi suất giảm mạnh, trong khi nền tảng vốn và chất lượng tài sản chưa được cải thiện, chính sách sẽ tự tạo ra sức ép ngược chiều.
Về dài hạn, cần tăng vai trò của các chuẩn mực vốn, thanh khoản và quản trị rủi ro trong điều tiết tín dụng. Đây cũng là hướng cải cách được IMF đề xuất đối với Việt Nam: hiện đại hóa khuôn khổ tiền tệ và chuyển dần từ giới hạn tăng trưởng tín dụng sang cơ chế giám sát an toàn thận trọng phù hợp.

articles.title: Spotify confirms Family Plan crackdown, but calls it a 'routine improvement' | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Spotify confirmed the reports of its crackdown on Family Plan sharing during its third-quarter call with investors, calling its new method “a routine improvement” to its existing verification tools.
Over the past several days, reports had surfaced indicating that Spotify was rolling out a “QR code verification” method, where the app would prompt members on its Family Plan to verify they lived with the plan manager by scanning a QR code. This code appears on the plan manager’s phone, which the plan member then needs to scan with their own phone, according to Spotify’s support documentation.
Plan members have seven days to complete the QR code after getting a notification, which means they could be out of luck if they live outside the home and aren’t planning a return visit anytime soon. If the verification window is missed, they won’t be able to join another Family or Duo plan for 12 months, but would instead have to shift to an individual plan that they pay for themselves.
The move is meant to boost subscriptions to Spotify’s profitable Premium plans, rather than allowing adult children or friends who live apart from gaming the system to get a cheaper plan by splitting a Family Plan subscription.
During the earnings call, an investor asked a question about the crackdown and what it means, but Spotify co-CEO Alex Norström downplayed the change, calling it a “routine improvement,” not a “crackdown.”
“Family Plan has existed for a long while. It has been around for, I think it is now close to 12, 13 years in Spotify history, and it makes up a pretty significant proportion of our subscriber base,” said Norström. “As such, it is important for us to just make sure over time that we improve the verification methods that we have. There are certainly ways, over time, to find holes around it. As that happens, we figure out how to improve it over time,” he added.
The executive said that the company’s attempt to better verify its users is not something that would have an end date or would ever be complete, but would be considered an ongoing routine improvement.

articles.title: Zurich startup Enact raises $30M to give robots a sense of touch
articles.text:
Zurich-based Enact Intelligence has emerged from stealth with a $30M pre-seed round from redalpine, Notion Capital and firstminute capital. It builds robots that sense force and touch through their motors, not only cameras. Founder Manuel Yves Galliker previously led software for 1X’s NEO humanoid.
Enact Intelligence, a Zurich startup building robots that can feel force and touch, has come out of stealth with $30M in pre-seed funding, the company said on Thursday. Venture firms redalpine, Notion Capital and firstminute capital backed the round.
Angel investors include Mistral founder Arthur Mensch and Yann LeCun, whose own AI lab, AMI Labs, raised about $1B in March. Andrew Lonsberry, founder of Path Robotics, also invested.
Sifted reported it is the largest pre-seed round ever raised in Switzerland. It is about four times the $7.2M that Budapest’s Allonic raised in February to rebuild robot bodies, which its investors called a Hungarian record.
Most robots today rely mainly on cameras to understand the world, Enact says. That makes it hard for them to handle objects, work reliably and learn from experience.
Touch sensors can help, but they tend to be too costly and fragile for factory work, the company adds. The UK’s ARIA research agency is spending £52M on robot dexterity projects, including electronic skin, because robot hardware has lagged behind software.
Enact measures force inside a robot’s motors instead of with separate sensors. It compares this to the way people feel tension in their muscles, not only at their fingertips. The company says the approach works for anything from a simple robot arm to a full humanoid.
“We can build on top of existing models, like video models, and adapt them to output robot actions for interacting with the real world,” said Manuel Yves Galliker, Enact’s founder.
Galliker founded Enact in March. He previously led software for the NEO humanoid at 1X, whose new hands can sense touch, and then worked at robotics lab Physical Intelligence. Enact’s 12-person team includes engineers from DeepMind, Amazon Robotics and defence firm Helsing.
He chose Zurich over the Bay Area on purpose. “Silicon Valley has traditionally been very strong in software and AI, but it’s lacking in robotics and hardware engineering talent,” he said. Zurich is also home to Gravis Robotics, which raised $200M in August for software that lets diggers work on their own.
Enact plans to grow its team fivefold by the end of 2027 and speed up its hardware work. It is in talks with large European companies in manufacturing, infrastructure, retail and food processing to put its first robots to work.

articles.title: The FCC is beginning to block gadgets with ‘foreign surveillance chips’
articles.text:
On October 13th, Brendan Carr’s FCC gave itself a new power — it can block gadgets for containing any computer chip made by any company on its list of potential threats to national security. Today, it’s exercising that power for the first time, blocking two gadgets because they contain “foreign surveillance chips,” the FCC claims.
The FCC is beginning to block gadgets with ‘foreign surveillance chips’
The first exercise of a new FCC power.
The first exercise of a new FCC power.
The agency doesn’t say which specific gadgets it blocked, and it didn’t immediately respond to our request for comment, but it does name the “surveillance chip”: it’s a HiVision Hi3516CV610 UHD Smart Vision SoC, a chip that turns a raw camera sensor into a home security camera, a dashcam, or the like. It’s often sold as a package with a Sony camera sensor and sometimes even a lens already on board, according to listings we viewed on AliExpress.
The FCC is calling it a foreign surveillance chip because HiVision advertises it as “designed for the surveillance market” with “[b]uilt in detection algorithms for human faces,” the FCC explains — and because HiVision is a subsidiary of Huawei, one of the first telecom companies the US government decided to call a national security risk.
Huawei is indeed on the FCC’s Covered List, and the FCC’s new power helps it close a loophole where companies could sneak in banned companies’ products inside another company’s gadgets. It did something similar when it gave itself the power to retroactively ban gadgets, and when it gave itself the power to block modular radio transmitters.
As with the router ban and the Roomba ban, he question remains: is the FCC keeping people safer, or just picking winners and losers while making a show of enforcement? We’ve asked the agency many times to chat about its efforts, but it won’t engage.

articles.title: Tăng tiền đặt cọc đấu giá đất lên 50%: Ngăn được đại gia tiềm lực giấu mặt vung tiền?
articles.text:
Tiền đặt trước cao có thể gây bất lợi cho người mua ở thực
Dự án Luật Đấu giá tài sản (sửa đổi) vừa được trình Quốc hội sáng 19/10, trong đó đề xuất nâng mức tiền đặt trước tối thiểu khi đấu giá quyền sử dụng đất để giao đất ở cho cá nhân từ 10% lên 20% giá khởi điểm, giữ nguyên mức tối đa 50%.
Các đề xuất này được kỳ vọng hạn chế tình trạng trả giá cao bất thường rồi bỏ cọc, gây nhiễu loạn thị trường bất động sản. Tuy nhiên, theo các chuyên gia, tăng tiền đặt trước hay siết quyền tham gia đấu giá chưa đủ để giải quyết tận gốc tình trạng đầu cơ, thổi giá đất.
Chia sẻ với PV VietNamNet, TS Lê Bá Chí Nhân, chuyên gia kinh tế, cho rằng nâng mức tiền đặt trước lên 20-50% giá khởi điểm là biện pháp nhằm tăng trách nhiệm tài chính của người tham gia, hạn chế tình trạng trả giá vượt xa giá trị thực rồi bỏ cọc.
Theo ông Nhân, mức đặt trước tối đa 50% có thể tạo ra rào cản tài chính đáng kể, buộc người tham gia cân nhắc kỹ năng lực vốn và khả năng thực hiện nghĩa vụ sau đấu giá. Qua đó, chính sách góp phần sàng lọc những người thiếu năng lực tài chính, hạn chế hành vi trả giá tùy tiện.
Tuy nhiên, nếu tỷ lệ đặt trước quá cao, người có nhu cầu mua đất để ở nhưng nguồn vốn hạn chế có thể gặp khó khăn khi tham gia. Trong khi đó, những tổ chức, cá nhân sở hữu nguồn tiền lớn vẫn có lợi thế hơn.
Vì vậy, theo ông Nhân, chính sách cần bảo đảm hài hòa giữa việc thiết lập kỷ luật thị trường và quyền tiếp cận bình đẳng của người tham gia đấu giá.
Vị chuyên gia nhấn mạnh, bỏ cọc không phải nguyên nhân duy nhất khiến giá đất bị méo mó. Giá đất còn chịu tác động của thông tin quy hoạch, tình trạng khan hiếm nguồn cung, tâm lý đám đông và hoạt động đầu cơ có tổ chức.
Nếu chỉ tăng tiền đặt trước mà thiếu cơ chế giám sát hành vi thông đồng, minh bạch thông tin và kiểm soát các giao dịch bất thường, thị trường vẫn có thể xuất hiện những phương thức thao túng khác.
Để hạn chế tình trạng này, ông Nhân đề xuất thiết kế mức đặt trước linh hoạt theo tính chất, quy mô và rủi ro của từng cuộc đấu giá, thay vì áp dụng cứng một mức tối đa. Đồng thời, cần công khai đầy đủ thông tin quy hoạch, giá khởi điểm, điều kiện pháp lý và nghĩa vụ tài chính; xử lý nghiêm hành vi thông đồng, cung cấp thông tin sai lệch và cố tình bỏ cọc.
Cùng với đó, cơ quan quản lý cần theo dõi giá trúng đấu giá so với mặt bằng thị trường, kết hợp kiểm tra nguồn vốn và việc thực hiện nghĩa vụ thanh toán theo quy định.
TS Trần Xuân Lượng, Phó Viện trưởng Viện Nghiên cứu Đánh giá thị trường bất động sản Việt Nam, cho rằng biện pháp này có thể hạn chế người thiếu năng lực tài chính, nhưng chưa chắc ngăn được nhà đầu tư lớn có tiềm lực.
Với những người kỳ vọng thu lợi lớn từ việc đẩy giá đất, khoản tiền đặt trước bị mất có thể không đủ sức răn đe. Một số đối tượng còn có thể sử dụng người khác đứng tên tham gia đấu giá.
Theo chuyên gia này, cần phân biệt rõ mục đích tham gia đấu giá, gồm mua đất để ở, đầu tư phát triển dự án hay đầu cơ, mua đi bán lại kiếm lời trong thời gian ngắn. Việc quản lý nên gắn với nguồn tiền, lịch sử sở hữu bất động sản và quá trình sử dụng đất sau khi trúng đấu giá.
Ông cũng đề xuất nghiên cứu chính sách thuế phù hợp để hạn chế đầu cơ ngắn hạn, đồng thời xây dựng cơ sở dữ liệu đất đai thống nhất nhằm hỗ trợ cơ quan quản lý xác định lịch sử sở hữu và phát hiện các trường hợp có dấu hiệu bất thường.
Theo ông Lượng, nâng tiền đặt trước lên quá cao chưa chắc mang lại hiệu quả như kỳ vọng, bởi người có tiềm lực tài chính vẫn có thể sử dụng người khác đứng tên tham gia đấu giá.
Cần phân biệt từng trường hợp bỏ cọc để áp “lệnh” cấm
Bên cạnh việc nâng tiền đặt trước, dự luật đề xuất cấm tham gia đấu giá quyền sử dụng đất trên phạm vi toàn quốc từ 6 tháng đến 5 năm đối với người trúng đấu giá nhưng không nộp đủ tiền, dẫn đến kết quả đấu giá bị hủy.
TS Lê Bá Chí Nhân nhận xét đây là biện pháp tăng tính răn đe, nâng cao trách nhiệm của người tham gia và hạn chế tình trạng trả giá cao bất thường nhằm tạo mặt bằng giá ảo rồi rút lui.
“Khi một số cá nhân cố tình đẩy giá lên cao nhưng không thực hiện nghĩa vụ tài chính, hậu quả không chỉ dừng lại ở một cuộc đấu giá thất bại. Giá trúng đấu giá bất thường còn có thể trở thành thông tin tham chiếu sai lệch, kích thích tâm lý đầu cơ, đẩy kỳ vọng giá đất lên cao, làm tăng chi phí tiếp cận nhà ở và gây méo mó quyết định đầu tư của doanh nghiệp”, ông nói.
Do đó, theo ông Nhân, xử lý hành vi bỏ cọc có chủ đích cũng là cách bảo vệ tính minh bạch của thị trường.
Nếu được thiết kế hợp lý, quy định cấm tham gia đấu giá trong một thời hạn xác định sẽ buộc người tham gia cân nhắc kỹ năng lực tài chính trước khi trả giá, góp phần sàng lọc những trường hợp tham gia nhằm đầu cơ ngắn hạn, trục lợi hoặc thao túng tâm lý thị trường.
Tuy nhiên, ông Nhân lưu ý không nên đánh đồng mọi trường hợp bỏ cọc. Cần phân biệt hành vi cố tình vi phạm, thông đồng, thao túng với những tình huống bất khả kháng hoặc phát sinh tranh chấp khách quan.
Chế tài cần có căn cứ pháp lý rõ ràng, thời hạn áp dụng tương xứng, đồng thời bảo đảm quyền giải trình và cơ chế khiếu nại. Cùng với đó, cần xây dựng cơ sở dữ liệu thống nhất về người vi phạm, công khai kết quả đấu giá và tăng cường giám sát các giao dịch có dấu hiệu bất thường.
TS Trần Xuân Lượng cũng cho rằng cần thận trọng khi áp dụng lệnh cấm, bởi việc bỏ cọc có thể xuất phát từ nhiều nguyên nhân, không phải trường hợp nào cũng nhằm thao túng thị trường hoặc trục lợi.
Chẳng hạn, người trúng đấu giá có thể gặp biến cố cá nhân hoặc thay đổi về khả năng tài chính khiến họ không thể tiếp tục giao dịch. Vì vậy, nếu áp dụng lệnh cấm một cách cứng nhắc, chính sách có thể chưa phản ánh đúng bản chất của từng trường hợp.
Ngoài các biện pháp trên, ông Lượng đề xuất nghiên cứu cơ chế xác định giá sàn và giá trần trong đấu giá quyền sử dụng đất, dựa trên căn cứ phù hợp về giá trị đất đai và điều kiện thị trường. Theo đó, giá sàn nhằm hạn chế nguy cơ thất thoát tài sản Nhà nước, còn giá trần có thể góp phần hạn chế tình trạng giá trúng đấu giá bị đẩy lên quá cao, gây tác động tiêu cực đến mặt bằng giá bất động sản.
“Nâng tiền đặt cọc hay hạn chế quyền tham gia đấu giá của người từng bỏ cọc chỉ là những giải pháp riêng lẻ. Muốn kiểm soát hiệu quả tình trạng đầu cơ, thổi giá đất, cần quản lý chặt mục đích sử dụng đất, minh bạch nguồn tiền, hoàn thiện dữ liệu và xây dựng chính sách thuế phù hợp, đồng thời có cơ chế giám sát việc thực hiện cam kết sau đấu giá”, ông Lượng nêu quan điểm.

articles.title: Investors break down how founders can raise a Series A today | TechCrunch
articles.text:
In today’s market, no single metric defines what a Series A is, or how to raise one. At this year’s TechCrunch Disrupt, three investors offered founders advice on raising one, and one of them tacked on a warning. With money pouring into AI and revenue numbers being inflated to justify sky-high valuations, a correction could come as soon as 2027.
The warning came from Shailendra Singh, a managing director at Peak XV, who spoke alongside Jahanvi Sardana, a partner at Index Ventures, and Janelle Teng Wade, a partner at Bessemer. “Seed and venture, I’ve never seen it as dysfunctional as it is now,” Singh said, adding that the current market is one of the hardest to raise in that he has seen.
“The burden is high to convince any top firm that you are amongst the few special companies that can break out, and then the dispersion is very high on the terms you might get, how much capital you can raise, and what terms you can raise it,” he continued. In fact, it’s common now to see a company trying to close a round with as many as three different prices at once. “[I]’s a crazy sign of market froth,” he said.
“We’re calling it the ‘tranchopalooza,’” Sardana added, referring to the way rounds are being split into tranches, or separate chunks.
Beyond the warnings, the investors laid out what they look for in a Series A pitch, including, first, a persuasive story about why a founder has a shot at building a big company. “Founders who can attract very high-quality talent have an advantage,” Singh added.
What a founder builds matters, too. Teng Wade said capital is flowing into areas such as defense, robotics, and AI infrastructure. She also noted that foundational model companies are moving toward vertical integration (taking on more of the stack themselves), but there’s still room for newer players, including neo-clouds that rent out AI computing power and neo-labs focused on AI research.
Metrics, meanwhile, still help a lot, but they are less defined than they used to be, especially in an era like AI where it’s incredibly expensive to run a company. Teng Wade gave an example of how her firm evaluated Anthropic in its early days, when its margins were negative, and it was spending heavily on compute.
One partner on her team, however, felt that AI was going to be “bigger than everything we’ve ever expected in terms of price premium on the frontier models,” she said, “becoming a substitute for other types of software.” The logic was that even with money-losing margins, the market would be big enough to pay off if the company became one of the top three players. Anthropic is now reportedly preparing an IPO at a valuation of around $2 trillion. It told investors this month it was profitable on an adjusted basis, though that measure excludes some costs.
The investors also spoke about the importance of honesty in a market like this, where inflated annual recurring revenue (ARR) numbers are swirling alongside headline valuations. “I tell founders, If you ever show a chart which shows cumulative revenue or cumulative ARR, that is a massive red flag,” Singh said. “It means that your time series data is not good because cumulative data is a big lie.” Added Singh: It’s important for a company to be intellectually honest in how they are presenting and engaging in bull cycles.”
Singh said the market is full of “false positives” because “it can’t be that every company is going to be successful. This is as optimistic as I’ve seen the venture world in two decades, and normally it’s a sign. I think 2027 will be different. I think we will see a correction.”
Finally, the panelists were asked to give founders at least one piece of parting advice. Singh went first, reminding founders that building a company is one of the “most excruciatingly difficult things” one can do. And with that, “deal with it,” he said. He also urged founders not to rush into something, to watch out for weak product-market fit, and always hold the bar very high for what they are trying to solve.
Sardana said it is important to know how to pitch but that founders should be careful not to let that dictate what they build. “It feels like [founders are] deciding what to build based on what’s getting funded, which is really scary,” she continued. Teng Wade, meanwhile, said her typical advice of telling founders to be conservative with their projections and requests hasn’t really held up.
“I would say just be audacious in your ask,” she now says, and see how the market responds, “and then you can tailor from there.”

articles.title: Universal Music Group licenses songs to AI gaming music service TYGER
articles.text:
Universal Music Group (UMG) will license music from its artists and songwriters to TYGER. The service uses AI to make songs follow the action in a video game as people play.
The two companies announced the deal today, with UMG the first major music company to license the service, they said.
Under the agreement, selected recordings and songs from UMG’s record and publishing catalogues will join TYGER’s paid, on-demand subscription. Some UMG recordings will also appear on its free tier, which carries ads.
TYGER runs alongside games rather than inside them, so studios do not have to build it in. Players choose the music. The licensed tracks then change in real time to match what happens on screen, using what the company calls its patented technology.
The service works on PC, console and mobile, according to TYGER. It is in closed beta across more than 20 games, which together have more than 540 million monthly players, the company said.
Its library holds more than 400,000 songs, mostly from independent artists.
“Gaming is where the next generation spends its time, discovers culture and connects with friends, but music has never had a native way to reach those audiences,” said Nick Venti, TYGER’s chief executive and co-founder.
For UMG, the deal offers its artists a new way to reach players. The company said it expects music to play a bigger part in gaming.
Michael Nash, UMG’s chief digital officer, said its artists “will now be able to soundtrack personalized gameplay experiences and connect with millions of gamers and fans around the world.”
With the UMG catalogue added, TYGER plans to relaunch later this year. The relaunch will bring an updated free, ad-supported tier and a new subscription offer.

articles.title: Sure, let’s smoosh SpaceX and Tesla together, who cares
articles.text:
Oh sure, SpaceX’s credit risk is pretty high because it’s about to borrow another $40 billion to spend on Nvidia chips, but who cares about that? SpaceX and Tesla have formed special committees to discuss a merger!
Sure, let’s smoosh SpaceX and Tesla together, who cares
Yes, of course there are pay package incentives in play for Musk. But that’s not all.
Sure, let’s smoosh SpaceX and Tesla together, who cares
Yes, of course there are pay package incentives in play for Musk. But that’s not all.
The degree to which you find this merger compelling likely has to do with the degree to which you believe Elon Musk about wanting to go to Mars, or “spread the light of consciousness,” as he put it in this week’s SpaceX earnings call (and earlier S-1). Now, a reasonably informed person knows that we don’t have the technology — or, frankly, even the raw information to build the technology — in order to support human life in space. So that means robots. But a lag between Earth and the Moon or Mars makes for difficulty in controlling the robots. So having artificially intelligent robots who can make decisions on their own with minimal supervision from Earth is the next sci-fi logic step.
“There’s a lot to be gained from cooperating on developing superintelligence software.”
If you believe Musk’s story, the technology we are talking about is being developed through self-driving cars (Tesla), LLMs (SpaceX), and humanoid robots (Tesla), all of which require data centers (SpaceX). Conveniently, we have just had earnings for both companies. On the other hand, if you view Mars as a useful fiction Musk uses to explain his antics in public, well, there’s a lot of money and a lot of control Musk gets from the merger.
Musk said on the recent SpaceX earnings call that “there’s a lot of merit to combining” SpaceX and Tesla. Why? “There’s a lot to be gained from cooperating on developing superintelligence software.” But artificial intelligence — ah, excuse me, super intelligence software isn’t the business SpaceX is really in right now. In its Q3 earnings on Tuesday, SpaceX reported $7.56 billion in revenue from the artificial intelligence — sorry, sorry, super intelligence division. The subcategory “SI solutions & infrastructure revenues” — which I think is Grok, Cursor, and the neocloud business wrapped together — jumped to $7 billion, or more than three times what it was last quarter. Now some of this was getting Cursor stapled on, which added $608 million in revenue. Most of the rest of that $7 billion was likely renting out compute to Anthropic and Google; Grok is probably contributing less, says Gil Luria, an analyst at DA Davidson.
At first blush, this may look comparable to the revenue of a company like Anthropic, whose leaked S-1 shows the company had $16.3 billion in revenue in the first half of this year from its frontier models. But SpaceX’s AI business looks more like CoreWeave than Anthropic. While we are told in the press release there was “increased Grok adoption across enterprise customers and consumers,” that number wasn’t broken out from bare-metal revenue. And if Musk wanted to brag about it, he would.
As for Tesla, which released Q3 results on Wednesday, its earnings sucked — a second consecutive quarter of declining profits. That’s because Musk is apparently not especially interested in normal cars anymore. Instead, Tesla is focusing on robots and, I guess, self-driving taxis. (There was also a Roadster hopping car demo recently, but that’s not going into production for a couple years, it’s very expensive, and Tesla cannot guarantee it will be delivered.) Musk did not elaborate on his comments about the merger on the Tesla call.
Macroharder
SpaceX and Tesla have some tie-ups already; SpaceX, for instance, bought $131 million of the low-selling Cybertrucks from Tesla. It has, in the past, held Tesla bonds. More crucially, the companies have also announced two AI — fuck it, we’re just sticking with AI — projects together: Terafab and Macrohard.
Terafab is the chip-making venture that Musk intends to build in Texas and run to supply himself with chips; Intel is partnered, kinda, with Musk to develop the technology. Macrohard is, uh, an AI project that lets people simulate software already made by Microsoft. At least, I think that’s what it’s supposed to be. Typing the name of the latter makes me pray for the asteroid to hit us all right now, so perhaps it’s fortunate that we haven’t heard much about it since the announcement in March.
“Musk has a history of setting timelines that his companies have missed,” Reuters notes, with a degree of what I can only describe as wry understatement
SpaceX’s S-1 from May said that Terafab and Microhard “are in the very early stages, as a result of which we and Tesla have not finalized a variety of details relating to our collaboration, including, but not limited to, financial terms, intellectual property rights, and the ultimate term of our collaboration.” As of earlier this month, Intel’s CEO said the company remained committed to the partnership, but it’s not obligated to remain part of Terafab and the S-1 says there may never be a definitive agreement. Intel’s Thomas Hannaford didn’t immediately respond to my emails asking if anything had been signed in the interim.
On this week’s call with SpaceX investors, Musk claimed the Terafab will reach volume production in the second half of 2028. He also said the company will have its first test chip from the facility in May or June 2027. “Musk has a history of setting timelines that his companies have missed,” Reuters notes, with a degree of what I can only describe as wry understatement. When an analyst on the call asked if Musk had placed orders for machines needed to make cutting-edge equipment, Musk did not answer.
Companies often are doing more privately than they announce publicly, so I do not view the S-1 filing as fully definitive. But Macrohard isn’t mentioned in the last 10Q. Neither is Terafab.
The Matt Levine case for the SpaceX-Tesla merger
Musk is going to pound the table about the Moon, Mars, “and beyond,” and a significant chunk of his fan base is very into this. But there are maybe some boring financial reasons shareholders may have an interest.
Let’s say you are constitutionally very different from me, and much richer, and for this reason you own a number of shares in Tesla. You’re a big believer in Elon Musk — obviously — but you notice that the man has an attention span of a squirrel on cocaine. He’s on X basically constantly and often racistly. He keeps showing up at the White House to do stuff that pisses off would-be Tesla customers. Then he publicly feuds with the president. Sometimes he’s very excited about rockets, and sometimes he’s very excited about Dogecoin and sometimes he’s really into Grok and sometimes he thinks about cars. But you notice that one way or the other he’s been thinking about cars a lot less lately.
Basically all you have to do is say “Nvidia” and someone will give you a fuckton of money
Since he seems to be focused — insofar as he can be said to focus — on AI, you notice some pretty big conflicts of interest. Musk’s companies “all need the same scarce Nvidia chips to power their AI, for instance,” notes Matt Levine, a longtime Musk observer. But if you combine the companies, well, maybe you build the best general-purpose AI. And then? “If you build the best general-purpose AI model, maybe it can drive the cars and operate the robots and upload people’s brains and serve right-wing takes on Twitter.”
Also, there’s a massive AI infrastructure buildout happening, and so basically all you have to do is say “Nvidia” and someone will give you a fuckton of money. The merger puts all the AI projects in one pile, plus also some cars and rockets and satellites I guess. “‘Give us $100 billion to build data centers in space, but if for some reason we don’t build data centers in space you can repossess our car factories and data centers on earth’ is a good pitch to credit investors,” Levine writes.
Musk also has a history — not always successful — of building physical infrastructure. This is, at least from my point of view, a better bet when it comes to building data centers than some Bitcoin miners who pivoted. “If Elon builds at the rate he talked about, he will have lots of extra capacity and be able to sell much of it,” says Luria.
From this point of view, obviously SpaceX and Tesla should merge, Levine writes:
It’s crazy that they are separate companies! One guy runs two gigantic physical AI companies with huge overlaps! What a nightmare of conflicts of interest and red tape! Just merge them, so that the one guy can come into the office each day with a simple mandate: Make the choices that maximize overall value for the giant AI complex, and for the shareholders of that complex. If some chips or engineers or drills or whatever should be working on robots, work on the robots; if they should be working on data centers, work on the data centers. The shareholders have come this far; surely they trust Musk to make those decisions. It’s just that right now, working on the robots is good for Tesla and bad for SpaceX; working on the data centers is bad for Tesla and good for SpaceX. Musk can’t put both of their interests first. There’s an easy fix.
It’s not exactly that simple, of course. The details of the deal matter; a lot of people are assuming a stock-for-stock merger. (“I assume the acquirer would be SpaceX, in part because it has a bigger market capitalization but mostly because of Musk’s greater control there,” Levine writes.) So does the regulatory environment. The case that SpaceX and Tesla should combine due to AI is also kind of an antitrust reason they shouldn’t?
The current regulatory environment is, in large part due to Musk’s meddling via his DOGE cronies, let’s say lax. Donald Trump, the current president, has two more years left in his term. Also, the markets have started getting waves of nervousness around AI. Earlier this summer, there was the Situational Awareness thing, and then there was the more recent CoreWeave thing, and, well, investor sentiment may be changing. That means “there’s a push to announce a deal by the first half of 2027 so that it closes during this administration,” Bloomberg writes, attributing this to “people who are familiar with the matter.”
Musk has more control at SpaceX than he does at Tesla. His voting power is above 50 percent, because he owns special supervoting shares. He is the CEO, CTO, and chairman of the board. Shareholders are very limited in how they can legally challenge that power. The filing puts it this way: “This will limit or preclude your ability to influence corporate matters and the election of our directors.”
At Tesla, however, Musk only has about 20 percent of the vote. (“Only!”) So in a stock-for-stock merger, where SpaceX is the acquirer, Musk suddenly has voting control of the whole enchilada. “He gets voting control of Tesla in the only way he can,” says Ann Lipton, a professor at the University of Colorado Boulder’s law school. “He can’t change it to a dual-class entity now that it’s publicly traded. This is the only way to do it.”
If SpaceX pays $2 trillion or more for Tesla, Musk gets a payout
Both companies are based in Texas, which makes it very difficult for shareholders to sue, says Lipton. “The chances of a shareholder being able to sue on the Tesla or SpaceX side are vanishingly small because Texas has erected so many barriers to shareholder litigation.” So there’s that risk gone.
Leave aside the more complicated issues of national security (for SpaceX) and antitrust. At a federal level, securities laws are largely “Did you disclose it?” notes Lipton. So the SEC, or what remains of it, will want to see that everything is disclosed to shareholders before the vote. As long as the disclosures are accurate, that’s that. At the state level, there may be some issues — it’s a breach of fiduciary duty to create an unfair transaction as a result of conflicts of interest — but Shari Redstone did merge Paramount and CBS, so it’s not impossible.
What does Musk get from this merger? Well, control, a thing he historically loves most of all. Potentially also, the combination adds $110 billion to his net worth, according to Bloomberg. More interesting, however, is how the merger interacts with Musk’s massive Tesla compensation package. If there’s a legal change of control — for instance, because SpaceX buys Tesla — the operational milestones in Musk’s enormous pay package fall away.
What matters then is Tesla’s valuation. If SpaceX pays $2 trillion or more, Musk gets a payout. At $2 trillion, Musk gets $6 billion of shares. He also gets accelerated vesting of shares from his 2018 pay package — which would otherwise have vested in 2028. The change of control also means he can sell them sooner.
Is that good for SpaceX? Assuming we wind up at or around the $2 trillion figure, we’re looking at basically a merger of equals — which means current SpaceX shareholders get diluted all to hell. Worse, Tesla’s business is stagnating, and its AI ambitions are expensive. “It’s likely that SpaceX and Tesla combined will spend close to a staggering $50 billion on capex in Q4, and their businesses won’t come close to covering that number,” writes Shawn Tully in Fortune.
So on a numbers basis, I kind of think no, not really, not that good for SpaceX. But none of Musk’s businesses are about numbers in the end — they are, to some extent, about how much you believe in Elon Musk. That’s what the Tesla valuation versus regular automakers was about in the first place. So sure, fine, slap them together and see what happens. The people who are buying what Musk’s selling, at this point, surely know what they signed up for.

articles.title: Spotify's current AI bet is about being the music service that agents choose | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Spotify had a strong third quarter, reaching 788 million monthly active users and generating nearly €5 billion (around $5.6 billion USD) in revenue. But the more interesting takeaway from its earnings call was how the company sees people listening to music in the future, and why the rise of AI agents could be good news for its business.
Co-CEO Gustav Söderström thinks the music streaming giant is particularly well-suited to this shift.
“Spotify is in one of the few categories that actually stands to thrive in the agentic age,” Söderström tells investors. “This is because agents excel at replacing and taking care of things people would rather not do. People love getting rid of chores. But entertainment is the opposite. Nobody asks an agent to ‘summarize a song’ for them.”
Instead of opening Spotify, searching for an artist, and building a playlist themselves, listeners could ask an AI assistant to do the work for them. They might want music for a run, a podcast about something they’ve been discussing with an AI, or an audiobook recap that picks up exactly where they left off.
Spotify wants to be the service those agents turn to, letting people discover music and interact with Spotify through conversations rather than just its own app. Notably, Spotify was the first music service to integrate with Meta’s Muse assistant, and it also integrates with ChatGPT and Claude.
“Our goal is to be the media service that you use from any agent, really turning the growth of agents into a tailwind rather than a headwind. That is exactly what we are seeing now. We are seeing really good adoption of Spotify inside these agents. While other companies are maybe trying to figure out what to do and many are leaning out, we are actually leaning in and participating in the growth instead of standing by the roadside and looking at it,” said Söderström.
The market is already showing signs of friction over how agents access third-party services. Amazon, for example, has blocked Meta’s Muse from shopping on its platform, illustrating how major players may restrict outside agents when questions arise around access, security, privacy, or commercial control.
Spotify’s pitch isn’t just that AI should just make entertainment easier to find. It should make the experience more personal, too.
Söderström describes Spotify today as “an intelligent media service encapsulated as an agent, whether you use it directly through our application or via another agent…Spotify is now an agent that you can not only click on in our app, but talk to, ask questions of, and instruct. We can do things today that no other media services can do,” he said.
“For example, you can ask Spotify to go through your listening history song by song back to 2008, picking your true favorites, beat-stretching them by speeding them up or down, and then sorting them by key and BPM. Then you can ask it to mix them together into the perfect running playlist at your exact cadence,” Söderström explained.
Spotify has years of listening history to draw on, including the artists people return to, the songs they skip, and the music they discover. That information can help it make recommendations that feel more personal than a generic playlist generated by an AI assistant that doesn’t know much about someone’s tastes.
However, Söderström also emphasized that Spotify isn’t sending its listener data to partners. Instead, the agent asks Spotify for something, and Spotify uses its own systems to reason about the request and choose what to play.

articles.title: Meta reports $825B in future lease and contract commitments
articles.text:
Meta has signed up to about $825bn in future leases and contracts, most of them for the data centres and computing power behind its AI push. The figures are in its quarterly filing with US regulators, dated October 22, 2026.
Bloomberg reported the total by adding together three items in the filing. In July, the news agency put Meta’s commitments at almost $700bn.
The largest item is $454.5bn in contracts that Meta cannot cancel. According to the filing, these mostly cover cloud capacity bought from other companies, plus servers and network equipment. They also include energy supply for data centres and hardware for Reality Labs, its virtual reality unit.
About $45.9bn of those contracts fall due in the rest of 2026, and $121.4bn in 2027.
Meta also has $355.7bn in leases that have not started yet, so they do not appear on its balance sheet. They cover data centres, energy infrastructure, shared server space and network equipment. The leases begin between now and 2036 and run for up to 30 years.
The third item is a deal to buy up to $14.7bn of cloud capacity over five years. That amount could shrink if the cloud provider sells the capacity to other customers, the filing says.
The commitments come on top of heavy spending now. In its third-quarter results on Wednesday, Meta said capital expenditure, including finance lease payments, reached $34.9bn in the three months to September 30. Free cash flow was negative $2.1bn.
Meta now expects to spend $135bn to $145bn this year, narrowing an earlier range of $130bn to $145bn.
“Our investments are paying off, the core business is strong, and we’re seeing velocity across the board,” said Mark Zuckerberg, Meta’s chief executive, in the results statement.
At the same time, Meta plans to create non-voting Class C shares, effective from January 19, 2027. The filing says the company expects to use them to sell new shares to investors in the future.
Meta’s shares fell about 3% in pre-market trading on Thursday. The cost of insuring Meta’s debt against default also hit a record. Its five-year credit default swaps reached about 119 basis points, according to ICE Data Services figures cited in market reports.

articles.title: Etsy bans AI-generated recipes and patterns from its online marketplace
articles.text:
Etsy said Thursday it will no longer allow merchants to sell AI-generated recipes and patterns on its online marketplace, as part of a wider push to set firmer rules around the use of artificial intelligence on its platform.
In a blog post, Etsy said it's banning the sale of "functional guides" that are created using AI, including patterns, cooking recipes and instructions. The products are usually marketed as digital downloads, such as crochet or sewing patterns. Users then "put in effort to achieve a finished product," the company said.
Sellers will also be required to show an actual item made using the instructions, not an AI-generated or simulated result, "so buyers know what to expect," Etsy said.
Etsy said in a separate notice to sellers that it was making the changes as AI threatens to erode buyers' and sellers' trust in the platform.
"Today, many active buyers say they can't tell which items involve AI-generated content," the company wrote. "It's become a top-three barrier to shopping more often on Etsy. And you, our seller community, have told us you're concerned about your work appearing alongside items that use AI in misleading ways, and that it's becoming harder for buyers to recognize your role in creating your items."
As part of the move, Etsy said it's barring sellers from creating bot-generated listings without any human involvement. Sellers will also be required to include at least one unedited photo of the actual item they're selling.
Etsy told sellers it will continue to allow AI-generated art on its platform as long as merchants "play a clear role in what they create and are transparent about the process."
"Sellers must still disclose when an item is created using AI and cannot misrepresent AI-generated work as handmade or entirely their own creation," the company added.
Founded in 2005, Etsy is known for its mix of craft makers and artisan goods. The company has been leaning more into that reputation as it has battled an influx of generic, mass-produced items from resellers and increasing competition from Amazon and Walmart, as well as newer e-commerce upstarts like TikTok, Temu and Shein.
Misleading, AI-generated products or images present a new challenge for Etsy and other online marketplaces. Etsy has in recent years struggled to curb the proliferation of AI-made crochet patterns and other AI "slop." Amazon recently required sellers to label photos or videos that feature AI-generated people in response to recent legislation mandating the disclosure.
While Etsy has cracked down on the use of AI in listings, it's been infusing the technology throughout more of its website. The company has used AI to build more detailed profiles of shoppers and surface relevant products in search results.
Etsy has also partnered with OpenAI on shopping features, including launching a ChatGPT app for product discovery.

articles.title: Japan core inflation in September surges to its highest this year at 2.1%
articles.text:
Japan's core inflation in September hit its highest this year at 2.1%, overshooting analysts' expectations, on the back of elevated energy prices and higher import costs due to a weak yen.
Core inflation, which strips out prices of fresh food, was in line with than the 2.1% forecast by economists polled by Reuters, and accelerated from the 1.7% in the month before.
Headline inflation came in at 2.1%, while the so-called "core-core" inflation, which excludes prices of fresh food and energy and is the Bank of Japan's preferred gauge, was at 2.4%.
Higher inflation could push the Bank of Japan for another rate hike this year, after a 25 basis points increase in September, as the central bank normalizes its monetary approach after decades of reflationary policy. Japan raised rates to a three-decade high of 1.25% in September.
Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama reportedly told parliament on Wednesday that Japan was "on the cusp of shifting to a period of sustained inflation driven by rising wages," while acknowledging that higher import costs were also contributing to price growth.
Oil import costs have risen as Japan buys energy from more expensive U.S. sources and switches away from Middle Eastern suppliers oil due to the Iranian conflict. Weakness in yen is also making oil cost more for Japan.
When Katayama was asked by a lawmaker whether the government's tax cut plan could conflict with the central bank's efforts to combat inflation with interest rate hikes, he said, "I see no gap between the view of the government and that of the BOJ," Reuters reported.
On Tuesday, Japan's Lower House began debating a bill to cut the consumption tax on food to 1% from 8% for two years, public broadcaster NHK reported. It also includes provisions for support payments to workers based on income levels.
