articles.title: Stock futures are little changed after tech sector sell-off: Live updates
articles.text:
U.S. equity futures were about flat on Thursday evening after tech stocks sold off on concerns that the artificial intelligence trade may be faltering, at least for the near term.
Futures tied to the Dow Jones Industrial Average advanced 52 points, or 0.1%. S&P 500 futures gained 0.06%, and Nasdaq-100 futures slipped 0.1%.
In regular trading, the S&P 500 sank 1.2%, and the Nasdaq Composite slid 2.6%. The broad market benchmark posted its worst session since July, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq had its worst day since June. The Dow Industrials bucked the trend and closed marginally higher.
In Asia, South Korea's benchmark Kospi Index fell 2.42%, while Japan's Nikkei 225 lost 0.49%. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 was 0.21% lower.
Worries around artificial intelligence spending weighed down the market and dragged the U.S. tech sector to a 3% decline on the day. Nvidia dropped 4.4%, Alphabet fell 3.2%, and Advanced Micro Devices declined 8.1% as losses occurred in different parts of the technology sector.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told CNBC on Thursday he thought capital within the AI buildout was becoming scarce.
"There's a scarcity of capital. The demand [for] the capital is much greater than the availability of the capital," Huang said when asked about the neocloud segment of the AI buildout, which is proving to be fragile.
Ed Yardeni, president of Yardeni Research, described the AI trade on Thursday as a "bubble" but said that some depressurization wouldn't be all bad.
"Taking some air out of the AI bubble is a good thing. I don't think it's going to burst and create problems for the economy," he said, pointing to the bond market as a source of capital competition for equities.
Bond yields eased on Thursday, with the 10-year Treasury sliding 18.5 basis points to 4.961% as traders bid up safe-haven assets. The yield on the 30-year slid 15 basis points, and the 2-year yield fell 17.5 basis points.
Brent crude prices spiked following a report that the U.S. and Israel were drawing up plans for renewed attacks on Iran as part of the regional war that started in late February. Brent jumped 4% to end the session at $113.17, the highest settle since May.
On the week, the S&P 500 is heading for a slim gain, up less than 0.1%, while the Nasdaq is down 0.5% in the period. The Dow is tracking for a 1.7% advance.
On the economic front, traders will be watching for the final reading of the University of Michigan's consumer sentiment report.

articles.title: Meta’s deal to keep Zuckerberg in California adds fuel to wealth tax debate ahead of election
articles.text:
In case there were any doubts, Mark Zuckerberg is staying in California.
Meta was apparently concerned enough that its founder and CEO might depart its home state that the company put in place a new stock plan that could help offset the burden of higher taxes should a billionaires tax, known as Proposition 40, pass on Election Day on Nov. 3.
The disclosure came in a filing on Wednesday that coincided with Meta's third-quarter earnings report, and represents a first among California's mega-cap tech companies. Zuckerberg, the sixth-richest person in the world, is one of the few among his peers to still reside in the state, along with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.
Elon Musk and Michael Dell live in Texas, while Amazon founder Jeff Bezos' primary residence has always been elsewhere. Google co-founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin moved out of California ahead of the election and bought luxury homes in Florida, the same state that Oracle founder Larry Ellison officially calls home.
Prop. 40 would impose a 5% tax on Californians worth over $1 billion. Zuckerberg's net worth is currently about $225 billion.
"If the California wealth tax is enacted and Mr. Zuckerberg becomes liable for a tax payment, Mr. Zuckerberg would effectively be paying to serve as the Company's chief executive officer while residing in California," the filing said, noting the CEO's "salary of only $1 each year."
Meta said in the filing that Zuckerberg committed to remaining in California for eight years, "unless there are material unforeseen circumstances that would render it prudent or advisable for Mr. Zuckerberg to reside elsewhere."
The company created a new class of non-voting Class C common stock to take effect in January. Zuckerberg will essentially be granted a portion of the new stock via a dividend. He will be able to "immediately sell or transfer up to 20%" of the shares he's granted "for any reason, including so that he may pay his potential tax liability under California Proposition 40, if enacted into law, without affecting his majority voting control," the filing said.
"There were many driving factors that led the board and special committee to approve the Class C shares, and it would be misleading to attribute it to any single reason," Meta told CNBC in a statement.
The tech industry, by and large, has been unified in its objection to the ballot measure.
In addition to the Google co-founders, a number of big-name techies have put spending into opposing Prop. 40. They include former Google CEO Eric Schmidt, Stripe CEO Patrick Collison, venture investor Peter Thiel and DoorDash CEO Tony Xu, according to various media reports based on campaign filings.
Collison and Xu are members of Meta's board of directors while Thiel left the company's board in 2022, having served since 2005.
Brin told The New York Times in April he fled the Soviet Union with his family in 1979, and said, "I don't want California to end up in the same place."
Huang, however, recently told CBS Sunday Morning that it would be a "privilege" to pay the tax. Huang is just behind Zuckerberg in Forbes' billionaire ranking, with a net worth of $185 billion.
Although Prop. 40 advocates, including Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., have been urging voters to pass the ballot measure, recent polling has suggested that it may fail to garner the majority support required to make it law. A recent Citrin-Politico poll showed 46% are in favor of the measure compared with 43% who oppose it.
Meta, with the help of a special committee, views Zuckerberg as key to the company's future and its efforts to become a major player in artificial intelligence, according to the filing. In particular, the company said it doesn't want to jeopardize Zuckerberg's close working arrangement with the Meta Superintelligence Labs, which is led by AI chief Alexandr Wang.
"The Special Committee believes that Mr. Zuckerberg's talent and leadership have been crucial to our growth, strategy, and stability since our inception, and the Special Committee wants that to continue," the filing said.
Although Meta considered the possibility of issuing Class A common stock to help raise funds, the filing noted that Zuckerberg made clear "that he would not support a significant equity financing that would have the effect of reducing his voting power in the Company."
Instead, the new stock incentive will help Meta receive "critical equity capital without impacting Mr. Zuckerberg's voting power and the unique and creative vision and exceptional management abilities which helped to deliver the long-term value as noted above," the filing said.
WATCH: 'Fast Money' traders react to Meta's Q3 results as stock climbs in extended trading.

articles.title: OpenAI nears up to $30 billion funding round at $1.25 trillion valuation led by UAE investors
articles.text:
OpenAI is closing in on a funding round that could value the artificial intelligence giant at more than $1 trillion ahead of a potential initial public offering.
The San Francisco-based AI company is raising up to $30 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation, according to people familiar with the deal, who asked not to be named because the details were confidential. That valuation does not include new capital raised.
Investors from the United Arab Emirates are leading the round alongside Coatue, according to the people. The financing is being positioned as an "opportunistic" bridge ahead of a potential IPO.
OpenAI kickstarted discussions for a new funding round after investors approached the company with proposals in September, as CNBC previously reported. OpenAI told investors on Thursday that it is aiming to secure signatures by the end of next week, but the final size of the round is still being determined, the people said.
Alongside the new investment, OpenAI is negotiating a commercial deal that would secure more computing capacity from the UAE, according to one person. OpenAI told investors in February that it's targeting roughly $600 billion in total compute spend by 2030.
The company confidentially filed its prospectus with the Securities and Exchange Commission in June, but it has not disclosed exactly when it plans to debut.
OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar told employees in August that the AI lab "will be a public company in 2027." The following month, CEO Sam Altman said that "right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public."
Anthropic, OpenAI's chief rival, is also gearing up for what is widely expected to be a massive IPO. The company confidentially filed its prospectus with regulators in June and is actively engaging in meetings with prospective investors, as CNBC previously reported.
The company is reportedly seeking a valuation between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion in its offering. In May, Anthropic closed a $65 billion funding round at a $965 billion valuation.

articles.title: A lesson from poker tells us not to fold on Meta after its earnings sell-off. Here’s why
articles.text: Meta's strong quarterly results were overshadowed by artificial intelligence spending concerns on Thursday, sending shares down 7%. The sellers made a mistake — and a trip to the poker table helps illustrate their folly. The bulls and bears seem to have hands of equal rank. There's a pair of reasons to stay away (a potential equity raise looms and other negative headlines dampen sentiment), balanced out by a pair of reasons to buy the weakness (the core business is on fire and the stock is cheap). To break the tie, we can take a lesson from poker. When you first start to learn the game (Texas Hold 'em for me), the first thing you learn is which hands have a higher value — a pair, two pair, three of a kind, and so on. Once you've committed that to memory, the next concept to learn is that of the "kicker." The kicker is the card that breaks a tie. Let's say you have a pair of kings with a queen kicker, while your opponent has a pair of kings with an ace kicker. Your opponent wins because the kings cancel out while the ace trumps the queen. Understanding the importance of a kicker may be the key to figuring out what to do with Meta shares going forward. With Thursday's decline, the stock has now given up nearly all of its gains following the exciting launch of its Muse personal agent app on Sept. 8. Is Meta's kicker a deuce, or a trillion-dollar ace in the hole? META YTD mountain Meta's year-to-date stock performance. The bear case Let's start with two reasons to sell the stock and stay away in the coming months. 1. The newest reason arrived alongside Wednesday's earnings release: Meta plans to create new Class C non-voting shares that the company can use to fund its AI infrastructure plans. Each shareholder of Meta's voting Class A will get one Class C, which effectively splits the stock. If Meta were to do a secondary offering of Class C shares down the line, then existing shareholders will see their financial interest in the company watered down, giving them a smaller claim to future earnings. To be sure, nothing is confirmed about what Meta plans to do with this new Class C stock, but the prospect of investing in a company is less attractive when a dilution event may be just around the corner. And a securities filing Wednesday makes clear that such an event could be coming, and that the scale of the fund-raising in the coming years may be more than some investors initially thought. Meta's free cash flow entering negative territory in the third quarter adds to the concern. "The scale of investment required to compete, sustain our growth, expand our infrastructure, and pursue new strategic initiatives amidst the dramatic transformation taking place in the tech industry and global economy related to artificial intelligence is unprecedented," the filing said. Some quick math: Based on a $650 share price, the team has to sell about 15.4 million shares to raise $10 billion. Given there are about 2.7 billion shares outstanding (on a fully diluted basis), a 15.4 million share sale would result in about 0.567% dilution. This translates to more than 5% dilution if they were to raise $100 billion in an initial secondary sale. 2. A second reason to stay away is the headline risk. The latest example is that a New Mexico judge on Wednesday ordered the company to pay a $25 billion penalty relating to the Cambridge Analytica data privacy scandal. Though Meta intends to appeal the decision, it nonetheless serves as the latest reminder that social media is a hot-button political issue, with many looking to clamp down on some of the practices that helped the company grow to its current juggernaut status. In other words, they're looking to alter one of the most profitable business models in history. This new financial penalty comes less than two months after Meta settled with a coalition of state attorneys general to resolve a lawsuit focused on youth mental health issues and social media usage. Meta took a $9.89 billion legal settlement charge in its just-reported third quarter. Meta also faces headline risk tied to data centers, which have gotten a lot of pushback from community residents and politicians during this election cycle. With the midterm elections less than two weeks away, this has become a hot-button political issue. Whether that remains the case coming out of the elections remains to be seen. For now, it is very much an overhang on the entire AI trade. The bull case Now let's get into two main reasons to stick with Meta and consider buying the weakness. 1. The fundamentals are arguably as strong as ever. Muse is off to an incredible start, and in addition to opening up entirely new revenue streams, Meta's AI model investments are clearly strengthening the core Family of Apps business. "This quarter, we also began moving our content understanding models onto our first-party Muse model family," CFO Susan Li said on Wednesday's earnings call. "In offline evaluations, these models are outperforming our prior production models and are reducing per-unit content processing costs by more than 80% across Instagram, Threads, Facebook and ads. Beyond improving quality, owning more of this stack gives us greater flexibility to develop models around the signals that matter the most for personalization." The company's wildly profitable core advertising business gives Meta Superintelligence Labs (MSL) — the company's AI division formed in 2025 and led by Alexandr Wang — a structural advantage versus pure-play AI labs like Anthropic and OpenAI. In addition to the top-line strength being delivered from AI, Zuckerberg called out his expectation for a 10-fold increase in computing power efficiency to serve Muse in the next year, "which will enable it to be profitable once the revenue lines are at scale." Moreover, the team has found religion in the money-losing Reality Labs segment, which is home to its smart-glasses business and other virtual reality efforts. Zuckerberg said its operating loss should come down to around $15 billion next year and trend "towards profitability from there." We're encouraged that the Reality Labs strategy has shifted to reduce its drag on earnings growth. 2. Meta shares are trading at an undemanding valuation. Using a roughly $650 share price, the stock trades at roughly 19 times 2027 consensus earnings estimates. That compares to the S & P 500 trading at roughly 18.5 times earnings, which we can use as the proxy valuation for the "average" company in the index. We would argue Meta is far better than average and therefore deserves a premium valuation to the market. On that note, Wall Street expects Meta to keep growing earnings at a healthy clip in the years ahead. The implied compound annual growth rate (CAGR) for earnings between fiscal 2026 and fiscal 2031 is 17.1%, based on consensus FactSet estimates for each year. In other words, this is not a company with worsening prospects where a discounted multiple would be warranted. The upshot is that Meta's multiple is so low that it provides the hedge we need to counterbalance the potential equity raise next year. Say you pay the 19-times valuation now, and we're later confronted with a $100 billion equity raise early next year — creating more shares outstanding and lowering Meta's earnings per share (all else equal). That might mean you actually paid a little over 20 times earnings. Not ideal, but we would argue it is still highly attractive given the underlying business momentum on display Wednesday night. The kicker On their own, we would argue the positives around the core business and valuation serve to offset the negatives. That's us putting our finger on the scale. However, playing it straight, the kicker here really favors the bulls. The kicker, in our view, is that we've yet to see the true upside that can come out of Meta Superintelligence Labs. Consider this: Meta has a market cap of about $1.75 trillion. The leading frontier labs, Anthropic and OpenAI, are reportedly being valued in the ballpark of $1.5 trillion . To be sure, there is plenty of debate on whether the pure-play labs, which are believed to be losing tens of billions per year, are being properly valued. While that debate rages on, what is clear is Meta's own lab, which is now very much pumping out frontier-level models , isn't being valued anywhere near the levels of Anthropic and OpenAI. Meta shares are probably getting some credit for the benefits that MSL is bringing to the company internally — i.e., the benefits to engagement and monetization of Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp. But we would argue the stock is being awarded no value for the revenue streams that MSL itself may create for the entire company. For example, Meta is openly building an enterprise platform and hired the CEO of another public company , CJ Desai from MongoDB , to lead the effort. So, it's no secret that Meta has its eyes on the enterprise customers from which Anthropic currently derives nearly all of its revenue. The most bearish investors out there may argue that MSL is indeed worthless or worse, in that it's driving AI investments to unsustainable and unhealthy levels. However, we believe the hype is real, and that Muse is a clear example of the lab generating what will ultimately prove to be a new, multi-billion revenue stream. But, as is the case with most startups, the fixed costs need to be taken in advance of the revenue realization. So, is MSL worth nothing? We would strongly push back on that view. Whether it's worth $500 billion, $1.5 trillion, or something in between is a worthwhile debate to have. As it stands now, though, we think figuring out the exact right number is less material to the decision of what to do with the stock now. More important is that long-term investors understand that while the pros and cons of stepping into the stock now may counterbalance each other, the kicker — that there is a business hidden inside of Meta that could, conservatively, be worth hundreds of billions over time as the infrastructure comes online and the Muse business scales — is very much an ace in the hole. The kicker is in the hands of the bulls. Bottom line We didn't make a move Thursday, content with the stock's 3.6% weighting in our portfolio. But having sold shares much higher in September during the height of the Muse excitement, and remaining bullish on Meta for the long term, we are actively looking for an opportunity to upgrade the stock to our buy-equivalent 1 from its current 2 rating. For those without a position, current levels are attractive, as long as there's an understanding that while the bearish pair may result in further near-term downside, the bullish pair — coupled with the MSL kicker — means that decline will be worth buying into. In stocks, like in poker, you have to know when to hold them and know when to fold them. With Meta, we see no reason to fold them. (Jim Cramer's Charitable Trust is long META. See here for a full list of the stocks.) As a subscriber to the CNBC Investing Club with Jim Cramer, you will receive a trade alert before Jim makes a trade. Jim waits 45 minutes after sending a trade alert before buying or selling a stock in his charitable trust's portfolio. If Jim has talked about a stock on CNBC TV, he waits 72 hours after issuing the trade alert before executing the trade. articles.title: These funds can juice your tax-free portfolio income. Just be sure to mind the risk
articles.text: The recent run-up in rates has dented municipal bond prices, leaving one corner of the market offering especially attractive tax-free income. Municipal bonds posted a negative return of 6.35% in the third quarter, the worst quarter since 1981, according to Nuveen. This was largely driven by a sharp spike in rates rather than credit deterioration, the firm found. Bond yields and prices move in opposite directions, so even as prices took a hit, income generation was on sale. At around the start of October, the yield on the Bloomberg Municipal Bond Index reached 4.78%. "What that's provided, in our view, is a very good opportunity set," said Dan Close, head of Nuveen Municipals. "It's almost impossible to call the absolute bottom, but if you can pick up the rates we get right now, you're certainly being paid to wait." He added that the "higher for longer" theme for interest rate policy has returned as market expectations point to a greater likelihood of the Federal Reserve raising rates in December. Fed funds futures trading suggests a roughly 71% likelihood of policymakers hiking rates at their final meeting of the year, according to the CME FedWatch tool. The recent decline in muni bonds is especially attractive for high income investors, who benefit from their tax-free treatment at the federal level – and generally tax-exempt status at the state and local level, if an investor lives in the issuing state. Consider an investor who is in the 32% marginal federal income tax bracket and is subject to the 3.8% net investment income tax. Buying a muni bond yielding 3.5% would equal a taxable bond with a yield of 5.45%, according to New York Life Investment Management . There are different ways to tap this market, and for those who are eyeing hefty yields and can stomach volatility, closed-end funds can provide compelling income generation — albeit with an added dose of complexity. Closed-end funds Closed-end funds differ from open-ended mutual funds and exchange-traded funds in several ways. First, they have a limited number of shares and trade throughout the day on a stock exchange, and trade at a premium or discount to their net asset value. Second, closed ends also use leverage, which can enhance returns over time but can also introduce price volatility – including magnifying losses. Finally, fees are almost always higher for closed-end funds versus their ETF cousins. That's because they're actively managed and leverage adds to expenses. Expense ratios on closed-end funds can top 1%, and higher costs eat into returns. Investors in closed-end funds that use municipal bonds still get monthly tax-free income, but what's distributed can come from a combination of interest payments, realized capital gains from the sale of underlying holdings and return of capital. Consider that Nuveen's Quality Municipal Income Fund (NAD) has a distribution rate of 8.2% and trades at a discount of 3.64%. BlackRock offers the MuniHoldings Fund (MHD) , which has a distribution rate of 6.79% and sells at a discount of 9%. "For clients looking for a pure income play and who can close their eyes to daily volatility on net asset value and market price, these tend to be very efficient vehicles for distributing high levels of tax-exempt income," said Close at Nuveen. But investors should be aware of the trade-offs if they're thinking about getting in. "Most of our clients are retirees whose priority is generating tax-efficient income and managing risk," said Tyler McConville, CFP and private wealth advisor at The Capital Group in Madison, Wisconsin. "Closed-end funds can give you yield, but they include discount to NAV risk and leverage, and that may not align with every retiree's objective." Individual issues and ETFs Investors seeking simplicity – and who have the cash to manage the purchase – may consider building a portfolio of laddered municipal bonds as a way to manage the risk of rising interest rates. A ladder involves purchasing bonds with varying maturities and then reinvesting the proceeds into new issues as holdings mature. "I can match cash needs and hold to maturity, and many investors find that reassuring," said Eileen Olson, CFP and founder of Emerald Wealth in Daufuskie Island, South Carolina. The catch is that a significant pool of money is needed to build a diversified portfolio of munis. Olson estimates clients need at least $250,000. For those with more modest savings, an ETF can provide diversification even if investors don't have that kind of money. But investors have to be mindful that they'll see price fluctuations as rates move, and should be aware of interest rate risk – or duration – as they decide on a fund. Vanguard has an actively-managed Core Tax-Exempt Bond ETF (VCRM) , with an average duration of 7.5 years and a 30-day SEC yield of 4.49%. But the largest muni bond funds by assets include the passively managed Vanguard Tax-Exempt Bond ETF (VTEB) and iShares National Muni Bond ETF (MUB) . "The bigger theme here is this is an interesting time for the muni market," said Matthew Wrzesniewsky, Vanguard's head of fixed income client portfolio management. His team likes the intermediate part of the muni yield curve. "Those windows of opportunity have opened up, and we're still there," Wrzesniewsky said.

articles.title: 68% of adults say they've gotten used to living with uncertainty. They're coping by making rash decisions, experts say
articles.text:
Psychiatrist and author Suzan Song has seen her clients make some rash decisions lately.
Some are pushing for commitment in romantic relationships early on, for example, says the Washington, D.C.-based Song. Others are leaving work without another position lined up. She and other mental health professionals are also seeing clients turn to AI to interpret interactions, predict outcomes or tell them what decisions to make. Some people are even gravitating toward religious organizations and turning to mystical practices like psychics and love spells to find a partner.
The underlying motivation for many of these behaviors? Uncertainty, they say. Just over two-thirds of U.S. adults say they've become accustomed to living with uncertainty, according to the American Psychological Association's 2026 Stress in America report. Twenty-eight percent also say they have little to no control over their future, up from 23% in 2025. The sample data is accurate to within plus or minus 2.5 percentage points using a 95% confidence level.
With a constant barrage of doomsday predictions about everything from AI to climate change, you may be wondering how to cope. Here's what mental health experts have to say.
The level of uncertainty has not changed — our exposure to it has
There has always been uncertainty — in people's personal lives as well as in the world at large. What's different now is the level of ambiguity around seemingly everything people need to navigate from jobs and finances to relationships, experts say.
The proliferation of smartphones, for example, has meant people are both steeped in their day-to-day worries and fielding an endless stream of headlines about the horrors of the world.
Historically, for example, "I could read up on the Cold War with newspapers," says Carrboro, North Carolina-based psychologist Julie Pike as an example, "but I couldn't go down a rabbit hole of TikToks and Instagram reels."
There's nothing to suggest that whatever happens next, you can't handle that.Natalie DattiloPsychologist
Between regular exposure to the mundane and increased access to everything else, worries stack — and so does stress and anxiety. In fact, uncertainty can be an anxiety generator.
Beyond making us feel like we're drowning in unknowns, the ubiquity of information might also mean people's tolerance for uncertainty has gone down, says Natalie Dattilo, an Indianapolis-based psychologist. In the past, people had no choice but to sit with their uncertainty and cope with it.
Today, chatbots can run the actuarial numbers, potentially alleviating some uncertainty concerns by, say, offering a close approximation for achieving life milestones. But even chatbots can't predict the future, and ultimately the uncertainty remains.
'The present is where uncertainty has the hardest time getting a grip'
When you feel like you're drowning in the unknown, New York-based psychotherapist Andrew Tepper recommends trying to focus on physical sensations in your body:
- Splash cold water on your face: "Cold water on the face triggers a part of your nervous system, which helps you to calm down," he says. "It's one of the fastest ways I know to take the edge off when anxiety spikes."
- Take your shoes off and stand in the grass: "I have clients, teenagers included, who now do this as a habit," he says. "Feeling the ground under your feet, the temperature, the texture, pulls your attention into the present. The present is where uncertainty has the hardest time getting a grip."
- Go outside and move: "Walk, hike, bike, just get outside. It's hard to spiral about next year when you're present in nature and engaged in an exhilarating activity."
You can also try repeating a mantra like "I am certain that no matter what happens, I will handle it," says Dattilo. You can repeat it weekly, daily — however often you need. These kinds of phrases are grounding and can help contain some of that anxiety. Plus, they're true.
"There's nothing to suggest that whatever happens next, you can't handle," she says.

articles.title: Reported fraud losses among older Americans hit $3 billion in 2025 as big losses surge: FTC report
articles.text:
Fraud losses reported by older Americans jumped in 2025, driven largely by an increase in victims losing sums of at least six figures, according to a new report from the Federal Trade Commission.
Americans ages 60 and older reported losing about $3 billion to fraud last year, a 25% increase from $2.4 billion in 2024, according to the FTC's annual report to Congress, released Monday, on fraud among older adults. That figure is up 400% from $600 million reported lost in 2020.
Just 6% of older fraud victims reported losing $100,000 or more last year, but those losses accounted for 70% of the age group's total reported losses. The number reporting losses of that magnitude rose nearly sixfold to 6,769 in 2025 from 1,136 in 2020.
Additionally, because many scams go unreported, the FTC estimates actual losses in 2025 could have been anywhere from $13.3 billion to $119.5 billion. In 2024, the estimated range was from $10.1 billion to $81.5 billion.
"The numbers and the increases are staggering," said Bob Blancato, national coordinator for the Elder Justice Coalition, an advocacy group for ending elder abuse. "Part of it is that the perpetrators are always ahead. They seem to be one step ahead of everybody."
Investment scam losses spiked 42% in 2025
The rising losses come as scammers increasingly target Americans' life savings by impersonating banks, businesses and government agencies, according to an August 2025 analysis by the FTC. The schemes often involve fabricated emergencies that convince victims to transfer money to supposedly protect their accounts from being compromised.
The volume of scams has increased with the use of artificial intelligence. AI-generated scams are also increasingly difficult to detect and easier to produce, according to the FBI.
In many impersonation schemes, criminals pose as representatives of banks or government agencies and falsely warn that a consumer's money is in danger of being stolen. Victims are then instructed to transfer funds, mail cash or deposit money into crypto ATMs, supposedly to protect their assets.
However, investment scams were the costliest fraud type reported by older Americans last year, with losses exceeding $1 billion, a 42% jump from 2024, the FTC's new report shows. These scams often begin with social media ads promoting investment opportunities or messages from people posing as financial advisors, according to the FTC. Victims may then be directed to fraudulent trading platforms.
Government impersonation scams ranked second in total reported losses among older consumers of $448 million, followed by business impersonation scams, which resulted in $422 million in reported losses.
Lawmakers weigh relief for victims
The growing financial toll comes as Congress considers legislation intended to provide additional protections and relief for people who lose money to scams.
The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 temporarily restricted victims' ability to claim their fraud losses in certain cases. as a deduction on their tax return. Prior to that legislation, fraud losses were generally deductible. The provision was scheduled to expire in 2025, but President Donald Trump's "big beautiful bill" law enacted last year made that change permanent.
While investment fraud losses may be deductible, according to an IRS memorandum issued in March 2025, money lost to other scams — such as some impersonator or romance scams — is not, experts said.
You get scammed out of $100,000 and then you're paying taxes on that $100,000. That's crazy.Bob BlancatoNational coordinator for the Elder Justice Coalition
In addition, if the victim tapped a tax-deferred retirement account such as a traditional 401(k) or individual retirement account as part of the fraud, income taxes may be due on the distribution. And if the victim is younger than age 59½, an early-withdrawal penalty of 10% may be imposed.
"You get scammed out of $100,000 and then you're paying taxes on that $100,000," Blancato said. "That's crazy."
The bipartisan Tax Relief for Fraud Victims Act, which was passed by the House in September in a 408-17 vote, would eliminate the deductibility restrictions and waive the 10% penalty if it applies, among other provisions. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee. It's uncertain whether it will gain traction in the upper chamber before this session of Congress is over.
Separately, the Financial Exploitation Prevention Act, which cleared the House in June by a vote of 414-2, would allow certain financial institutions such as mutual fund companies to temporarily delay transactions when they reasonably believe a customer is being financially exploited. It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee; whether it will get a floor vote is unknown.
Already, many banks and other financial institutions ask accountholders for a "trusted contact," which is someone who can be contacted in certain circumstances, including when financial exploitation is suspected. That person may be able to intervene to prevent the fraud by reaching out to the accountholder. The Financial Industry Regulatory Authority, or FINRA, requires brokerages to make a reasonable effort to add a trusted contact to accounts, although investors are not required to provide one.
Approach potential victims with care
If you suspect an older adult in your life is being victimized, it's important to approach the situation with care, experts say.
"It's usually best to start with an open, nonjudgmental, compassionate approach," said Marti DeLiema, an associate professor at the University of Minnesota and associate director of education for the school's Center for Healthy Aging and Innovation.
"You never say 'you're being scammed,' because they'll throw their guard up," DeLiema said. "Scammers will try to intentionally isolate the target from potential interveners. They'll say don't tell anyone about our relationship or don't tell anyone that you won the lottery."
If the money is already gone, it's important not to blame the victim, DeLiema said. "We do that to scam victims all the time. We say, 'What were you thinking? How could you be so foolish?'" she said.
"We really need to move away from the shame, because I guarantee you, they're already doing that to themselves," DeLiema said. "They're already pointing the finger inward."

articles.title: Trump defends Ramaswamy ad with Acton's estranged mom after bipartisan criticism
articles.text:
President Donald Trump on Thursday defended a controversial ad by the campaign of Vivek Ramaswamy featuring the estranged mother of Amy Acton, his Democratic opponent in the Ohio gubernatorial race, calling Acton a liar.
Trump's defense of the ad came after widespread bipartisan backlash to it, which focused on the fact that Acton's stepfather, Cledith Arthur, was charged with raping her when she was a child and was married to Acton's mother, Donna Arthur.
In the ad, Donna Arthur says Acton has "lied her entire life."
"Don't vote for people who lie," Arthur says in the ad. "Don't let her become your governor. If you think she'll make your life better, you're fooling yourself. It will only get worse."
Acton has said she has not seen Arthur since she was 12 years old. Cledith Arthur fled after his arrest and remained a fugitive until his death in Pennsylvania in 2004.
Trump, in a Truth Social post on Thursday, said, "Vivek Ramaswamy put up a very powerful Ad about a mother saying that her daughter, Amy Acton, who is running for Governor of Ohio, is a liar, and much worse."
"The Press, in a concerted and well coordinated attack, is trying to get Vivek Ramaswamy to 'take down the Ad,' " Trump said. "Frankly, anybody whose mother spoke about a daughter in that way would normally lead to the daughter being precluded from serving in Office, let alone the Office of Governor."
Trump also criticized Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine for calling for the ad to be taken down, even as DeWine continued to support his fellow Republican Ramaswamy's candidacy to succeed him.
"The ad, on its face, is deeply, deeply troubling," DeWine said in a press conference earlier Thursday.
Trump said DeWine "probably wants a Dumocrat to win, and certainly doesn't want someone who will do a much better job than he is capable of doing."
"I suggested, on the other hand, that Vivek should keep it up, and let everyone listen to the mother of a defective, dishonest, and incapable Candidate, explain how the daughter is a DISASTER who, uncontrollably, lies, cheats, and steals!" Trump said.
Trump later told reporters that he had "no idea" about Acton's allegation of being raped by her mother's husband, and questioned when Acton had made that claim.
Trump's comments came a day after his vice president, JD Vance, during a visit to Cincinnati and said it was "not really my concern" whether the ad was appropriate.
But Vance also said, "I'm a little bit disgusted when I see Republicans across the country who are whining more about that advertisement than they are about what the congressional Democrats and other Democrats want to do to the United States of America."
"The media and the Democrats in the state of Ohio are obsessed because guess what? Vivek Ramaswamy had the audacity to run a TV commercial which calls it out like it is and calls Amy Acton a liar," Vance said. "Whatever you think about any of the TV advertisements, focus on the substance and focus on the facts."
Ramaswamy's campaign has spent nearly $95,000 to air the ad so far, according to AdImpact, with more than 100 airings concentrated in Cleveland, Columbus, and Cincinnati — three of Ohio's biggest media markets.
Ramaswamy's campaign has said it committed $4 million to air the ad.
Acton on Thursday said of the ad, "It was a horrible and hideous thing to do. A sad thing. And I feel like it was an exploitative thing to do."
"My mother is not well," Acton said.
Her brother, Philip Stearns, told The New York Times in a statement earlier this week that he and Acton were removed from their mother's custody after their stepfather was arrested.
"Our birth mother stayed married to Amy's rapist until he died," Stearns said. "This desperate, disgusting attack reveals exactly who Vivek Ramaswamy is at his core — a pathetic excuse for a man who is willing to hurt anyone as long as it gets him what he wants."
Former Ohio Sen. Rob Portman, a Republican, told Politico on Thursday that the ad should be taken down.
"The increasing incivility in the political arena should concern us all," Portman said, according to Politico's Jonathan Martin. "This ad is an unfortunate example of that broader trend. It crosses the line. I hope the ad will be taken down and the final days of the campaign will focus on policy differences."
— CNBC's Luke Fountain contributed to this article.

articles.title: Trump asked Musk to lift Starlink slowdown, WSJ reports
articles.text:
President Donald Trump asked Elon Musk to ease restrictions he had imposed on the military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink system in Ukraine, The Wall Street Journal reported Thursday, citing U.S. officials.
The Starshield system, which Ukraine depends on in its war against Russia, was "working more normally Thursday, shortly after" Trump spoke to Musk by phone, U.S. and Ukrainian officials told the Journal.
Trump said later Thursday he did not "want to comment one way or the other" about whether he made the call to Musk.
"Whether I called or whether somebody else called, doesn't make any difference," Trump told reporters outside the White House as he departed for a campaign rally in Iowa.
"The bottom line, he put it back," Trump said of Musk.
The Journal reported Tuesday that Musk, the founder and CEO of SpaceX and a critic of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, had ordered the Starlink slowdown.
Two unnamed sources in that report said Trump and Musk had discussed the decision to throttle Starlink "soon after" the change first became public last week, while one source said Musk had spoken to Trump prior to imposing the speed cap.
Trump has repeatedly denied involvement in the decision and said he does not know if Musk was behind it.
"I don't know who did it, but I was not involved," Trump said Wednesday.
The Starlink controversy, which drew bipartisan concern and criticism from lawmakers, emerged as Trump has ramped up criticism of Zelenskyy for continuing to target Russian energy infrastructure. At the same time, Trump has pursued a deal to ease sanctions on Russia so it can supply some diesel on the global market.
Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday that he does not believe Musk would throttle Starlink without "at least the acquiescence of the White House."
Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., the ranking member of the Senate homeland security committee's investigations subcommittee, on Thursday launched an inquiry into how SpaceX's satellite tech was "degraded for Ukraine without notice."
"This decision to limit critical technology for a key ally not only put Ukrainian forces at risk and their people in peril, but raises serious questions about who controls critical capabilities the U.S. government has spent billions of dollars to procure," Blumenthal said in letters to Musk and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
The White House and an email associated with Musk did not immediately respond to CNBC's requests for comment on Thursday's report that Trump had asked Musk to lift the restrictions.

articles.title: Moderna shares plunge after cancer vaccine data leaks — despite positive results
articles.text:
Moderna shares dropped as much as 25% on Thursday following the leak of partial data on its closely watched cancer vaccine developed with Merck.
Shares of both drugmakers fell even though the data, released in full later Thursday following the leak, appeared meaningful for patients and positive relative to Wall Street expectations.
The personalized vaccine, known as intismeran autogene, paired with Merck's immunotherapy Keytruda reduced the risk of recurrence or death in certain melanoma patients by 42% compared with Keytruda alone.
The data also showed that the shot along with Keytruda reduced the risk of cancer spreading to distant parts of the body or death by 38%, compared with just the immunotherapy.
The companies said about 82% of patients who received the personalized cancer vaccine alongside Keytruda were alive without their melanoma returning at two years after receiving the shot, compared with 70% of those who received Keytruda alone.
"This is a huge development for our patients," said Dr. Hussein Tawbi, a melanoma expert and trial investigator at the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center, about the results.
He said that the added benefit of the vaccine also comes with much milder toxicity, or side effects like injection-site pain, compared to other cancer treatments.
The detailed phase 3 trial results were set to be presented at the European Society for Medical Oncology conference this weekend.
"Whenever you put a therapy on top of something that works really well, like Keytruda, sometimes it's harder to show additional benefit. We have no problems of showing additional benefit here," Dr. Dean Li, Merck Research Laboratories president, said in an interview ahead of the results.
The benefit appeared even larger after the six-month vaccine regimen, with a separate analysis showing a 58% reduction in risk of recurrence or death. The companies say it is still too early to determine whether the treatment helps patients live longer overall.
Several analysts acknowledged investors' elevated expectations ahead of the release, but noted that the data is overall positive.
"We assert this relative reduction in recurrence/death is clinically meaningful," BMO Capital Markets analyst Evan Seigerman said in a research note on Thursday following the leak. "Such a [stock] reaction likely reflects inflated expectations into the full data release, rather than a true indictment on the efficacy of the combo therapy."
Oncologists and investors see the targeted vaccine as a possible breakthrough treatment, with the potential to be used to treat other forms of cancer in the future. Merck and Moderna are studying the vaccine in several trials across other tumors, such as non-small cell lung cancer, bladder cancer and renal cell carcinoma.
But Li acknowledged the companies have more work to show the product can be effective across tumor types.
"I can dream of creating a log cabin, but we got some wood chops, and we've just knocked down one tree," Li said. "Knocking one tree does not give you a cabin or a village."
The shot is designed to target the specific mutations in each patient's tumor rather than using a one-size-fits-all approach. The idea is to train the immune system to recognize and kill those unique cancer markers and then pair that response with Keytruda, which helps the body attack the cancer more effectively.
It could also offer Moderna a critical additional commercial product in its pipeline, following vaccines for Covid-19, the flu and respiratory syncytial virus.
In a research note Thursday, UBS analysts said "this is overall a strong data set" and gives more confidence in upcoming studies of the vaccine in kidney and bladder cancers. They added the stock reaction may be due more to massive expectations than disappointing data.
Against the backdrop of those high expectations, Moderna shares have spiked more than 530% year-to-date as of Thursday afternoon.
Shares of Merck, a much larger drugmaker, fell by about 1% on Thursday. The company's stock has climbed nearly 41% this year.
Since the vaccine is personalized, the complicated manufacturing process can take six weeks. But Merck CEO Robert Davis told CNBC last week that the company believes it can shorten that timeline in the future, potentially allowing the shot to reach more patients more quickly.

articles.title: SpaceX and Tesla have high election stakes as Elon Musk pours $366 million into campaigns
articles.text:
Elon Musk's business empire is tying itself ever closer to the federal government just as he spends record sums to help decide who controls it in the 2026 midterm election.
SpaceX has racked up at least $6.78 billion in federal work so far through Oct. 1 this year, according to FedScout, a research firm that tracks government spending and contracts, nearly twice its total for all of 2024. Tesla, SpaceX, including Musk's artificial intelligence business, also face high-stakes government decisions over defense spending, launch licenses, spectrum, autonomous vehicles, electricity and data centers.
At the same time, Musk has committed roughly $366 million to the 2026 election cycle across at least 40 races, making the world's richest person the midterms' biggest individual donor so far.
At least $276 million of that money has flowed to Republican groups and Musk's own political operation, America PAC, since July, according to a CNBC analysis of Federal Election Commission filings, as Republican candidates have faced attacks on the cost of living and the war in Iran.
For Musk, Republican victories could help preserve his influence and a favorable political environment for his companies. Democratic control of either chamber could instead bring subpoenas and investigations into his businesses, federal contracts and his work leading President Donald Trump's Department of Government Efficiency.
Democrats are favored to win control of the House, while the battle for the Senate remains a toss-up.
"With all that spending, [Musk] wants favors in Congress and from the administration and influence on regulatory contracts as well as being shielded from oversight," said Bruce Freed, president and co-founder of the nonpartisan Center for Political Accountability and a former chief investigator for the Senate banking committee.
Musk did not respond to CNBC's request for a comment on this story. However, he lashed out at the possibility of Democrat-led investigations in a Wednesday post on X, which he owns, saying: "Live by the sword, die by the sword."
"Those who pick fights with me should understand that I will find out who is really pulling the strings and come for them, not just their puppets," he wrote.
Musk's Texas empire
Nowhere is the overlap between Musk's business interests and political spending clearer than in his home state of Texas.
Tesla is headquartered in Austin, where it operates its largest U.S. vehicle factory. SpaceX operates a launch facility at its company town, Starbase, in South Texas. Musk's tunneling venture, The Boring Co., is based in Pflugerville.
That gives Texas officials sway over taxes, electricity, permitting, infrastructure and economic-development incentives that can carry enormous consequences for Musk's companies.
At least $189.6 million of his political money is targeted to help elect Republican Ken Paxton through various avenues, prompting his Democratic opponent, James Talarico, to accuse Musk of trying to "buy this Senate seat in Texas."
Musk went after Talarico on Wednesday, saying on X that "There is something deeply wrong" with the Democrat.
"There is something deeply wrong with a political system that allows one trillionaire to buy his own personal U.S. Senator," Talarico responded.
Musk is spending at the state level, too. According to the nonpartisan Transparency USA, which tracks money in state politics, Musk and his trust have given at least $6 million this cycle to state candidates and political groups, including Gov. Greg Abbott, Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick and House Speaker Dustin Burrows.
The Musk-Abbott connection also extends to personnel: Tesla policy chief Karen Steakley previously served as Abbott's deputy director for legislative affairs.
Tesla and SpaceX are also planning to build a sprawling AI chip factory with Intel outside of Austin in Grimes County, Texas, where longtime Musk lawyer and America PAC attorney Chris Gober is running for Congress.
A $30 billion government business
For SpaceX, the federal government is one of its most important customers.
Since 2008, the company has received more than $30.7 billion in federal work, according to FedScout. The figure excludes classified contracts and some state-funded spending on services such as Starlink terminals and satellite internet service, which states have used during disaster recovery.
That federal business has accelerated during Trump's second administration, FedScout found. SpaceX has racked up $6.78 billion in 2026 so far, compared with $3.97 billion in 2025 and $3.8 billion for all of 2024.
In late May alone, the Space Force awarded SpaceX $2.29 billion for a military communications network tied to the "Golden Dome" missile shield and, three days later, another $4.16 billion for threat-detection satellites.
Congress does not award those contracts, but it funds and oversees the agencies that do, including the Defense Department and NASA, each a major SpaceX customer.
"Keeping allies in committee powers in Washington helps [Musk] wield power in the halls of Congress better," said Hilary Braseth, executive director of OpenSecrets, a nonpartisan research group that tracks money in politics.
Musk's America PAC is backing Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, who is chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, which helps write funding bills for NASA and the Pentagon.
Collins' Democratic opponent, Troy Jackson, has accused Musk of trying to "buy a government that serves his interests."
Musk has already learned how quickly that kind of political influence can evaporate.
After spending nearly $300 million to help elect Trump and congressional Republicans in 2024, Musk gained extraordinary access to the administration. He led DOGE's push to slash the federal workforce and pressed for deregulation on several fronts.
Then the relationship blew up. A June 2025 feud over Trump's tax-and-spending bill escalated into threats from the president to cut government support and contracts for Musk's companies.
Now Musk is back in Trump's orbit. In recent weeks, he has attended Trump's state dinner with Chinese President Xi Jinping, sat beside the president at his AI summit and received the National Medal of Science. On Sept. 30, the DOD appointed Musk to co-lead Project Meridian, advising the Pentagon on future warfare.
Expanding reach
Musk’s political spending extends well beyond the states where his business empire is concentrated.
Across six other battleground states, America PAC had spent about $22.7 million on general election expenditures through Oct. 20, according to a CNBC analysis of FEC filings, including roughly $8.9 million in Ohio, $7.2 million in Michigan and $2 million in Maine.
In Michigan, America PAC is paying for digital ads, mailers, printing and postage, and text and phone outreach supporting Republican Mike Rogers and attacking Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, according to FEC filings.
Rogers backs a one-year moratorium on new data centers; El-Sayed wants to pause advanced AI development and new data centers until tougher federal safeguards are in place.
In Ohio, America PAC is funding ads, text and phone outreach among other measures helping Republican Jon Husted against Democrat Sherrod Brown, according to FEC filings. Husted wants large data centers to shoulder more grid costs; Brown has attacked industry tax breaks and pledged to make data centers pay their full electricity costs.
Those debates matter more as Musk pushes deeper into AI.
SpaceX's AI division, formerly known as xAI, was awarded a Pentagon contract last July with a $200 million ceiling, while a General Services Administration agreement makes the company's Grok chatbot available across federal agencies through March 2027.
Musk's companies also depend on a web of federal regulators whose decisions can directly affect their ability to expand.
The Federal Aviation Administration licenses SpaceX launches, while the Federal Communications Commission controls satellite licenses and spectrum used by Starlink. Congress funds and oversees both agencies, and the Senate confirms FCC commissioners.
Tesla has its own stakes in Washington, where Congress and federal agencies can reshape electric-vehicle tax breaks, battery subsidies, autonomous-vehicle rules and trade policy affecting Chinese competitors.
Musk's companies are spending directly on those fights, too.
Since January 2025, SpaceX has spent about $5.3 million lobbying on issues including NASA funding, defense spending, military launches, missile defense and procurement, while Tesla has spent about $3.6 million lobbying Washington, according to disclosure reports.
"Elon's spending is virtually unprecedented in recent elections for its scale in such a short period for one individual donor," Freed told CNBC. "He seems to be spending with basically no budget, and he got the money to do so."

articles.title: The perfect storm behind the Nasdaq's rout — plus, some of the bright spots in the market
articles.text: Every weekday, the CNBC Investing Club with Jim Cramer releases the Homestretch — an actionable afternoon update, just in time for the last hour of trading on Wall Street. Stocks are falling on Thursday , with chip stocks and AI infrastructure names getting hit the hardest on growing concerns about the scarcity of capital to fund the AI buildout. The Nasdaq is leading the way lower, sinking 2.5%. The issue started to get a lot more attention last Monday when Broadcom CEO Hock Tan warned about how a capital crunch could become AI's next bottleneck. It then played out through CoreWeave 's bonds selling off, making it tougher for the neocloud to raise new debt to fund its expansion plans. While Meta Platforms posted strong earnings on Wednesday evening, its results were overshadowed by free cash flow going negative for the first time since its 2012 initial public offering, and the company's SEC filing that mentioned the company's long-term forecast requiring the need to raise "hundreds of billions of dollars over a period of several years beginning as early as fall 2026." Meta also noted the "increasingly challenging environment for raising capital." Even Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang acknowledged the challenges of raising sufficient capital to support aggressive AI investment plans for neoclouds, saying Thursday that the "demand of the capital is much greater than the availability of the capital." However, Huang expressed confidence that the funding gap for neoclouds would eventually be resolved. More on Meta's capital needs, which is contributing to its 7.5% decline on Thursday. The SEC filing mentioned above was about how the company formed a special committee to review the establishment of its Class C common stock. The idea behind the Class C shares is to create a vehicle that Meta can raise funds to support acquisitions and investments without diluting CEO Mark Zuckerberg's voting power. Zuckerberg maintaining control of the company he founded is not the main gripe of investors nowadays (as it had been in the past. The current concern is about the "hundreds of billions of dollars" that must be raised, as well as an acknowledgement of how timing is important to secure capital before "competitors saturate various funding options." The filing called out Alphabet and SpaceX , the yet-to-go-public AI labs Anthropic and OpenAI, as well as other notable companies that recently raised capital to fund the same AI growth. This disclosure underscores the growing race among AI companies to secure financing before their competitors do. We saw something similar in June, when Alphabet moved quickly to raise about $85 billion through equity sales just days ahead of SpaceX's blockbuster IPO. By the way, markets tend to struggle when they know they need to absorb excess supply. We don't raise these concerns to sound overly bearish on the AI buildout, especially when signs continue to point to strong demand. AI adoption is not slowing down. In fact, we went against the selloff on Thursday and nibbled on some GE Vernova shares, marking our first AI-related purchase in weeks. But understanding why certain stocks are falling is important to identifying what needs to happen to support the next rally. In the market background , the rally in bonds on Thursday is worth highlighting as investors flock to safety. The 10-year Treasury yield dipped below 5% for the first time since Sept. 23. The drop in yields is helping high dividend yield stocks like Kimberly-Clark and rate-sensitive groups like housing and Home Depot outperform in an otherwise rough day for stocks. Both KMB and HD are Club names. Thursday's rotation is being reflected in the nearly flat Dow Jones Industrial Average . The two most important earnings reports after the closing bell are Western Digital and Bloom Energy . Western Digital's comments will provide insight into demand and shortages for storage products used in AI data centers, while Bloom Energy provides a window into whether data center operations are accelerating near- and long-term investments in power infrastructure. Before Friday's bell, American Express and SLB report their quarterly results. On the data side, Friday morning brings October S & P Global U.S. manufacturing and services PMI and October University of Michigan survey of consumer sentiment and 1-year inflation expectations.
