articles.title: The RealReal CEO started as its first employee—her No. 1 lesson over 15 years: Don't 'get too attached to being right'
articles.text:
Rati Sahi Levesque never wants to forget the "really hard" times she experienced while working at The RealReal, she says. After all, they taught her how to lead a company worth north of $1 billion.
Levesque, 45, started working at the luxury resale marketplace in 2011 as its first employee and remembers struggling to get old-school fashion houses to understand its online business model. Later, as The RealReal's chief operating officer during the Covid-19 pandemic, she keenly felt the company's loss of "hundreds of millions of dollars," she says.
Now, she's The RealReal's CEO, credited with overseeing one of the retail industry's more successful post-Covid turnaround stories. Since her appointment in October 2024, Levesque has helped add nearly $1 billion to The RealReal's market value, which sits at nearly $1.3 billion as of Thursday afternoon. The company brought in more than $692 million in 2025 revenue, according to its annual report. In September, Levesque landed on the 2026 Time100 Next List of the "world's most influential rising stars."
The rise from founding employee to chief executive gave Levesque firsthand experience in many of the roles at her company, and empathy for the 3,000-plus employees who work those jobs, she says. The No. 1 lesson she learned from her 15 years at the company, she says: Never lose your "growth mindset," stay open to reevaluating your preconceived notions and be willing to accept when your strategy isn't working.
"One of the biggest lessons I've learned is not to get too attached to being right," says Levesque, 45. "We've made plenty of decisions over the years that we thought were the right ones at the time, only to learn there was a better way. You have to be able to laugh at yourself, acknowledge what isn't working and move forward."
Advice from a CEO: Practice being wrong
The RealReal's post-Covid success revolves around an acknowledgment of being wrong, Levesque says.
Like many venture-backed startups, The RealReal's leadership team spent much of its first decade focused on growth at all costs, absorbing annual losses to prioritize acquiring new customers. Levesque was part of the team behind that strategy. But when the pandemic sent sales plummeting, the company's leaders realized the need to "pare back" from less profitable categories, like home goods and children's apparel, that they had previously added in the name of growing revenue, then-CEO John Koryl told The New York Times in August 2023.
The RealReal's pandemic lows pushed the company to experiment and grow in other ways too, Levesque says. At the time, The RealReal ran several large, expensive brick-and-mortar retail locations — including a 6,000-square-foot store in New York City and a 12,000-square-foot one in Los Angeles — meant to allow shoppers to interact with some luxury items and staff in person before making a purchase. Depressed consumer foot traffic pushed the company's leadership into taking "big bets" on closing those large stores in favor of a more efficient and economical approach, says Levesque.
The RealReal now manages a larger number of smaller stores, aiming for efficiency over spectacle, the company told The Wall Street Journal in 2024.
Analysts have credited The RealReal's recent growth to Levesque and Koryl's strategy, which included other cost-cutting measures such as layoffs and the introduction of artificial intelligence-powered tools meant to help authenticate large numbers of luxury goods efficiently. The moves helped give The RealReal "one of the best turnarounds" in the retail industry, Wells Fargo senior analyst Ike Boruchow wrote in an October 2025 research note.
The pandemic, of course, gave plenty of business leaders reason to change strategic course. Realizing you're wrong and reacting with humility isn't always so easy to do in regular day-to-day life, Levesque says.
As CEO, she observes how employees respond to setbacks to get a sense of their growth mindset, she says: Do they try to dodge responsibility or spin a loss as a win? Do they take accountability and show a willingness to learn something that will make them more effective in the future?
Levesque also suggests practicing being wrong, so you're familiar with the feeling of knowing when your original idea is still worth pursuing and when to change course. She got a lot of practice by working in a whole host of different environments during her first 15 years at The RealReal, she notes.
"You're going to fail. Like, it's going to happen," she says. "You're going to get things wrong. But taking accountability for it really helps."

articles.title: AI debt and French bonds face a stress test — why it may not be over
articles.text:
From AI companies financing data center projects to France's heavily indebted government, credit markets are flashing warnings as investors grow warier of borrowing risks.
Five-year credit default swap spreads have widened for CoreWeave, Oracle and SoftBank Group, as well as France and Italy, according to CNBC's analysis of FactSet data.
AI-related bonds have been selling off as markets raise the cost of capital amid concerns of a financing crunch. Neocloud demand is "off the charts," Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told CNBC on Thursday, but he warned of a "scarcity of capital." "The demand of the capital is much greater than the availability of the capital," he said, adding, "that's going to get solved."
Countries like France face a similar crunch. Pressure is building in bond markets as investors demand more compensation to finance public debt. Recent mass protests and rioting in France have heightened the market's concerns.
"Markets may no longer want to underwrite massive capex, heavy leverage, and uncertain future cash flows, and that same shift is widening French sovereign spreads as investors demand more compensation to hold long‑duration, debt‑financed obligations from a strained state," FedWatch Advisors CIO and founder Ben Emons wrote on his "French Neoclouds" Substack post.
Insurance costs rise for AI-linked debt
CoreWeave, Oracle and SoftBank are at the heart of the AI infrastructure buildout, spanning data centers, cloud services and financing.
Their five-year CDS spreads offer a window into investors' anxiety about the cost of it all and eventual payoff. Higher spreads mean more expensive default protection and can signal greater concern about a borrower's creditworthiness.
CoreWeave has experienced some of the sharpest increases in default-protection costs. Its five-year CDS spread reached 1,065.84 basis points on Oct. 21, according to FactSet, reflecting heightened concerns about the debt-heavy company's ability to finance its expansion.
At the same time Oracle's spread rose to 308.25 basis points on Oct. 21, up from 141 on Jan. 2. S&P Credit Ratings downgraded Oracle's debt to the lowest level of investment grade in July, citing the expanding infrastructure business raised the overall credit risk.
Softbank is a major AI investor with a large stake in OpenAI and investments in data centers and power infrastructure, including an $87 billion commitment for data centers in France. Its five-year CDS spread stood near a four-year high of 432 basis points on Oct. 20, up from 284 basis points on Jan. 5.
France's default-protection costs climb above Italy's
France isn't in a full-fledged debt crisis, but markets are signaling unease with the cost of protecting against a sovereign default rising above that of Italy's, which has also increased.
France's five-year credit default swap spread reached 89.8 basis points on Oct. 21, up from 29.74 basis points on Jan. 2, according to CNBC's analysis. Italy's spread increased to 67.1 basis points on Oct. 22 from 28.33 on Jan 2. France's budget uncertainty and debt burden have become a focus, raising concerns that the risk could spill over to other countries in Europe.
Germany's spread also rose but remained much lower at 12.15 basis points on Oct. 22, compared with 7.47 at the start of the period.
Thierry Wizman, global FX and rates strategist at Macquarie Group, pointed to France's mounting debt burden and persistent fiscal deficits as key drivers of rising default-protection costs.
"The key drivers are the large amount of French sovereign debt (120% of GDP) and the inability to reduce the deficit," Wizman told CNBC. In comparison to France, German government debt is 65% of the country's GDP.
Investors are also watching the spread between French and German bonds, considered the European benchmark of creditworthiness, which has also surged to 1.6 percentage points. France's 10-year bond yield also topped 5% for the first time since 2002. The spread between the 10-year yield on French OATs and German Bunds is the extra payment investors demand to hold French bonds instead of German.
While the Franco-German spread is relatively wide, the Eurozone saw far larger gaps in borrowing costs during the Eurozone debt crisis of the early 2010s.
France faces another test on Oct. 23 when Moody's is scheduled to review its Aa3 sovereign rating, which carries a negative outlook. The review comes as political divisions complicate efforts to repair the country's public finances.
Spillover effects to bond indexes
While stresses are popping up in some pockets of AI financing, debt markets are also pricing in higher costs. S&P Global warned on Oct. 19 that major cloud providers may have more AI-linked debt exposure than publicly recognized.
CDS indexes offer a broader picture of credit-market pressure by tracking default-protection costs across baskets of companies.
North America's CDX High Yield index captures credit risk across speculative-grade companies. Its five-year midpoint spread reached 355.35 basis points on Oct. 20, up about 39 basis points from the end of 2025, according to data from LSEG.
The widening suggests investors are demanding more compensation for credit risk beyond AI-linked borrowers.

articles.title: Personal agents like Meta's Muse could fuel AI’s growth — and challenge Amazon and Apple
articles.text: Hopes are high on Wall Street that autonomous AI agents will drive a new revenue phase for the AI build-out. But these bots are still a show-me story while concerns mount about online privacy and cybersecurity. Meta Platforms' Muse epitomizes the excitement with the app off to a fast start. Data from Sensor Tower provided to CNBC shows that while it took Anthropic's Claude 670 days to hit 9 million U.S. downloads, it took Muse just 36 days to hit the same number. Despite a recent pullback, Meta's stock has gained 5.7% since the launch as analysts pencil in billions of additional revenue. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg highlighted Muse on Wednesday's earnings call, calling it "the centerpiece of our vision for what we're building." He said the bot's adoption by users was so fast that the company had to coordinate with payment processor Stripe to raise credit limits. Muse is potentially just the vanguard for a new age of personal AI agents. Apps like OpenAI's Dots and SpaceXAI's Grok Bot could also take off. What's more, they're all supposed to get smarter as they learn about your lifestyle habits and personal preferences. The stakes for these personal bots are high. As open-source and freemium AI products proliferate, they could erode pricing for enterprise-scale AI and token pricing for frontier labs, endangering returns on invested capital. Personal agents could generate new revenue streams and another large source of token demand. "Agentic AI tools are what is driving this next era of AI infrastructure build-out because they are driving usage in a way that expands the amount of AI compute that's necessary," said Bob O'Donnell, president of Technalysis Research. "They're doing tasks that are being repeated over and over, and they're driving more and more demand for it." Meta and others selling personal agents also aim to gain e-commerce power, capturing more sales and fees from online sellers and exchanges. The goal: controlling e-commerce through robot operators that can act as brokers, shoppers and task managers. "Muse is reshaping how we surf, search, compare, and transact across the Internet, saving users time, money, and improving productivity as it becomes that always on, daily habit," Citi analysts said in a recent note. Muse could bring in $27 billion of revenue for Meta over the next several years through subscription and transaction revenue, Citi estimates. Personal agents start a new AI knife fight While the apps show promise for online shopping, they're a long way from ubiquity. While they may be welcome by small businesses and mom-and-pop sellers, they also pose threats to large e-commerce sites and proprietary application systems. Amazon.com has taken steps to limit the access of agents to their online stores and the user-oriented recommendation systems that generate additional sales. "We think it's fairly straightforward that third-party applications that offer to make purchases on behalf of customers from other businesses should operate openly and respect service provider decisions," an Amazon spokesperson told CNBC in September when the company blocked Meta's Muse. Wall Street also sees a threat to Apple 's App Store. "It is not a stretch to imagine that AI apps will route outside of in-app purchases to avoid paying Apple's toll," Craig Moffett at MoffettNathanson wrote in a Tuesday note. Agents could also leave application interfaces behind entirely, by being routed through text-messaging services, as Spear Street Technology's Instinct does. "Users interact with Instinct purely via text messages, WhatsApp and phone calls without a traditional app or web dashboard. Apple has no way to monetize this digital interaction," Moffett said. The trust factor Another major hurdle is privacy, data security, and protection from AI hacking. Since personal agents act like AI butlers — getting to know your personal habits, shopping preferences, and details of your private life — they need vast access to your personal data. "There are a huge range of risks," said Calli Schroeder, senior counsel at Electronic Privacy Information Center, an advocacy group. "You could have the AI agent collecting its own information and also combining what it learns with information it buys from data brokers. So it can get extremely, extremely specific about you in ways that I don't think users are aware of." Some potential privacy breaches may fall under product safety laws that attorneys general can prosecute under UDAP statutes , Schroeder said, acknowledging the possibility of broader AI legislation coming out of the next Congress. Meta says it built a dedicated cloud-based "virtual machine" to run Muse, including "state of the art privacy and security," as Zuckerberg put it Wednesday. Still, there may be holes. Researchers recently discovered some vulnerabilities in Muse; security firm Claroc found that user-shared Muse pages could be discovered easily through searching domain names, revealing "people's personal files and companies' internal documents." "If you had asked us beforehand, we would have guessed that gathering these would take real effort. It took one query," Claroc researchers wrote. A Meta spokesperson told CNBC that the company has "paused this functionality while we review this report and consider changes to how these links can be discovered." Meta's data protection practices, more broadly, have generated large fines in legal cases. The company was ordered by a New Mexico judge to pay $25 billion in penalties on Wednesday over some of its data practices. The company said it would appeal the order. There's no guarantee, moreover, that personal agents will add economic value -- if they just take from one source and shift it to another. And until they start generating material revenue growth, they aren't likely to ease the market's rising anxiety about AI capex and debt. Wall Street remains bullish, though, viewing Muse in particular as a potentially new killer app. Analysts expect Muse and related revenue to help fuel revenue growth for Meta from $255 billion this year to $430 billion in 2029, according to consensus forecasts. Deutsche Bank's Benjamin Black said Muse has put Meta "back in the frontier discussion," according to a recent note, maintaining a buy on the stock and $820 target. For now, markets appear more concerned about rising AI capex, debt levels and equity issuance — reasons why Meta's stock slumped 6% Wednesday even after a solid earnings report.

articles.title: We're dipping back into the AI trade with our first data center buy in weeks
articles.text: We are buying 10 shares of GE Vernova at roughly $818. Following the trade, Jim Cramer's Charitable Trust will own 100 shares of GEV, increasing its weighting in the portfolio to about 2.15% from 1.9%. After holding off on data center-related stocks since our last Micron buy five weeks ago, we are nibbling on the power company GE Vernova into Thursday's sell-off. AI-related semiconductors and industrial stocks are getting hit hard as investors grow increasingly concerned about the source of capital to support the data center buildout. It's less about demand for AI products and more about how these investments will be funded as cash flows get used up and debt-related financing becomes less attractive to investors. GE Vernova, which makes heavy-duty gas turbines that power data centers, as well as other electrical equipment used inside them, is the third-worst performer in the S & P 500 on Thursday, reflecting concerns about the durability of the buildout. With Thursday's move, GE Vernova stock is now trading more than $100, or about 12% below where it stood on Aug. 24 when we downgraded our rating to a 2 and talked about our need to get more cautious around AI-related stocks. We acknowledge that the capital requirements to fuel the next leg of the AI buildout still need some sorting out. But after steering clear of the group for so long, we are dipping back in with GE Vernova and upgrading our rating to a 1 again to play for a bounce here, with demand for intelligence and AI applications continuing to strengthen. articles.title: Japan Food Inflation
articles.text:
Japan’s annual food inflation rate eased to 2.8% in September 2026 from 3.1% in the previous month, marking its slowest pace since February 2022. Price growth moderated for dairy products and eggs (1.0% vs 1.3% in August) and cakes and candies (4.3% vs 5.0%). Meanwhile, fresh vegetable prices fell for the first time in six months (-0.3% vs 5.5%), and cereal prices extended their decline for a fifth month (-5.0% vs -3.4%). Rice prices plunged 20.6%, falling for a fifth consecutive month and recording the steepest decrease on record. In contrast, inflation held steady for beverages (at 6.0%) but accelerated for fresh fruit (1.0% vs 0.1%), fish and seafood (10.7% vs 9.9%), oils, fats and seasonings (4.6% vs 4.0%), meat (4.3% vs 3.3%), alcoholic beverages (0.6% vs 0.4%), prepared foods (4.2% vs 3.3%), and meals eaten out (2.5% vs 2.1%). source: Ministry of Internal Affairs & Communications

articles.title: A couple bought and renovated a $1.5 million brownstone while dating—now it's their full-time job
articles.text:
Barry Bordelon and Jordan Slocum had been dating for just seven months when they began looking for a Brooklyn, New York, brownstone to buy together. Eight years later, they've parlayed their experience renovating their home into a successful business.
In 2018, Slocum and Bordelon purchased a $1.5 million brownstone built in 1890, and spent the next eight months bringing the home back to life.
Now, Bordelon, 46, and Slocum, 42, are the founders of The Brownstone Boys, an interior design and restoration company they launched in 2020.
They've written a book about renovation and design, appeared on HGTV and helped dozens of aspiring DIYers highlight their homes' vintage charm.
Today, Slocum and Bordelon employ four other designers and project managers at The Brownstone Boys, and they've completed more than 32 full renovations in New York City.
Searching for a home with 'good bones'
The couple met in early 2017 on a dating app. "For me, it was kind of love at first sight," says Slocum. On their second date, they discovered that they shared a passion for historic architecture, particularly Brooklyn brownstones.
At the time, Bordelon worked in software sales and Slocum worked for an ice cream company, helping design and develop new store locations.
The couple decided "very early on" that they wanted to buy a home together, Bordelon says, and they started looking at brownstones in summer 2017.
Not everyone was excited about their plan. "I freaked my parents out when I told them that I was buying a property with someone that I had only been dating for such a short period of time," Slocum says. "I just remember my mom telling me I was crazy."
Before buying a home together, they had "a full, honest conversation around finances" and what it would take to achieve their goal, according to Slocum. Bordelon already had experience renovating and reselling apartments as a hobby, and Slocum had been saving up to buy his own apartment.
Their aim was to find a home with "good bones" that they "could bring back to life and restore," Bordelon says. "We wanted a beautiful, tree-lined street. We wanted a stoop out front that we could sit on and have a glass of wine or a cup of coffee."
In October 2018, Bordelon and Slocum purchased a 2,400-square-foot brownstone in the Bedford-Stuyvesant neighborhood of Brooklyn for about $1.5 million.
"We had to really stretch our budget" to purchase the home, Slocum says. They pooled their savings for a down payment of approximately $475,000, according to Bordelon, and took out a mortgage for the rest.
Learning the art of renovation
When Bordelon and Slocum started renovating the brownstone at the end of 2018, their main challenge was their "very limited" budget, according to Bordelon.
When contractors quoted them up to $1 million for the project, the couple realized they would have to do most of the renovations themselves.
Brownstones can be challenging to renovate due to the age of the buildings and materials, according to Bordelon. New York City's brownstone rowhouses, named for their reddish-brown sandstone facades, were primarily built in the latter half of the 19th century. There are few craftspeople left who specialize in working with brownstone, Slocum says, so "replicating the beautiful craftsmanship" is difficult.
The couple took pains to preserve historical details like the house's original wooden shutters. Early on, they hired a wood restorer who showed them how to strip and restain the antique woodwork, which allowed them to "learn the craft" and then tackle the rest of the project themselves.
The brownstone was previously used as a short-term rental property, Bordelon says, so they had to modify the layout to turn it into a functional home. They transformed a former bedroom into a custom-built kitchen and dining area, and converted a small, "useless" room into a spacious guest bathroom.
The initial renovation cost was approximately $300,000, according to Slocum, which the couple funded from their savings. To save money, they also lived in the brownstone throughout most of the eight-month renovation project.
Today, Bordelon and Slocum occupy the second and third floors of their brownstone, which they transformed into a duplex with three bedrooms and two bathrooms. They turned the garden-level floor of the brownstone into a one-bed, one-bath apartment unit that they rent out for $2,500 per month, which covers about half of their $5,000 monthly mortgage payment.
The major renovations are largely finished, but for design fanatics like Bordelon and Slocum, "there's always going to be a project to do," Slocum says. The couple recently revamped their living room and kitchen, adding details like crown moldings, vintage lighting and custom banquette seating, which cost approximately $12,000.
It's all worth it to live in their "forever home," says Slocum. The couple even had their wedding on the stoop of their brownstone in October 2024. "This home truly is our love story," he continues.
Becoming 'The Brownstone Boys'
While they were renovating the brownstone, Slocum had the "really amazing idea" to chronicle their journey online, Bordelon says, so they started an Instagram page and a blog called The Brownstone Boys.
The blog got picked up by a larger Brooklyn real estate website, Brownstoner, and developed a dedicated online following of architecture enthusiasts and aspiring DIYers.
"We were telling our whole story: all the finances involved, what was working, what wasn't working, problems we had and how we solved them," Bordelon says. "It really became a community."
In 2019, a few months before they finished renovations, one of their Instagram followers reached out to Bordelon and Slocum asking for their help with a similar renovation project.
Bordelon and Slocum agreed to help with project management and design, and soon other potential clients started reaching out.
After taking on their third client, Bordelon and Slocum quit their jobs to focus on The Brownstone Boys full-time. They officially filed their LLC in January 2020. "Honestly, we haven't even had time to look back yet, because we've been so busy since," Bordelon says.
Running a business as a couple isn't always easy, Bordelon says, but having each other's support has been key to their success.
"There's two of us in almost everything that we do, every decision that we make," he says. "Although there are, of course, disagreements and hard moments to work through, I really think it's been a benefit and an asset throughout everything we've done."

articles.title: Hà Nội: Hiện trường vụ cháy lớn trong quán ăn có tiếng trên phố Hoàng Cầu
articles.text:
Hà Nội: Hiện trường vụ cháy lớn trong quán ăn có tiếng trên phố Hoàng Cầu
Tối 22/10, một vụ cháy xảy ra tại quán ăn trên phố Hoàng Cầu, Hà Nội. Ngọn lửa bùng lên bên trong nhà hàng, khói bốc cao khiến nhiều người dân xung quanh lo ngại.
Theo chia sẻ của một người dân sống đối diện hiện trường, đám cháy được cho là bắt nguồn từ khu vực bếp trên tầng 3 của nhà hàng vào khoảng 20h30-20h40 cùng ngày. Khi phát hiện hỏa hoạn, nhân viên quán đã hô hoán, kêu gọi người dân hỗ trợ.
Khoảng 10 phút sau, lực lượng cứu hỏa có mặt tại hiện trường, triển khai phun nước khống chế đám cháy. Ngọn lửa sau đó được dập tắt trong thời gian ngắn.
Hình ảnh ghi nhận tại hiện trường cho thấy lửa cháy lớn bên trong nhà hàng, khói bốc lên từ khu vực xảy ra hỏa hoạn. Sự việc thu hút sự chú ý của nhiều người dân, khiến khu vực xung quanh tập trung đông người theo dõi.
May mắn, theo ghi nhận ban đầu, vụ cháy không gây thiệt hại về người.
Nguyên nhân vụ cháy đang được cơ quan chức năng làm rõ.

articles.title: Elon Musk invests about $1 billion in Skydance
articles.text:
Elon Musk has made an investment in Skydance of roughly $1 billion, according to a person familiar with the matter who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to speak publicly.
The financial injection comes as the company looks to cut costs. Paramount closed its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery on Oct. 6, naming the combined entity Skydance. Co-CEOs David Ellison and Ynon Kreiz are tasked with merging two major film studios in Paramount and Warner Bros., two popular streaming platforms — Paramount+ and HBO Max — and a host of corporate functions to support a portfolio of TV networks and two news divisions.
Skydance has said it expects to see $6 billion in cost savings over three years, though it faces a debt burden of nearly $80 billion.
Musk's commitment is part of a wider effort by Skydance to raise equity investments, according to Semafor, which first reported the news Thursday. Representatives for Musk and Skydance did not immediately respond to CNBC's requests for comment.
Shares of Skydance were down about 1% Thursday.
Ellison's father, Larry Ellison, has a history with Musk. The Oracle co-founder invested $1 billion in Musk's 2022 deal to purchase Twitter, now called X. Larry Ellison also invested in Tesla in 2018 and served on the company's board of directors.
The elder Ellison also personally guaranteed more than $40 billion of equity financing in Paramount's offer to take over WBD.

articles.title: iPhone Duo bị thổi giá trên chợ đen, giá rao bán hơn 130 triệu đồng
articles.text:
iPhone Duo bị thổi giá trên chợ đen, giá rao bán hơn 130 triệu đồng
iPhone Duo, mẫu iPhone gập đầu tiên của Apple, hết hàng chỉ vài phút sau khi mở đặt trước ngày 16/10/2026. Trên eBay, một chiếc bản 2 TB được đánh dấu đã bán với giá 5.000 USD, tương đương khoảng 130,5 triệu đồng. Mức này cao hơn khoảng 26,5 triệu đồng so với bản đắt nhất Apple bán chính hãng tại Việt Nam.
- 22-10-2026Chiếc iPhone 13 triệu của Ronaldo
- 22-10-2026“Đập hộp” iPhone Duo chính hãng Việt Nam trước ngày giao hàng: điện thoại gập đầu tiên của Táo đóng gói ra sao?
- 22-10-2026Trải nghiệm thực tế nếp gấp màn hình trên iPhone Duo: Đã biến mất hay vẫn lộ rõ khi dùng?
Apple mở đặt trước iPhone Duo, mẫu iPhone gập đầu tiên của hãng, vào ngày 16/10/2026 và máy hết hàng chỉ sau vài phút. Ngày mở bán chính thức vẫn giữ nguyên là 23/10/2026, nhưng khách đặt mới tại Mỹ phải chờ đến 25/01/2027 mới nhận được máy. Thời gian chờ này áp dụng cho mọi phiên bản.
Theo trang công nghệ PhoneArena, nguyên nhân được cho là các nhóm đầu cơ dùng công cụ tự động (bot) để gom số lượng lớn, khiến nhiều khách hàng thông thường không kịp đặt mua.
Ngay sau khi hết hàng, iPhone Duo xuất hiện trên eBay với giá cao hơn nhiều so với niêm yết. Một chiếc màu Night Sky, bản 2 TB, được đánh dấu đã bán với giá 5.000 USD (khoảng 130,5 triệu đồng), trong khi Apple bán phiên bản này tại Mỹ với giá 3.199 USD (khoảng 83,5 triệu đồng). Người mua đã trả thêm khoảng 1.800 USD (hơn 46 triệu đồng). Một suất đặt trước bản 1 TB cùng màu cũng được bán với giá 4.400 USD (khoảng 113 triệu đồng), so với giá gốc 2.599 USD (khoảng 67 triệu đồng).
Phần lớn tin rao trên eBay là bán suất đặt trước, không phải máy có sẵn để giao ngay. Việc các giao dịch này đã hoàn tất hay chưa hiện chưa có thông tin xác nhận.
Mức giá đầu cơ iPhone Duo tại Mỹ lên đến 130,5 triệu đồng cao hơn bản 2 TB chính hãng tại Việt Nam khoảng 26,5 triệu đồng, tức đắt hơn khoảng 25%. So với bản 256 GB rẻ nhất, giá đầu cơ cao gấp khoảng 2 lần, chênh khoảng 65,5 triệu đồng.
Nhiều người dùng thất vọng vì cho rằng Apple chưa có biện pháp hiệu quả để ngăn bot gom hàng, dù đây không phải lần đầu sản phẩm mới của hãng bị đầu cơ. Trang PhoneArena nhận định Apple lẽ ra cần chuẩn bị kỹ hơn, vì cảnh báo về nguồn cung hạn chế đã xuất hiện từ trước khi tên gọi iPhone Duo được công bố. Bên cạnh đó, nếu không xử lý, khách hàng có thể phải chờ thêm nhiều tháng, đến lúc những thông tin đầu tiên về iPhone Duo 2 đã xuất hiện.
Về phía Apple, hãng mô tả nhu cầu đặt trước là “phi thường”. Apple cho biết sẽ nỗ lực đưa máy đến tay nhiều khách hàng hơn và tiếp tục nhận đơn trực tuyến.
Đầu cơ không phải nguyên nhân duy nhất. Theo ZDNet Korea, Apple đã yêu cầu các nhà cung cấp tăng sản lượng linh kiện cho iPhone Duo, nhưng việc này chưa chắc giúp hãng nhanh chóng bù đủ số máy đang thiếu.
PhoneArena cho biết một trở ngại lớn là nguồn cung T-Glass từ hãng Nitto Boseki (Nhật Bản) còn hạn chế. T-Glass là loại sợi thủy tinh chuyên dụng trong bảng mạch điện tử, giúp bảng mạch ổn định hơn và ít biến dạng do nhiệt. Nếu nguồn cung vật liệu này không cải thiện, Apple khó đẩy nhanh sản xuất, kể cả khi các linh kiện khác đã tăng sản lượng.
Một số tin đồn cho rằng lượng máy dành cho khách mua trực tiếp tại cửa hàng sẽ rất hạn chế. Tuy nhiên, một nhân viên Apple Store đã bác bỏ thông tin này khi trả lời PhoneArena
Thị trường Việt Nam mẫu iPhone gập đầu tiên của Apple cũng khan hàng. iPhone Duo mở đặt trước tại Việt Nam từ 19h00 ngày 16/10/2026 (giờ Việt Nam) và nhiều đại lý đã thông báo hết suất chỉ sau ít phút, khách có thể phải chờ đến tháng 12/2026 mới nhận được máy.
Sáng 23/10, iPhone Duo sẽ chính thức lên kệ tại thị trường Việt Nam. Dù vậy, lượng người dùng có thể nhận được máy trong ngày đầu mở bán không nhiều.

articles.title: Japan Core Inflation Rate
articles.text:
Japan’s core consumer price index, which excludes fresh food but includes energy, increased 2.1% year-on-year in September 2026, following a 1.7% rise in August. It was the highest reading since December 2025, matching market forecasts. The latest reading pushed inflation above the Bank of Japan’s 2% target for the first time in nine months, though government fuel subsidies helped offset price pressures from higher oil costs linked to the Middle East conflict. Meanwhile, the index excluding fresh food and fuel, which the Bank of Japan closely watches as a better gauge of demand-driven price movements, rose 2.4% year-on-year in September, marking the first increase since October 2025 and the fastest pace in six months. The BoJ raised interest rates by 25 bps to 1.25% at its September meeting, bringing borrowing costs to their highest level since April 1995. source: Statistics Bureau of Japan
Core consumer prices in Japan increased 2.10 percent in September of 2026 over the same month in the previous year. Core Inflation Rate in Japan averaged 2.40 percent from 1971 until 2026, reaching an all time high of 24.70 percent in October of 1974 and a record low of -2.40 percent in August of 2009.
